chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.text: This reference describes how IOMETE maps onto Kubernetes: the Helm chart structure, the full service inventory, feature flags, and infrastructure options. For a conceptual overview of each service, see the Architecture Overview. For installation steps, see the On-Premises Deployment Guide.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Helm Chart Structure
chunks.text: Everything ships as a single Helm chart (`iomete-data-plane-enterprise`), which deploys all platform services into one Kubernetes namespace. Services talk to each other over internal Kubernetes DNS.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Initialization Job
chunks.text: Before any service starts, a pre-install/pre-upgrade Helm hook job (`iomete-data-plane-init`) bootstraps the environment: 1. Creates PostgreSQL databases for each microservice 2. Creates the Hive Metastore secret 3. Creates the Hadoop configuration secret 4. Creates the Spark ConfigMap 5. Creates the Spark History folder in object storage Init Job Failures This job runs with `backoffLimit: 2`. If it fails, the entire Helm install or upgrade fails. When troubleshooting a failed deployment, check the init job logs first.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Configuration Distribution
chunks.text: All Helm values (including feature flags) are serialized to YAML and stored in a Kubernetes Secret named `data-plane`. Every backend microservice reads this secret at startup, so a Helm upgrade propagates config changes to all services on their next restart.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Service Inventory
chunks.text: Knowing which services run (and which are optional) helps you plan resource allocation and troubleshoot startup issues. The table below lists every service the Helm chart deploys. chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Gateway Routing
chunks.text: Every request into the platform passes through the Gateway (an Nginx reverse proxy), which routes traffic to the correct backend based on URI prefix. The tables below show the complete routing map.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: API Routes
chunks.text: /api/v/domains//sql, /api/v/domains//git: Backend Service iom-sql. /api/v/health-check: Backend Service iom-health-check. /api/v/admin/compaction, /api/v/domains//compaction: Backend Service iom-maintenance. /api/v/domains//data-catalog, /api/v/domains//data-product, /api/v/domains//governance, /api/v/admin/governance: Backend Service iom-catalog. /api/v/authz, /api/v/auth, /api/v/data-planes, /api/v/modules, /api/v/system-config, /api/v/admin/node-types, /api/v/admin/volumes: Backend Service iom-core. /api/v/domains//compute, /api/v/domains//spark/, /api/v/domains//jupyter-containers, /api/v/domains//namespaces, /api/v/domains//secrets, /api/v/domains//schedules, /api/v/domains//event-streams: Backend Service iom-cluster. /api/v/domains//roles, /api/v/domains//members, /api/v/admin/identity, /api/v/admin/domains, /api/v/users, /api/v/groups, /api/v/bundles, /api/v/identity: Backend Service iom-identity.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Non-API Routes
chunks.text: / (default), /domains/, /admin/: Backend Service iom-app, Protocol HTTP. /catalogs/: Backend Service iom-rest-catalog, Protocol HTTP. /socket.io: Backend Service iom-socket, Protocol WebSocket. /collaboration: Backend Service iom-collab, Protocol WebSocket (feature-flagged). /spark-history, /spark-ui, /monitoring: Backend Service iom-core, Protocol HTTP. /sso-proxy: Backend Service iom-core, Protocol HTTP. /service/(plugins\: Backend Service roles\, Protocol xusers\, tags), iom-identity, HTTP (Ranger admin API).

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Dynamic Workload Routes
chunks.text: /data-plane//lakehouse//...: Target cc- . :10000, Protocol HTTP (HiveServer2 JDBC). /spark.connect.: Target cc- . :15002, Protocol gRPC (Spark Connect). /arrow.flight.protocol.FlightService: Target cc- . :33333 or Spark Proxy, Protocol gRPC (Arrow Flight). /data-plane//jupyter//...: Target jc- . :8888, Protocol HTTP + WebSocket. /data-plane//event-stream//...: Target iom-event-stream-proxy, Protocol HTTP. The Gateway supports gRPC for Spark Connect and Arrow Flight, with keepalive enabled and a 24-hour read timeout (`86400s`).

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Node Placement
chunks.text: To keep platform services and Spark workloads on separate hardware, the chart exposes two pairs of node selectors and tolerations: controlPlaneNodeSelector / controlPlaneTolerations: Applied To All IOMETE platform services, Purpose Isolate control plane on dedicated nodes. dataPlaneNodeSelector / dataPlaneTolerations: Applied To Spark workloads (drivers, executors), Purpose Isolate compute on data nodes.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Multi-Namespace Support
chunks.text: If different teams need separate CPU and memory quotas, you can deploy Spark workloads (drivers and executors) into additional namespaces via the `namespaces` list in `values.yaml`. The data plane's own namespace is always included automatically. Each extra namespace gets its own copies of: - Prefect Worker - Spark Proxy Server (when Arrow Flight proxy is enabled) - Event Stream pods (when event streams are enabled) IOMETE doesn't create the quotas themselves. See Namespace Quotas. For details, see Connect Namespace. For full multi-cluster topology, see Multi-Cluster Setup.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Priority Classes
chunks.text: PriorityClasses let Kubernetes preempt lower-priority pods when resources are scarce. When `priorityClasses` is enabled, Spark workloads are assigned these classes: iomete-compute: Workload Type Compute clusters. iomete-spark-job: Workload Type Spark jobs. iomete-notebook: Workload Type Jupyter containers. iomete-operational-support: Workload Type Job Orchestrator workers.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Autoscaling
chunks.text: For services that handle variable load, you can turn on Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA). It's disabled by default and must be enabled per-service in `values.yaml`. iom-gateway: HPA Support Yes, Notes Disabled by default. iom-core: HPA Support Yes, Notes Disabled by default. iom-cluster: HPA Support Yes, Notes Disabled by default. iom-identity: HPA Support Yes, Notes Disabled by default. iom-catalog: HPA Support Yes, Notes Disabled by default. iom-rest-catalog: HPA Support Yes, Notes Disabled by default. spark-submit-service: HPA Support Yes, Notes Disabled by default. iom-collab: HPA Support Yes, Notes Memory-based (85%) primary, CPU (80%) secondary. iom-event-stream-proxy: HPA Support Yes, Notes Enabled by default (1-4 replicas, 80% CPU). iom-sql: HPA Support No, Notes Fixed at 1 replica.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Feature Flags
chunks.text: Feature flags control what gets deployed and how the platform behaves. Most live in `values.yaml` under `features:` and reach every service through the `data-plane` secret. A few flags use different paths (noted in the table).

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Deployment Flags
chunks.text: These flags control whether entire services or subsystems are deployed at all: enableCollaborativeSqlEditor: Services Deployed iom-collab, Default false. services.nats.enabled: Services Deployed NATS cluster, Default false. eventStream: Services Deployed iom-event-stream-proxy, Default false. sparkProxyForArrowFlight: Services Deployed spark-proxy-server (per-namespace), Default false. ratelimiter: Services Deployed iom-ratelimiter, Default false. jupyterContainers: Services Deployed jupyter-containers ConfigMap, Default false.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Runtime Behavior Flags
chunks.text: These flags toggle features without adding or removing services: arrowFlightConnection: Effect When Enabled Arrow Flight connections available for compute clusters, Default true. arrowFlightForDbExplorer: Effect When Enabled DB Explorer uses Arrow Flight instead of Spark Connect REST, Default false. activityMonitoring: Effect When Enabled Query monitoring and resource tracking, Default false. downloadQueryResults: Effect When Enabled SQL query result download in UI, Default true. caseInsensitiveIcebergIdentifiers: Effect When Enabled Iceberg table/database names are case-insensitive, Default false. iometeSparkLivenessProbe: Effect When Enabled Additional liveness probe on Spark driver pods, Default true. icebergRestCatalogStrictMode: Effect When Enabled Database must exist before creating tables, Default false. enforceUniqueIcebergTableLocations: Effect When Enabled Tables created without an explicit LOCATION get a unique storage directory, so a rename + recreate of the same name can't collide and let remove_orphan_files delete a live table's data (tables created with an explicit LOCATION are unaffected), Default true. priorityClasses: Effect When Enabled Spark workloads use PriorityClasses, Default false. emailNotifications: Effect When Enabled Email notifications available, Default true. sparkJobArchival: Effect When Enabled Archival of Spark job history, Default false. onboardComputeRas: Effect When Enabled Resource Access Service for compute clusters, Default false. onboardSparkJobRas: Effect When Enabled Resource Access Service for Spark jobs, Default false. onboardWorkspaceRas: Effect When Enabled Resource

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Object Storage
chunks.text: All table data, Spark event logs, and SQL results live in object storage, making it the most important infrastructure dependency. Configure the provider and credentials in `values.yaml`. S3-compatible (Apache Ozone, Dell ECS, IBM Cloud Object Storage, MinIO, and others): Config Key s3_compatible, URI Scheme s3a://, Required Settings endpoint, accessKey, secretKey. MinIO (deprecated): Config Key minio, URI Scheme s3a://, Required Settings endpoint, accessKey, secretKey. Dell ECS (deprecated): Config Key dell_ecs, URI Scheme s3a://, Required Settings endpoint, accessKey, secretKey. AWS S3: Config Key aws_s3, URI Scheme s3a://, Required Settings IAM role, cloud.region. Google Cloud Storage: Config Key gcs, URI Scheme gs://, Required Settings GCP service account. Azure Blob (Gen1): Config Key azure_gen1, URI Scheme wasbs://, Required Settings storageAccountName, storageAccountKey. Azure Data Lake (Gen2): Config Key azure_gen2, URI Scheme abfs://, Required Settings storageAccountName, storageAccountKey. From 3.19.1, use `s3_compatible` for any S3-compatible storage and set its endpoint and keys under `storage.s3CompatibleSettings`. The `minio` and `dell_ecs` types and their `storage.minioSettings` and `storage.dellEcsSettings` blocks are deprecated. **Object storage paths**: data/: Contents Lakehouse table data. iomete-assets/spark-history/: Contents Spark event logs. iomete-assets/sql-results/: Contents SQL query results. iomete-assets/sql-editor/worksheets/: Contents SQL editor worksheet content. ranger/audit: Contents Ranger audit logs (when HDFS audit is enabled).

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Database
chunks.text: All services share a single PostgreSQL server. The init job creates databases with a configurable prefix (default: `iomete_`): - ` metastore_db` (Hive Metastore) - ` ranger_db` (Ranger policies) - ` iceberg_db` (Iceberg catalog metadata) - Per-microservice databases (Core, Cluster, Identity, SQL, Catalog, etc.) - ` prefect_db` (Prefect job orchestrator) - ` mcp_db` (MCP server OAuth state) **Multi-cluster database support**: You can point `clusterDatabase` at a different server than the main `database`. This is handy in multi-region setups where high-volume operations (Kubernetes/Spark data) hit a local database while metadata stays on a global one. **SSL**: PostgreSQL SSL is optional. When `ssl.enabled` is true, JDBC connections use `sslmode=verify-full`. **Connection pooler**: If `database.host` points at a connection pooler (for example PgBouncer), set `database.directHost` / `database.directPort` to the actual PostgreSQL endpoint. Schema migrations (every platform service's, including the MCP server's, which run automatically at startup) hold a session-scoped advisory lock and cannot run through a transaction pooler; all other traffic keeps using the pooler.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Secret Store
chunks.text: You can choose where IOMETE keeps sensitive values like database passwords and API keys: kubernetes (default): Description Kubernetes Secrets. database: Description Encrypted in the IOMETE database. vault: Description HashiCorp Vault (requires endpoint, path, token).

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Logging
chunks.text: Depending on your observability stack, you can route logs to one of several backends: kubernetes (default): Description Reads logs directly from the Kubernetes API. loki: Description Grafana Loki (requires host, port). elasticsearch: Description Elasticsearch (requires endpoint, apiKey, indexPattern). splunk: Description Splunk Enterprise (requires endpoint, token, indexName). **Hot storage**: When `hotStorage.enabled` is true, the platform tries the Kubernetes API first (for recent logs), then falls back to the external backend for older entries.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Monitoring
chunks.text: If you run Prometheus, set `monitoring.enabled` to true. This adds scrape annotations to every service pod. Metrics endpoints differ by framework: - `/q/metrics` for Quarkus services (Core, Cluster, Identity, SQL, Catalog, REST Catalog) - `/metrics` for everything else (Spark Operator, Collab)

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: TLS and TrustStore
chunks.text: If your environment uses self-signed certificates, mount a Java TrustStore into all services via a Kubernetes Secret. The TrustStore must include both the default public certificates and your custom ones. See TrustStore Configuration for setup details.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Ingress
chunks.text: The Gateway expects an ingress controller in front of it. When `ingress.httpsEnabled` is true (the default), the Gateway sets the public-facing protocol to HTTPS in forwarded headers. See Configure Ingress for setup instructions.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: OpenAPI Documentation
chunks.text: Every backend service publishes an OpenAPI spec, and the Gateway proxies them all under `/openapi/`: /openapi/ui: Service Swagger UI (served by Core Service). /openapi/core: Service Core Service. /openapi/cluster: Service Cluster Service. /openapi/iam: Service Identity Service. /openapi/sql: Service SQL Service. /openapi/catalog: Service Catalog Service. /openapi/rest-catalog: Service Iceberg REST Catalog.

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Cloud Provider Support
chunks.text: IOMETE runs on AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises Kubernetes. The main differences between providers are scratch directory paths and zone-aware scheduling: On-Premises: Scratch Directory /local1, Zone-Aware Scheduling No. AWS: Scratch Directory /local1, Zone-Aware Scheduling Yes (region + availability zone). Azure: Scratch Directory /mnt, Zone-Aware Scheduling No. GCP: Scratch Directory /mnt/stateful_partition, Zone-Aware Scheduling No. Regardless of provider, Spark workload pods include tolerations for dedicated nodes (`k8s.iomete.com/dedicated`) and ARM64 architecture (`kubernetes.io/arch=arm64`).

chunks.title: Deployment Architecture
chunks.heading: Technology Stack
chunks.text: Backend language: Technology Kotlin. JVM: Technology Java. Backend framework: Technology Quarkus. Build system: Technology Gradle (Kotlin DSL). Frontend: Technology React, TypeScript, Vite. UI library: Technology Ant Design. Spark engine: Technology Apache Spark. Table format: Technology Apache Iceberg. Hive Metastore: Technology Apache Hive. Spark Operator: Technology Kubernetes Operator (Go). Event ingestion: Technology Rust. Job orchestration: Technology Prefect (Python). Messaging: Technology NATS JetStream. Search: Technology Typesense. Rate limiting: Technology Redis.

chunks.title: IOMETE Backend Databases
chunks.text: IOMETE requires a backend database to efficiently store and manage metadata. This database is essential for two primary types of metadata: 1. **IOMETE Internal Metadata:** This includes information about the operational and structural elements of IOMETE's architecture. 2. **Data Lake Metadata:** Specifically tailored for the Hive Metastore and Iceberg Metastore, this involves detailed metadata regarding data lake databases, tables, partitions, columns, and more. For optimal functionality, IOMETE supports the use of either MySQL or PostgreSQL databases. These databases are chosen for their reliability, scalability, and widespread support in the industry.

chunks.title: IOMETE Backend Databases
chunks.heading: IOMETE Internal Metadata
chunks.text: The database requirements for managing internal metadata are typically moderate. This includes operations such as creating and updating various IOMETE resources like clusters, spark jobs, users, etc.

chunks.title: IOMETE Backend Databases
chunks.heading: Metadata of Data Lake
chunks.text: This section pertains to the metadata storage for Hive Metastore and Iceberg Metastore. The load on these databases is directly influenced by the number of users and the volume of tables within the data lake.

chunks.title: IOMETE Backend Databases
chunks.heading: Database Resource Requirements
chunks.text: The IOMETE database has been optimized to operate effectively with modest resource requirements. The following specifications provide a guideline based on different user scales: The resource requirements outlined below are based on the assumption that both MySQL and PostgreSQL provide similar performance characteristics thus applicable to both databases.

chunks.title: IOMETE Backend Databases
chunks.heading: Small Scale (1-10 Users)
chunks.text: - **CPU**: 1-2 cores - **Memory**: 4GB - **Disk Space**: 20GB

chunks.title: IOMETE Backend Databases
chunks.heading: Large Scale (100-1000 Users)
chunks.text: - **CPU**: 8 cores - **Memory**: 32GB - **Disk Space**: 50GB Disk size depends on the data lake size and number of tables in the data lake. Typically, a range between 20GB to 100GB suffices. For enhanced database performance, especially in data-intensive operations, the use of SSD or NVMe SSD disk type is recommended. It is crucial to ensure that the database is configured with reliable backup and recovery mechanisms to safeguard data integrity and continuity.

chunks.title: Configure custom DNS for IOMETE Data Plane
chunks.text: This document aims to provide you with a straightforward, step-by-step approach to setting up a DNS name for your IOMETE data plane, enhancing its accessibility and ease of use. ---

chunks.title: Configure custom DNS for IOMETE Data Plane
chunks.heading: Understanding the Basics
chunks.text: Before we dive into the technical steps, let's clarify some key concepts: - **IOMETE Data Plane**: This is the infrastructure component that handles the processing and movement of data within the IOMETE ecosystem. - **DNS (Domain Name System)**: DNS translates human-friendly domain names (like `www.example.com`) into IP addresses that computers use to identify each other on the network. - **Istio Ingress Gateway**: This is a crucial component within the IOMETE setup that directs incoming traffic to the right destinations within your data plane.

chunks.title: Configure custom DNS for IOMETE Data Plane
chunks.heading: Identifying the Istio Ingress Gateway Address
chunks.text: The first step in configuring your DNS is to locate the external IP address of the Istio Ingress Gateway, as all traffic to the IOMETE data-plane goes through it.

chunks.title: Configure custom DNS for IOMETE Data Plane
chunks.heading: If Your Setup Uses a `LoadBalancer`
chunks.text: IOMETE typically configures the Istio **ingress gateway** as a `LoadBalancer`. To find its external address, use the following command in your terminal: kubectl get svc istio-ingress -n istio-system This command returns the external address of the ingress gateway. Note this address, as it could be either an **IP** or a **DNS** address.

chunks.title: Configure custom DNS for IOMETE Data Plane
chunks.heading: If Your Setup Uses a `NodePort`
chunks.text: In cases where the gateway is configured as a `NodePort`, you'll need to identify the IP address of a Kubernetes worker node, ideally the one hosting the Istio ingress gateway.

chunks.title: Configure custom DNS for IOMETE Data Plane
chunks.heading: Creating Your DNS Record
chunks.text: With the external address of the Istio Ingress Gateway in hand, you're ready to create a DNS record. This step involves going to your DNS provider and setting up the record that will point to the IOMETE data plane. - **For an IP Address**: Create an `A` record with your DNS provider, pointing to the IP address you've identified. - **For a DNS Name**: Create a `CNAME` record that points to the DNS name of the ingress gateway. Here's a simplified overview of what to do next: 1. **Access Your DNS Provider**: Log into the platform where your domain's DNS settings are managed. 2. **Navigate to DNS Management**: Look for the section where you can add or modify DNS records. 3. **Add the Record**: Depending on your external address: - For an IP address, add an `A` record pointing to this IP. - For a DNS name, add a `CNAME` record pointing to this name. 4. **Save Changes**: Apply and save your changes. DNS propagation can take some time, so it might not work immediately. Remember, DNS changes can take a while to propagate across the internet, so give it some time before testing.

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.text: This guide walks you through the process of installing ISTIO as an ingress controller on a Kubernetes cluster and configuring it for use with IOMETE.

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: Deploying ISTIO
chunks.text: For AWS, GCP, and Azure deployments, terraform script is already deployed ISTIO as an ingress controller. If that's the case, you can skip this section.

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: Adding the ISTIO Helm Repository
chunks.text: helm repo add istio https://istio-release.storage.googleapis.com/charts helm repo update

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: Deploy ISTIO Components via Helm
chunks.text: Execute these commands to install the necessary ISTIO components: helm upgrade --install -n istio-system base istio/base --version 1.17.2 helm upgrade --install -n istio-system istiod istio/istiod --version 1.17.2 helm upgrade --install -n istio-system istio-ingress istio/gateway --version 1.17.2

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: Configuring the Gateway
chunks.text: You need to configure the ISTIO ingress gateway to access the IOMETE Data Plane UI. ---

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: For HTTP (Non-TLS Mode)
chunks.text: Apply the following configuration for an HTTP gateway: Required file: gateway-http.yaml showLineNumbers

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: Download the HTTP gateway configuration:
chunks.text: wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iomete/iomete-deployment/main/istio-ingress/gateway-http.yaml

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: For HTTPS (TLS Mode)
chunks.text: To set up a secure gateway using TLS: 1. **Create a TLS Secret:** Use the template below, replacing placeholder values with your actual base64 encoded certificate and key. 2. **Deploy the HTTPS Gateway:** After creating the secret, apply the HTTPS gateway configuration.

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text: Before you begin, ensure you have the following ready: - **DNS Configuration**: The DNS for your IOMETE Data Plane must be set up. See Configure Custom DNS for IOMETE Data Plane. - **TLS Certificate and Private Key**: You need a TLS certificate and a private key, valid for your IOMETE Data Plane's DNS name. Why do I need a custom DNS? In order to set up HTTPS, you need to have a DNS address. This ensures that the TLS certificate is valid for the DNS name. Technically, you can enable HTTPs without a DNS, but creating TLS certificates for IP addresses is not recommended. Where can I get a TLS certificate? You can obtain a TLS certificate from a certificate authority (CA) or generate a self-signed certificate. Please, ask your network administrator or IT department for assistance. Alternatively, you can use services like Let's Encrypt to get a free TLS certificate.

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: Create a TLS Secret
chunks.text: Once you have your TLS certificate and private key, you need to create a Kubernetes secret to store them. This secret will be used by the ISTIO ingress gateway to enable TLS traffic. Given that the certificate and key are stored in `tls.crt` and `tls.key` files, respectively. You can create a secret using the following command: showLineNumbers kubectl -n istio-system \ create secret tls tls-secret \ --key tls.key --cert tls.crt Alternatively, you can create a secret using a YAML file with the following content: showLineNumbers title="tls-secret.yaml" apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: tls-secret # Replace with your secret name namespace: istio-system type: kubernetes.io/tls data: tls.crt: tls.key:

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: Deploy the HTTPS Gateway
chunks.text: After creating the secret, apply the HTTPS gateway configuration. If you use a different secret name, update the `tls-secret` value in the gateway-https.yaml file. Required file: gateway-https.yaml showLineNumbers

chunks.title: Configure ISTIO Ingress
chunks.heading: Download the HTTPS gateway configuration:

chunks.title: Install Data-Plane to Kubernetes Namespace
chunks.text: This document will guide you through the process of installing and connecting a new Data-Plane to the IOMETE Control-Plane. Namespace names In this document, we use `data-plane-ns` and `iomete-system` as the namespace names for the Data-Plane and Control-Plane instances. You can replace it with your desired namespace name. Note that the Control-Plane namespace should be the same as the one you used during the Control-Plane installation.

chunks.title: Install Data-Plane to Kubernetes Namespace
chunks.heading: Label the namespace for IOMETE
chunks.text: kubectl label namespace data-plane-ns iomete.com/managed=true

chunks.title: Install Data-Plane to Kubernetes Namespace
chunks.heading: Add the Namespace to Your Values File
chunks.text: In the `values.yaml` file of the IOMETE Control Plane, add the new namespace to the `namespaces` section: showLineNumbers

chunks.title: Install Data-Plane to Kubernetes Namespace
chunks.heading: Create the Service Account and Role
chunks.text: The new namespace needs `lakehouse-service-account` with its Role and RoleBinding. - **If `serviceAccount.create` is `true` in `values.yaml`**, skip this step. The Helm upgrade below creates them. - **If it is `false`**, have a Kubernetes administrator re-create the file from step 1 of Option 2 in the install guide and apply it before you upgrade. The file covers every namespace listed in `values.yaml`, so it includes the new one. - **On 3.19.0 or earlier**, create them manually before you upgrade, as shown in Installing 3.19.0 or Earlier.

chunks.title: Install Data-Plane to Kubernetes Namespace
chunks.heading: Add the Namespace to the Webhook
chunks.text: Skip this step if `webhook.create` is `true`. Helm updates the webhook during the upgrade. If an administrator created the webhook with the install guide commands, add the new namespace to it. List the Control Plane namespace and every namespace from `values.yaml`: kubectl patch mutatingwebhookconfiguration spark-operator-iomete-system \ --type=strategic \ -p='{"webhooks":[{"name":"webhook.sparkoperator.k8s.io","namespaceSelector":{"matchExpressions":[{"key":"kubernetes.io/metadata.name","operator":"In","values":["iomete-system","data-plane-ns"]}]}}]}' If the webhook was created with `gencerts.sh`, skip this step. The `iomete.com/managed=true` label you added to the namespace is enough.

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Installation
chunks.text: IOMETE is designed to operate within a Kubernetes environment. The installation process, streamlined through Helm, is well-organized, efficient, and straightforward. *Prerequisites*: 1. A pre-configured Kubernetes cluster. 2. Necessary credentials and access to external storage and database (a built-in database solution can also be used). *Steps for Installation*: 1. **Repository Cloning**: Clone the dedicated GitHub repository that contains the Helm charts and other essential files for deployment. 2. **Helm Installation**: Utilize the provided Helm charts from the repository to initiate the installation process. All required files, examples, and a comprehensive installation guide can be found in our GitHub repository. We highly recommend following the step-by-step guide provided in the repository and using the example configurations as templates.

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Installation Example
chunks.text: Here is an example for data plane installation. You'll only need to modify the values in the `data-plane-values.yaml` file and run the following command: helm upgrade --install -n iomete iomete-dataplane iomete/iomete-dataplane \ -f data-plane-values.yaml --version 1.0.5 Below is an example of the `data-plane-values.yaml` file that the Helm chart uses to install the IOMETE data plane: [code example]

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Upgrades
chunks.text: To ensure our customers benefit from the continuous improvements, feature additions, and optimizations we make, we release updates periodically. With every release, our primary focus remains the seamless transition of our users from one version to another, ensuring stability, data integrity, and operational continuity.

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Semantic Versioning
chunks.text: IOMETE follows the Semantic Versioning standard. This ensures that our customers can easily understand the impact of a new release and plan accordingly. - **Major Version**: A major version release indicates that the update contains significant changes. These changes can include new features, breaking changes, or other significant improvements. - **Minor Version**: A minor version release indicates that the update contains new features, improvements, and bug fixes. These changes are backward-compatible and do not require any significant changes to the existing setup. - **Patch Version**: A patch version release indicates that the update contains bug fixes and minor improvements. These changes are backward-compatible and do not require any significant changes to the existing setup. Each release is accompanied by a detailed changelog, which provides a comprehensive overview of the changes included in the update.

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Upgrade Notification and Support
chunks.text: Upon the release of a new update: 1. **Notification**: Customers will receive a notification regarding the new release. This will detail the new features, improvements, and any critical fixes included. 2. **Upgrade Guide**: Accompanying the notification, customers will be provided with a comprehensive upgrade guide. This manual will have step-by-step instructions, tailored to help users navigate through the upgrade process with ease. 3. **Dedicated Support**: Understanding that upgrades can sometimes be intricate, our support team is always ready to assist. Whether you need clarification on a step or face any technical challenges, our experts will be there to guide and ensure a successful upgrade.

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Upgrade Process
chunks.text: 1. **Backup**: Before starting the upgrade, take backups of configurations, databases, and any vital data. This precautionary step ensures data safety. 2. **Access New Release**: Fetch the updated Helm chart corresponding to the new release. 3. **Apply the Upgrade**: Use the Helm upgrade command with the fetched chart. Follow the instructions provided in the upgrade guide. Using Kubernetes replication and `RollingUpdate` strategies we ensure smooth transition of our services. 4. **Validation**: Post-upgrade, verify the platform's state. Check if all the services are running correctly and test key functionalities to ensure everything operates as expected.

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Upgrade Example
chunks.text: In most cases, just running the below command will be enough to upgrade the platform. Assuming `data-plane-values.yaml` is adjusted to the new version: Replace `--version 1.0.5` with the version you want to upgrade to helm upgrade --install -n iomete iomete-dataplane iomete/iomete-dataplane \ -f data-plane-values.yaml --version 1.0.5

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Rollback Process
chunks.text: While we strive to make every upgrade seamless, unforeseen issues can arise. In such scenarios, the platform is designed to support smooth rollbacks. 1. **Rollback Guide**: If the need arises, a rollback guide will be provided, detailing how to revert to the previous stable version without loss of data or functionality. 2. **Rollback Execution**: Use Helm's rollback command to revert to the previous state/version. Helm’s rollback feature ensures that the platform is restored to its previous operational state without hitches. 3. **Support During Rollback**: During a rollback, our support team remains available to address any challenges or concerns, ensuring that the system is restored to its optimal state without unnecessary downtime.

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Rollback Example
chunks.text: Again, in most cases, rollback is just running helm upgrade commands with the previous version. Assuming `data-plane-values.yaml` is adjusted to the previous version: It is recommended to keep a copy of the previous version of the file. Version control systems like Git can be used to track changes. helm upgrade --install -n iomete iomete-dataplane iomete/iomete-dataplane \ -f data-plane-values.yaml --version 1.0.5

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: Monitoring and Management
chunks.text: Monitoring and management are pivotal to ensuring the health and performance. We've integrated leading monitoring tools such as Prometheus, Loki, and Grafana. *Monitoring Features*: 1. **Prometheus**: Collects metrics from configured targets at specified intervals, evaluates rule expressions, and can trigger alerts if certain conditions are observed. 2. **Loki**: A horizontally scalable, highly available, multi-tenant log aggregation system. 3. **Grafana**: Offers visualization panels to view metrics and logs. IOMETE provides built-in monitoring for Spark services Monitoring Kubernetes nodes through Grafana.

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: High Availability / Disaster Recovery
chunks.text: **1. External Dependencies and HA** - **MySQL Database**: - Our platform integrates with a high-availability MySQL database setup. This ensures that database operations remain resilient to failures, guaranteeing uninterrupted data access. - Features like automated failover, replication, and backup capabilities of the MySQL setup mean that the platform can continue its operations even if a primary database node fails. - **Storage Solution**: - The platform is designed to work seamlessly with high-availability storage solutions. This guarantees that the data remains accessible and safe. - Through redundancy, data replication, and failover protocols present in these storage solutions, data loss or inaccessibility issues are effectively negated. **2. Stateless Architecture** One of the foundational strengths of our platform is its stateless nature: - Being stateless ensures that no session or user-specific data is stored on any single server or node. This means, in the event of a node failure, another node can easily take over without any loss of data or disruption to the user. - This architecture also aids in effortless horizontal scaling, as new nodes can be added without needing any unique configurations or data. **3. Kubernetes-driven Replication and Failover** Leveraging Kubernetes' powerful orchestration capabilities, our platform achieves enhanced availability: -

chunks.title: Life Cycle Management (LCM)
chunks.heading: High Availability / Disaster Recovery
chunks.text: scaling, as new nodes can be added without needing any unique configurations or data. **3. Kubernetes-driven Replication and Failover** Leveraging Kubernetes' powerful orchestration capabilities, our platform achieves enhanced availability: - **Replication Across Nodes**: Kubernetes ensures that the platform's services and pods are replicated across multiple nodes. If a node faces issues or goes down, traffic is automatically directed to healthy nodes, ensuring uninterrupted service. **4. Disaster Recovery and Quick Switching** In the improbable event of a complete Kubernetes cluster failure: - Customers have the option to maintain a separate standby Kubernetes cluster with our platform deployed. - This standby instance can be quickly pointed to the same high-availability database and storage. This ensures a swift switch without any data loss or significant downtime.

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Starting from version **3.16.x**, IOMETE supports multi-cluster deployments. This allows multiple IOMETE instances — each running in its own Kubernetes cluster — to share a set of common resources through a shared global database. This is useful when you have IOMETE deployed across multiple data centers or environments and want certain resources (like users, catalogs, and domains) to stay in sync without manually duplicating them. Current Limitation This implementation does **not** provide a unified control plane or a single view across instances. Each IOMETE instance is still operated and maintained independently. A true single control plane architecture is planned for a future release. See Roadmap below. ---

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Deployment Models
chunks.text: IOMETE can be deployed in three ways depending on your scale and requirements. ---

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Single Installation
chunks.text: The simplest setup: one IOMETE instance, one Kubernetes cluster, one database. The `clusterDatabase` is not configured, so IOMETE uses the same database for both global and cluster-scoped data. This is the default and requires no additional configuration. ---

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Multiple Independent Installations
chunks.text: As teams and environments grow, you may run many separate IOMETE instances — each fully independent, with its own database, its own users, and its own workloads. There is no shared state between them. This is common when different business units, regions, or environments (dev, staging, production) each need their own isolated IOMETE deployment. Each instance is managed separately, and there is no synchronization between them. ---

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Multi-Cluster Setup (Shared Global Database)
chunks.text: When you need certain resources — users, catalogs, domains — to be consistent across multiple instances, you configure a shared global database. Each instance still runs independently and has its own cluster-local database for Kubernetes and Spark workloads, but all instances read from and write to the same global database for shared resources. **Example:** Instance A (data center A) and Instance B (data center B) both point to the same global database. A user created in Instance A is immediately visible in Instance B. Each instance still manages its own Spark jobs and clusters locally. This is what the `clusterDatabase` configuration enables. When provided, IOMETE routes cluster-specific, high-volume operations to the local database and uses the global database only for shared resources. ---

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: How It Works
chunks.text: Each IOMETE instance uses two databases: - **Global database** (`database`) — shared across all instances. Stores resources that are common across the fleet, such as users, catalogs, and domains. This is always required. - **Cluster database** (`clusterDatabase`) — local to each instance. Stores Kubernetes and Spark-related data specific to that installation, such as clusters, jobs, and workloads. When `clusterDatabase` is **not configured**, IOMETE treats the deployment as a single-instance setup and uses the same database for both global and cluster-scoped data. When `clusterDatabase` **is configured**, the global database is shared with other instances while high-volume cluster-specific operations are offloaded to the local database. ---

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Global vs. Cluster Resources
chunks.text: The tables below list which databases and services are global (shared across all instances) and which are cluster-local (specific to each instance).

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Databases
chunks.text: iomete_catalog_db: Scope Global. iomete_core_db: Scope Both, Notes Tables are split — some in global, some in cluster-local. iomete_iam_db: Scope Global. iomete_iceberg_db: Scope Global. iomete_metastore_db: Scope Global. iomete_prefect_db: Scope Cluster-local. iomete_sql_db: Scope Cluster-local.

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Services
chunks.text: iom-catalog: Database Scope Global. iom-cluster: Database Scope Cluster-local. iom-core: Database Scope Global. data-plane-init: Database Scope Both, Notes Initializes both global and cluster-local databases. iom-identity: Database Scope Global. iom-rest-catalog: Database Scope Global. iom-sql: Database Scope Cluster-local. prefect-server + prefect-worker: Database Scope Cluster-local. metastore: Database Scope Global. ---

chunks.heading: Single Instance (Default)
chunks.text: No changes needed. When `clusterDatabase` is omitted, both the global and cluster-scoped data go into the same database. title="data-plane-values.yaml" database: type: postgresql host: "postgresql" port: "5432" user: "iomete_user" password: "iomete_pass" prefix: "iomete_"

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.text: Add the `clusterDatabase` section alongside the main `database` block. The `database` section becomes the shared global database; `clusterDatabase` is the instance-local database. [code example] Repeat this on every IOMETE instance, each with its own `clusterDatabase` host, all pointing to the **same** `database` (global) host. The global database must be reachable from every participating Kubernetes cluster. Verify firewall rules and network policies allow connectivity from each cluster to the global database host before deployment.

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Applying the Configuration
chunks.text: helm upgrade --install -n iomete-system data-plane \ iomete/iomete-data-plane-enterprise \ -f data-plane-values.yaml Run this on each instance after updating its values file. ---

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Behavior and Expectations
chunks.text: - Changes to global resources (users, catalogs, domains) on any instance are immediately visible on all connected instances. - Each instance has its own UI and access endpoint. There is no aggregated view across instances. - Instances can be upgraded independently, as long as all connected instances remain compatible with the global database schema. - If the global database becomes unavailable, operations that depend on global resources will be affected across all instances. ---

chunks.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
chunks.heading: Roadmap
chunks.text: The current multi-cluster implementation is a first step. In upcoming releases, IOMETE plans to introduce a **single control plane** architecture: - One main control plane managing configuration and global state. - Multiple lightweight data planes (B, C, …) running in separate environments with a reduced set of services. - A unified view across all data planes from the control plane UI. This will replace the shared-database approach with a proper distributed control model. ---

chunks.title: MySQL Deployment
chunks.text: IOMETE requires a database to store metadata and other information. Refer Backend Databases for more details. You can use your own database, or you can use the provided `mysql` database. This mysql database is for testing purpose only. For production, please use your own database that is optimized for production use. Add `bitnami` helm repo if you haven't done so. showLineNumbers helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami helm repo update Deploy mysql database, and wait for it to be ready. Required file: mysql-values.yaml showLineNumbers wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iomete/iomete-deployment/main/database/mysql/mysql-values.yaml helm upgrade --install -n iomete-system \ mysql bitnami/mysql -f mysql-values.yaml Wait for mysql pod to be ready. It takes about **~1 minute** showLineNumbers kubectl get pods -n iomete-system \ -l app.kubernetes.io/name=mysql --watch When admin user credentials are provided to IOMETE deployment, IOMETE will create necessary users and databases automatically. If you want to create users and databases manually, you can use the following script: database-init-mysql.sql

chunks.title: Kubernetes Network Policies
chunks.text: IOMETE services rely on specific network configurations to function properly in a Kubernetes cluster. These network policies govern how different components communicate securely and efficiently.

chunks.title: Kubernetes Network Policies
chunks.heading: Spark Operator Webhook Policy
chunks.text: The webhook service plays a critical role in managing IOMETE resources. If resource creation times out or fails, there could be a connectivity issue between the Kubernetes API server and the webhook. This is often due to restrictive network policies that block incoming traffic. Kubernetes API server requires access to the Spark Operator webhook service. This policy allows controlled ingress traffic to the webhook while restricting external access. title="iomete-spark-operator.yaml" apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: iomete-spark-operator spec: podSelector: matchLabels: service: spark-operator ingress: - from: - ipBlock: cidr: [API_SERVER_IP]/32 # Replace with your API server's IP egress: - policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress **How to Find API Server IP** Use the following command to retrieve the API server IP and update the policy: kubectl cluster-info | grep master Replace `[API_SERVER_IP]` in the YAML file with the actual IP address. ---

chunks.title: Kubernetes Network Policies
chunks.heading: IOMETE Namespaces Communication Policy
chunks.text: This policy ensures that all IOMETE control plane and data plane services can communicate securely across namespaces, using the label `iomete.com/managed: "true"`. It leaves out Jupyter Container pods. Kubernetes combines policies by allowing anything any of them allows, so a policy that selects every pod would cancel out the Jupyter Containers policy. Use the `NotIn` selector below only when the Jupyter Containers policy is installed. Without it, notebooks match no policy and become fully open, so keep `podSelector: ` instead. title="iomete-ingress-egress.yaml" apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: iomete-ingress-egress spec: podSelector: matchExpressions: - key: iomete.com/appType operator: NotIn values: - jupyterContainer ingress: - from: - namespaceSelector: matchLabels: iomete.com/managed: "true" egress: - policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress ---

chunks.title: Kubernetes Network Policies
chunks.heading: Jupyter Containers Policy
chunks.text: Jupyter Containers run user code, so the data plane Helm chart can install a policy named `iomete-jupyter-containers` in the data plane namespace and every Spark namespace. It's off by default. To turn it on, set this in `values.yaml` and run the Helm upgrade: title="values.yaml" networkPolicies: jupyterContainers: enabled: true The policy only restricts traffic when your cluster's network plugin enforces NetworkPolicies, so check that before relying on it. With it: - Only the IOMETE gateway can reach notebooks. - Notebooks can reach DNS, your ingress controller and the internet over IPv4 and IPv6. - Apart from DNS, your ingress controller and any `extraEgress` entries, notebooks can't reach private, link-local (cloud metadata) or carrier-grade NAT addresses. If you applied `iomete-ingress-egress` before, it may still select every pod and cancel this policy. Re-apply the updated version and check its `podSelector` uses `NotIn jupyterContainer`: kubectl get networkpolicy iomete-ingress-egress -n -o yaml Notebooks connect to compute clusters through your ingress controller. The policy allows the `istio-system`, `istio-ingress`, `ingress-nginx`, `openshift-ingress` and `traefik` namespaces. If your controller runs elsewhere, or your platform host resolves to a private IP, adjust the policy in `values.yaml`: title="values.yaml" networkPolicies: jupyterContainers: ingressNamespaces: - my-ingress extraEgress: - to: - ipBlock: cidr: 10.20.30.40/32 #

chunks.title: Kubernetes Network Policies
chunks.heading: Jupyter Containers Policy
chunks.text: runs elsewhere, or your platform host resolves to a private IP, adjust the policy in `values.yaml`: title="values.yaml" networkPolicies: jupyterContainers: ingressNamespaces: - my-ingress extraEgress: - to: - ipBlock: cidr: 10.20.30.40/32 # internal load balancer or private data source ports: - protocol: TCP port: 443 ingressNamespaces: Use it to List the namespaces of the ingress controller serving the platform host. Setting it replaces the default list.. extraEgress: Use it to Allow an internal address notebooks need.. blockedCidrs: Use it to Change which IPv4 and IPv6 ranges count as internal.. dnsPorts: Use it to Change the ports notebooks use for DNS, for example add 5353 on OpenShift.. enabled: Use it to Turn the policy on.. If notebooks open but can't connect to a compute cluster, add your ingress controller's namespace to `ingressNamespaces`. To apply the policy yourself instead of through the chart, save it as `iomete-jupyter-containers.yaml`, replace ` ` with the data plane namespace, and apply it to the data plane namespace and every Spark namespace: [code example] kubectl apply -f iomete-jupyter-containers.yaml -n kubectl apply -f iomete-jupyter-containers.yaml -n ---

chunks.title: Kubernetes Network Policies
chunks.heading: Applying Network Policies
chunks.text: The following steps explain how to apply network policies to IOMETE control plane and data plane namespaces. 1. Save both `iomete-spark-operator.yaml` and `iomete-ingress-egress.yaml` files. 2. In the `iomete-spark-operator.yaml`, replace: `[API_SERVER_IP]` with your Kubernetes API server's IP address (obtain this using `kubectl cluster-info | grep master`). 3. Apply the policies using `kubectl` to the respective namespaces: kubectl apply -f iomete-spark-operator.yaml -n kubectl apply -f iomete-ingress-egress.yaml -n Ensure that both policies have been applied successfully ---

chunks.title: Kubernetes Network Policies
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.text: If issues arise, follow these troubleshooting steps: 1. **Verify Policy Application**: Ensure the policies are correctly applied: kubectl get networkpolicies -n 2. **Check API Server Access**: Confirm that the API server can reach the webhook: kubectl cluster-info | grep master 3. **Connectivity Issues**: If errors persist, review your network policies and consult with your networking team or system administrator for potential misconfigurations. ---

chunks.title: Kubernetes Network Policies
chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text: Ensuring proper network communication between IOMETE components is essential for the platform's security and performance. By applying the correct network policies and monitoring connectivity, you can maintain a secure and efficient IOMETE deployment.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.text: Nutanix Ready IOMETE Data Plane Enterprise is Nutanix Ready validated and supported on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP) 2.18. Validated on IOMETE 3.19.0 and supported on 3.19.0 and later. The whole platform runs inside your NKP cluster and uses Nutanix storage for both lakehouse data and persistent volumes, so you get a self-hosted lakehouse on your existing Nutanix infrastructure.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.heading: Validated Versions
chunks.text: IOMETE Data Plane Enterprise: Version 3.19.0. Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP): Version 2.18.0 (Kubernetes 1.35.2). Nutanix AOS: Version 7.6.0.6. Nutanix AHV: Version 11.2.0.2. Prism Central: Version 7.6.0.6. Node OS: Version Ubuntu 24.04.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.heading: Architecture on NKP
chunks.text: Platform services and Spark compute: Runs on NKP workload cluster. The Helm chart installs the platform services into a namespace such as iomete-system, and Spark workloads run there or in additional namespaces. Lakehouse data and Iceberg metadata: Runs on Nutanix Objects, through its S3-compatible API. Persistent volumes (event stream, search index, Spark shuffle and spill data): Runs on Nutanix Volumes, through the Nutanix CSI driver and the nutanix-volume StorageClass. Metadata database: Runs on PostgreSQL managed by CloudNativePG (CNPG), the operator that ships with NKP. User access to the IOMETE console: Runs on NKP's built-in Traefik ingress.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text: - An NKP 2.18 or later workload cluster with the capacity listed in the On-Premises Deployment Guide, and `kubectl` and `helm` set up for it. - A Nutanix Objects object store reachable from the cluster, with a bucket and an access key for IOMETE. - The CloudNativePG platform application enabled in your NKP workspace. - The `nutanix-volume` StorageClass, which is the default on NKP. - metrics-server, only if you plan to enable autoscaling.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.heading: Installing on NKP
chunks.text: Follow the On-Premises Deployment Guide and use the settings below for the NKP-specific parts. Istio is not needed on NKP: the built-in Traefik ingress gives users access to the IOMETE console.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.heading: Object Storage: Nutanix Objects
chunks.text: Create a bucket and an access key in Nutanix Objects, then point IOMETE at the Objects endpoint: title="data-plane-values.yaml" storage: type: "s3_compatible" bucketName: "iomete" s3CompatibleSettings: endpoint: "http:// " accessKey: " " secretKeySecret: name: " " key: " " `s3CompatibleSettings` needs IOMETE 3.19.1 or later. For earlier versions, see Object Storage. If the Objects endpoint uses HTTPS with a certificate from a private CA, add that CA to IOMETE's truststore. See Custom Java Truststore.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.heading: Metadata Database: CloudNativePG
chunks.text: Enable the CloudNativePG platform application in your NKP workspace and create a PostgreSQL cluster with at least three instances, so CNPG can fail over automatically. Then point IOMETE at the cluster's read-write service, which always routes to the current primary: title="data-plane-values.yaml" database: type: "postgresql" host: " -rw. .svc.cluster.local" port: "5432" user: " " passwordSecret: name: " " key: " " See Backend Databases for the user and databases IOMETE needs.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.heading: Persistent Volumes: Nutanix Volumes
chunks.text: IOMETE's own volumes, for the event stream and the search index, use the cluster's default StorageClass. `nutanix-volume` is the default on NKP, so they need no extra settings. If your cluster uses a different default, set the storage class explicitly: title="data-plane-values.yaml" services: eventStream: persistence: storageClassName: "nutanix-volume" typesense: persistence: storageClassName: "nutanix-volume" Spark writes shuffle data, and data that spills out of memory, to local disk. To put that on Nutanix Volumes, create an On-Demand PVC volume with the `nutanix-volume` storage class and attach it to your compute clusters and jobs.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.heading: Console Access: NKP Traefik Ingress
chunks.text: NKP ships with Traefik. Create an Ingress for the IOMETE gateway service: title="iomete-ingress.yaml" apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: iomete namespace: iomete-system spec: ingressClassName: kommander-traefik rules: - host: iomete.example.com http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: iom-gateway port: number: 80 NKP redirects HTTP to HTTPS and serves Traefik's default certificate. To use your own, add a `tls` section to the Ingress that references a certificate Secret, for example one issued by cert-manager, which NKP includes.

chunks.title: Deploying IOMETE on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)
chunks.heading: Autoscaling (Optional)
chunks.text: Several IOMETE services can scale with load through a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): - **Services:** `gateway`, `core`, `identity`, `dataCatalog`, `cluster`, `restCatalog` and any other service with an `autoscaling` block in your chart's `values.yaml`. - **Enabling:** set it per service, for example `services.gateway.autoscaling.enabled: true`. - **Resources:** from IOMETE 4.0, the chart requires a service's resource requests to equal its limits when autoscaling is on. - **Metrics:** the HPA needs metrics-server, which NKP workload clusters don't always run. Install it if `kubectl top nodes` returns an error.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.text: This guide provides detailed instructions for deploying IOMETE on-premises within a Kubernetes environment, ensuring you have a seamless setup process. Terraform option There is also a Terraform configuration that handles all the steps below in one go (Kubernetes cluster, PostgreSQL, Apache Ozone, data plane, and monitoring). This is currently available for Azure. Nutanix Kubernetes Platform Installing on Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP)? Follow this guide together with Deploying IOMETE on NKP, which covers the NKP-specific settings for Nutanix Objects, Nutanix Volumes, CloudNativePG and the built-in Traefik ingress. Istio is not needed on NKP.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Essential Requirements Before You Start
chunks.text: Have the following ready before you start: - **Kubernetes cluster** with room for two kinds of workloads: - **IOMETE services:** at least 12 CPU cores and 24GB of RAM. This includes headroom for Kubernetes system pods and Istio. - **Spark workloads:** at least one node with 4 CPU cores and 32GB of RAM for Spark drivers and executors. - **Object storage:** Apache Ozone, Dell ECS, IBM Cloud Object Storage, MinIO or any other S3-compatible storage, AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Google Cloud Storage. If you don't have one, see Apache Ozone deployment or MinIO deployment. - **PostgreSQL database** for IOMETE metadata. If you don't have one, see PostgreSQL deployment. - **Istio**, to give users access to the IOMETE UI. See Configure ISTIO Ingress Gateway. - **Tools:** - `kubectl` and `helm`, set up for the target cluster. - `yq` v4, only if an administrator creates the cluster-level resources (option 2 below). - `aws` CLI (optional), to create a bucket when you use Apache Ozone or MinIO.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Deployment Steps
chunks.text: Make sure `kubectl` points at the right Kubernetes cluster before you continue.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Create namespace for IOMETE
chunks.text: A dedicated namespace for IOMETE is recommended for better organization. Create it using the following command: title="Create and label the namespace" kubectl create namespace iomete-system

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Label the namespace for IOMETE
chunks.text: kubectl label namespace iomete-system iomete.com/managed=true Technically, you can deploy IOMETE in any namespace. If you choose to deploy in a different namespace, ensure you use the correct namespace in the following steps. To run Spark workloads in more namespaces, see Install Data-Plane (Namespace).

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Object Storage
chunks.text: If you need an object storage system, you can deploy Apache Ozone, an open-source S3-compatible object store. Follow the instructions in Apache Ozone deployment. You can also use MinIO.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Deploying Metadata Database (PostgreSQL)
chunks.text: For metadata storage, you need a PostgreSQL database. Please follow the instructions here.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Add IOMETE Helm Repository
chunks.text: Add the IOMETE helm repository for access to necessary charts: showLineNumbers title="Add the IOMETE Helm repository" helm repo add iomete https://chartmuseum.iomete.com helm repo update Set the chart version you are installing. Every `helm` command below uses it, so all of them work from the same chart: title="Set the chart version"

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Prepare Your Values File
chunks.text: [](https://artifacthub.io/packages/search?repo=iomete) Required file: example-data-plane-values.yaml title="Download the example values file" wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iomete/iomete-deployment/main/on-prem/example-data-plane-values.yaml This is a sample file. Edit it for your setup before you continue. For every available setting, see the IOMETE Data Plane Enterprise page on Artifact Hub.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Create Cluster-Level Resources
chunks.text: IOMETE needs three sets of Kubernetes resources before its pods can start: - The `lakehouse-service-account` service account, with its Role and RoleBinding. - The Spark Operator CRDs. - The Spark Operator webhook and its certificate. The Helm chart can create all of them for you. Use option 1 if your Helm user has permission to create them. If it doesn't, use option 2 and have a Kubernetes administrator create them. Installing 3.19.0 or earlier? The chart creates these resources from version 3.19.1 onward. On 3.19.0 or earlier, option 1 isn't available. Create the same resources by hand, as described in Installing 3.19.0 or Earlier.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Option 1: Let Helm Create Them (Recommended)
chunks.text: Add these lines to `example-data-plane-values.yaml`: title="example-data-plane-values.yaml" serviceAccount: create: true crds: create: true webhook: create: true With these set, Helm creates the resources during installation. It keeps the service account and the webhook up to date on every upgrade. It creates the CRDs only on the first installation and never updates them, so apply CRD changes yourself as described in Upgrading the CRDs. If another Helm release or an administrator already manages the Spark Operator CRDs, leave `crds.create` set to `false`. Helm 4 fails the installation when an existing CRD differs from the one in the chart. Your Helm user needs permission to create CRDs, a `MutatingWebhookConfiguration`, service accounts, Roles, RoleBindings and Secrets. If the installation fails with a `forbidden` error, set the failing switch back to `false` and use option 2 for that resource. Upgrading an existing installation If you created these resources by hand in an earlier installation, the chart leaves them as they are. You don't need to change anything. Turning on `crds.create` for an existing installation creates nothing, because Helm installs CRDs only on a release's first installation.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Option 1: Let Helm Create Them (Recommended)
chunks.text: nothing, because Helm installs CRDs only on a release's first installation.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Option 2: Have an Administrator Create Them
chunks.text: A Kubernetes administrator generates the resources from the chart and applies them. The commands need `yq` v4 and must run with the same values file you install with. 1. Create the service account, Role and RoleBinding: helm template data-plane iomete/iomete-data-plane-enterprise \ --namespace iomete-system \ --version "$IOMETE_VERSION" \ --values example-data-plane-values.yaml \ --set serviceAccount.create=true \ | yq 'select(.metadata.name == "lakehouse-service-account" or .metadata.name == "iomete-lakehouse-role" or .metadata.name == "iomete-lakehouse-role-binding") | del(.metadata.annotations."helm.sh/hook", .metadata.annotations."helm.sh/hook-weight")' \ > lakehouse-service-account.yaml kubectl apply -f lakehouse-service-account.yaml 2. Create the Spark Operator CRDs. The chart ships them as plain files, so download the chart and apply them from it. The CRD files are large, so they must be applied with `--server-side`: helm pull iomete/iomete-data-plane-enterprise \ --version "$IOMETE_VERSION" \ --untar --untardir "chart-$IOMETE_VERSION" kubectl apply --server-side -f "chart-$IOMETE_VERSION"/iomete-data-plane-enterprise/charts/operator-crds/crds/ 3. Create the webhook and its certificate: helm template data-plane iomete/iomete-data-plane-enterprise \ --namespace iomete-system \ --version "$IOMETE_VERSION" \ --values example-data-plane-values.yaml \ --set webhook.create=true \ | yq 'select(.kind == "MutatingWebhookConfiguration" or (.kind == "Secret" and .metadata.name == "spark-operator-webhook-certs"))' \ > spark-operator-webhook.yaml kubectl apply -f spark-operator-webhook.yaml 4. Keep all three switches off in `example-data-plane-values.yaml`, so Helm doesn't try to create them: title="example-data-plane-values.yaml" serviceAccount: create: false crds: create: false webhook: create: false Helm doesn't update resources an administrator

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Option 2: Have an Administrator Create Them
chunks.text: Keep all three switches off in `example-data-plane-values.yaml`, so Helm doesn't try to create them: title="example-data-plane-values.yaml" serviceAccount: create: false crds: create: false webhook: create: false Helm doesn't update resources an administrator created. Repeat step 1 after you add a namespace or change `namespaces`, `docker.imagePullSecrets` or `serviceAccount.annotations`, and apply CRD changes as described in Upgrading the CRDs when you upgrade to a new chart version. Mixing both options You can combine the two options. For example, let Helm create the service account and have an administrator create the CRDs and the webhook. Set each switch to `true` only for what Helm creates.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Upgrading the CRDs
chunks.text: `helm upgrade` never updates or deletes the Spark Operator CRDs, whether Helm or an administrator created them. When the release notes for the version you are upgrading to say the CRDs changed, apply them before you run the upgrade: helm pull iomete/iomete-data-plane-enterprise \ --version "$IOMETE_VERSION" \ --untar --untardir "chart-$IOMETE_VERSION" kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts -f "chart-$IOMETE_VERSION"/iomete-data-plane-enterprise/charts/operator-crds/crds/ `--force-conflicts` lets `kubectl` take over the fields Helm set when it created the CRDs. Without it, `kubectl` refuses the change.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Installing 3.19.0 or Earlier
chunks.text: Manual steps for chart versions 3.19.0 and earlier These are the same three resources as in option 2, but the files come from the iomete-deployment repository instead of the chart. A Kubernetes administrator runs them, since they create cluster-level objects. There are no `create` switches to set on these versions. 1. Create the service account, Role and RoleBinding: wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iomete/iomete-deployment/main/service-account.yaml kubectl apply -n iomete-system -f service-account.yaml 2. Create the Spark Operator CRDs: wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iomete/iomete-deployment/main/iomete-crds.yaml kubectl apply --server-side -f iomete-crds.yaml 3. Create the webhook and its certificate. The `gencerts.sh` script generates the certificate and writes `spark-operator-webhook.yaml`: wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iomete/iomete-deployment/main/gencerts.sh chmod +x gencerts.sh ./gencerts.sh -n iomete-system -s spark-operator-webhook -r spark-operator-webhook-certs kubectl apply -n iomete-system -f spark-operator-webhook.yaml When you later upgrade to 3.19.1 or newer, you don't need to redo anything. The chart finds these resources and leaves them as they are.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Launching IOMETE Data Plane
chunks.text: showLineNumbers title="Install the IOMETE data plane" helm upgrade --install -n iomete-system data-plane \ iomete/iomete-data-plane-enterprise \ --version "$IOMETE_VERSION" \ -f example-data-plane-values.yaml Run the same command later to upgrade.

chunks.title: On-Premises Deployment Guide
chunks.heading: Configure ISTIO Ingress Gateway
chunks.text: Please follow the Configure ISTIO Ingress Gateway to configure the Ingress Gateway for IOMETE Data Plane to be able to access the UI.

The graph draws the control plane and every data plane connected to it, with each plane's address, connection status, and CPU and memory quota usage. The graph can be expanded to fullscreen. - **Remote Workloads**: Computes, Spark jobs and Jupyter containers can be created on a named data plane. chunks.text: - **Access Policy Patch Support**: Added PATCH support for data access policies so admins can append or remove individual resources and policy items without resending the full policy definition. - **`PATCH /access/policy//resources`**: Adds or removes a resource entry from an existing policy. - **`PATCH /access/policy//policy-items`**: Adds or removes allow/deny policy items, including users, groups, roles, and their associated access permissions. - **LDAP Identity Management Improvements**: - Added automatic service account detection for LDAP-synced identities based on directory attributes such as `employeeType=Service`, ensuring these identities are imported as `Service Account` instead of `Person`. See LDAP Configuration. - Improved LDAP filter validation for custom sync filters by always validating overall filter syntax, tightening validation for edited filter lines, handling spacing/indentation edge cases more reliably, and surfacing clearer save-time error messages for invalid filters. See LDAP Configuration. - **Identity soft-delete** (behind the `identitySoftDelete` feature flag): When enabled, deleted users and groups are archived instead of permanently removed. This applies across all identity surfaces: - **LDAP sync**: LDAP-origin users and groups are reconciled incrementally: new identities are created, returning identities are restored, existing identities are updated in place, and identities no longer present in LDAP are archived instead of being hard-deleted. Instead, the catalog handles data access on behalf of clients — they only need a catalog-level access token. IOMETE implements both modes defined by the Iceberg REST specification: - **Credential Vending** — The catalog issues temporary, scoped credentials per table. Permissions are derived from Apache Ranger policies (`SELECT` → read-only, `INSERT`/`DELETE` → read-write). Credentials are short-lived and automatically scoped to the table's path. - **Remote Signing** — The catalog signs requests on behalf of clients using presigned requests. Credentials never leave the server. Both modes are disabled by default. They can be enabled globally via System Configs (`iceberg-catalog.vended-credentials.enabled` / `iceberg-catalog.remote-signing.enabled`) or per catalog via additional catalog properties. 📄 Learn more: Iceberg REST Catalog — Access Delegation 📝 Deep dive with our blog post: Access Delegation in Apache Iceberg - **Enterprise Catalog** A new **preview** IOMETE-managed catalog that simplifies multi-format table management. chunks.text: - **IOMETE Spark**: Spark version spark-3.5.5 is a default version set. - **PriorityClass Mappings**: Implemented Priority Class Mappings, which enables to configure priority classes mappings in helm charts. - **Log Management**: - Built Executor Logs feature enabling real-time viewing of compute and Spark job executor logs in the UI. - Added support for downloading logs from external logging systems including Splunk, Loki, and EFK. - **Tag Filtering on Spark/Streaming Job List**: You can **search** and **filter** the Spark/Streaming job list by **resource tags**. - **New SQL Chart Types**: You can now visualize SQL query results with **Pie Charts**, **Scatter Plots**, **Treemaps**, and **Composed Charts**. - **Parent-Child Relationship for Groups**: - On the **Group Details** page, users can now see both their **directly assigned** and **parent** groups. - Added two tabs: - **Sub groups** (Inheriting to) - **Parent groups** (Inherited from) - Same updates applied to **Domain Group Members**. - ***Note**: Currently, group relationships apply only to LDAP members.* - **Job Orchestrator**: - Job Priority Restrictions: - Only Domain Admins can upgrade jobs to HIGH priority. - Regular users can manage NORMAL jobs, edit HIGH, and downgrade to NORMAL. - Existing jobs and normal operations remain unaffected. - Worker Deployment Changes:

chunks.heading: Platform 3.11.0 (August 11, 2025)
chunks.text: upgrade jobs to HIGH priority. - Regular users can manage NORMAL jobs, edit HIGH, and downgrade to NORMAL. - Existing jobs and normal operations remain unaffected. - Worker Deployment Changes: Workers moved to respective data planes, reduced resource usage, and added per-namespace configurations. - Spark Job Quota Enhancements: Added PriorityClass quota support; system now applies the most restrictive limit across namespace and job-specific quotas for CPU, Memory, and Pods. - **API Improvements**: Implemented exposing the token management operations in the API / swagger. - Fixed an issue where resources quotas in the homepage picked up the priority class quota instead of the namespace quota. - Fixed an issue where the USE command on a catalog failed with access_denied when the user had access to only specific databases, by adding proper catalog-level USE privilege support.

chunks.title: IOMETE Release Notes
chunks.heading: Platform 3.10.2 (August 3, 2025)
chunks.text: - Fixed an issue where the `spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled` flag was always set to false. - Fixed an issue where the `spark.executor.instances` was set to 1 even when dynamic allocation was disabled. - Fixed an issue where the user failed to query the view when they lack the permission to the underlying table, even if the user has a permission to the view. - Disabled `delete table` button in database explorer within SQL Editor sidebar.

chunks.title: IOMETE Release Notes
chunks.heading: Platform 3.9.3 (July 23, 2025)
chunks.text: - Patched `antiAffinity` rules, customers can now configure soft affinity rules for Spark driver pods to help distribute them across nodes and reduce the probability of most drivers ending up on the same node. This can be enabled by setting the flag `iometeSparkDriverAntiAffinity.enabled` to true in values.yaml during installation. - The iom-core pod now dynamically reloads any `docker.tagAliases` defined in `values.yaml`, removing the need to restart the pod.

chunks.title: IOMETE Release Notes
chunks.heading: Platform 3.10.1 (July 22nd, 2025)
chunks.text: - Fixed an issue where column descriptions and tags were being unintentionally overridden by the catalog-sync job. - Descriptions will now be preserved if already present. - Tags from the sync job will be merged with existing tags instead of replacing them. - Added validations of tags and label names based on the rules mentioned here. - It has been implemented in API level, so that integrated tools to be validated as well. - It has been implemented in UI level as well, so the users to be informed about valid syntax formats.

chunks.title: IOMETE Release Notes
chunks.heading: Platform 3.10.0 (July 15, 2025)
chunks.text: - **Job Orchestrator [Beta]**: This is the beta release of our broader initiative to bring orchestration to IOMETE. To enable it, set the flag `jobOrchestrator.enabled` in `values.yaml`. - **Priority-based Scheduling**: Users can now prioritize the scheduling of business-critical jobs over regular-priority jobs. - **Resource-aware Execution**: Jobs are only submitted when there is sufficient cluster capacity, helping prevent failed or stuck jobs. - **Built-in observability**: We've added rich metrics to monitor queue state, job wait times, and scheduling patterns in real time. For an in-depth overview, check out the official press release. - **Jupyter Containers [Beta]**: Jupyter Containers is a powerful new feature that brings familiar Jupyter development environments directly into your IOMETE Platform. This enhancement enables data engineers and analysts to spin up dedicated, pre-configured Jupyter environments with just a few clicks. Key highlights: - Create isolated Jupyter containers with customizable resource allocation. - Each container comes with JupyterLab pre-installed and ready to use. Click "Open JupyterLab" to directly access Jupyter environment from IOMETE UI. - Pre-installed Spark libraries for immediate access to distributed computing. - Direct connectivity to IOMETE Compute clusters via Spark Connect. - Essential developer tools pre-installed: git, aws cli, sparksql-magic, pandas, other libraries and extensions. -

chunks.text: - Fixed an issue where queries run from the SQL Editor were missing automatic `LIMIT` clauses.
