chunks.title: Getting Started with Airflow
chunks.heading: Getting Started with Airflow
chunks.text: The IOMETE Airflow Plugin lets you trigger and manage IOMETE Spark jobs from an Airflow DAG. It submits each job run, monitors its status, and cancels the run if its Airflow task is killed.

chunks.title: Getting Started with Airflow
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text: - Python 3.10–3.13 - Apache Airflow `>=2.10.5, } link="user-guide/access-tokens/personal" > Create a personal access token for the IOMETE API } link="https://github.com/iomete/iomete-integrations/tree/main/iomete-airflow-plugin" > View the plugin source and examples } link="deployment/on-prem/release-notes/integrations" > Review changes before upgrading the plugin

chunks.title: IometeOperator Reference
chunks.heading: IometeOperator Reference
chunks.text: `IometeOperator` submits an existing IOMETE Spark job and monitors its run from an Airflow task. Complete Getting Started with Airflow before using this reference.

chunks.title: IometeOperator Reference
chunks.heading: Parameters
chunks.text: task_id: Type str, Required Yes, Default —, Description Unique identifier for the task in the DAG.. job_id: Type str, Required Yes, Default —, Description IOMETE Spark job ID or name.. host: Type str, Required Yes, Default —, Description IOMETE platform URL.. domain: Type str, Required Yes, Default —, Description IOMETE domain identifier.. access_token: Type str, Required One token option, Default —, Description Personal access token passed as a raw string. This field is not templatable.. access_token_variable: Type str, Required One token option, Default —, Description Name of an Airflow Variable containing the token. The plugin resolves it when the task runs.. host_verify: Type bool, Required No, Default True, Description Verifies the IOMETE host's TLS certificate.. config_override: Type dict or str, Required No, Default , Description Overrides arguments, environment variables, or Spark configuration for this run.. polling_period_seconds: Type int, Required No, Default 10, Description Seconds between job status checks.. do_xcom_push: Type bool, Required No, Default False, Description Pushes job_id and job_run_id to XCom.. Set either `access_token` or `access_token_variable`, never both.

chunks.title: IometeOperator Reference
chunks.heading: Template Fields
chunks.text: Airflow applies Jinja templating to: - `job_id` - `config_override` - `host` - `domain` - `access_token_variable` The raw `access_token` field is intentionally excluded because Airflow stores rendered fields in its metadata database and displays them in the UI.

chunks.title: IometeOperator Reference
chunks.heading: Configuration Overrides
chunks.text: `config_override` accepts a dictionary or JSON string with these optional fields: , "sparkConf": } See DAG Examples for a templated runtime override.

chunks.title: IometeOperator Reference
chunks.heading: Job Run States
chunks.text: ENQUEUED: Description Job is queued., Final? No. SUBMITTED: Description Job is being deployed., Final? No. RUNNING: Description Job is running., Final? No. COMPLETED: Description Job completed successfully., Final? Yes. FAILED: Description Job failed., Final? Yes. ABORTED: Description Job was cancelled., Final? Yes. ABORTING: Description Job cancellation is in progress., Final? No. A `FAILED` or `ABORTED` run raises an `AirflowException`. If the Airflow task is killed, the operator cancels the active IOMETE job run.

chunks.title: IometeOperator Reference
chunks.heading: Retries
chunks.text: Configure retries on the Airflow task with `retries` and `retry_delay`, either on the operator or in `default_args`. Each Airflow retry submits a new IOMETE job run, so every attempt appears in the Airflow UI with its own logs. Keep the job's Restart Policy set to **Never**, the default. The operator fails the task on the first `FAILED` state it sees and doesn't wait for IOMETE to restart the run. With **Always** or **OnFailure**, IOMETE can restart the job after Airflow has already marked the task failed, and that restart can overlap with an Airflow retry.

chunks.title: IometeOperator Reference
chunks.heading: XCom Values
chunks.text: When `do_xcom_push=True`, the operator publishes: job_id: Description Value passed to the operator's job_id parameter, which is either the job's ID or its name.. job_run_id: Description ID of the specific job run.. See Passing Run Details with XCom for usage.

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.text: Hi! In this guide, we will explain how to effortlessly integrate **IOMETE** with one of the most popular BI tools: Apache Superset.

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.text: Apache Superset is a modern data exploration and visualization platform. Superset is fast, lightweight, intuitive, and loaded with options that make it easy for users of all skill sets to explore and visualize their data, from simple line charts to highly detailed geospatial charts.

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Adding iomete database drivers in docker
chunks.text: Superset requires a Python database driver to be installed for each additional type of database you want to connect to. When setting up Superset locally via `docker-compose`, the drivers and packages contained in `requirements.txt` and `requirements-dev.txt` will be installed automatically. In this section, we'll walk through how to install the connector library for iomete lakehouse.

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Install driver for iomete
chunks.text: As we are currently running inside a Docker container via `docker-compose`, we cannot simply run `pip install py-hive-iomete` on our local shell and expect the drivers to be installed within the Docker containers for superset. In order to address this, the Superset `docker-compose` setup comes with a mechanism for you to install packages locally, which will be ignored by Git for the purposes of local development. Please follow these steps: Create `requirements-local.txt`

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: From the repo root...
chunks.text: touch ./docker/requirements-local.txt Add the driver selected in the step above: echo "py-hive-iomete" >> ./docker/requirements-local.txt Rebuild your local image with the new driver baked in: docker-compose build --force-rm After the rebuild of the Docker images is complete (which make take a few minutes), you can relaunch using the following command: docker-compose up The other option is to start Superset via Docker Compose using the recipe in `docker-compose-non-dev.yml`, which will use pre-built frontend assets and skip the building of front-end assets: docker-compose -f docker-compose-non-dev.yml pull docker-compose -f docker-compose-non-dev.yml up

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connect to iomete
chunks.text: Now that you've got a `py-hive-iomete` driver installed locally, you should be able to test it out. We can now create a Datasource in Superset that can be used to connect the iomete lakehouse. Assuming your Lakehouse cluster is running and can be accessed.

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Get connection details from iomete
chunks.text: For connection details, go to the iomete app, select the lakehouse you want to connect to, and in the **Connection details,** you will find all the required information. Change highlighted parameters: - `access_token`: Generated Tokens are used instead of password for connecting to lakehouse. - Database: `default` database is specified in the connection string. If you want to use other database change it.

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Add a connection to Superset
chunks.text: Use the following connection string in “SQL Alchemy URI”, by going to Sources > Databases > + icon (to add a new datasource) in Superset.

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connection template
chunks.text: iomete://admin:@dev.iomete.cloud/default?lakehouse=demo Then click “Test Connection”, which should give you an `OK` message. If not, please look at your terminal for error messages, and reach out for help.

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Add dataset
chunks.text: Once connected to iomete, we can add datasets from iomete to Superset and create charts.

chunks.title: Apache Superset - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Create chart
chunks.text: Click on the added dataset to create a sample chart That’s all! Repeat the same process to add other datasets and enjoy the rich set of chart libraries of Superset.

chunks.title: Metabase
chunks.heading: Connecting Metabase to IOMETE
chunks.text: Metabase is an open-source business intelligence tool that lets teams build dashboards and explore data without writing SQL. It also supports SQL queries for advanced users. This guide walks you through connecting Metabase to your IOMETE compute cluster.

chunks.title: Metabase
chunks.heading: Running Metabase Locally
chunks.text: Skip this section if you already have a Metabase instance running. You can run Metabase locally using Docker: docker pull metabase/metabase:latest docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name metabase metabase/metabase Metabase will be available at `http://localhost:3000`. See the Metabase installation docs for other deployment options.

chunks.title: Metabase
chunks.heading: Adding IOMETE as a Data Source
chunks.text: You can add IOMETE during the initial Metabase setup or later from **Admin Settings**. 1. Select **Spark SQL** as your database type. 2. Fill in the connection fields using values from the compute cluster details page in the IOMETE console. Host: Value \. Port: Value \. Database: Value \. Username (User ID): Value \. Password: Value \. Additional JDBC options: Value ;transportMode=http;ssl=true;httpPath=data-plane//lakehouse/. 3. After connecting, Metabase syncs metadata from IOMETE. You can track progress in the bottom-right corner.

chunks.title: Metabase
chunks.heading: Exploring Data and Building Dashboards
chunks.text: Once the sync completes, your tables appear in the Metabase database explorer. From here you can create dashboards and visualizations.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The IOMETE Power BI connector connects Power BI to IOMETE through the IOMETE Arrow Flight SQL ODBC driver. It adds an **IOMETE Arrow Flight Connector** data source to Power BI and supports both Import and DirectQuery. You build reports in Power BI Desktop. To refresh published reports from the Power BI Service, you also install the driver and connector on an on-premises data gateway. Both setups use the same connector bundle. If you need the older Thrift Server connection instead, see Power BI (Thrift).

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text: Before you begin, make sure you have: - A running IOMETE compute cluster - An IOMETE username and personal access token - Administrator access to every Windows machine where you install the driver: your Power BI Desktop machine and, for scheduled refresh, every gateway node - Power BI Desktop, and for scheduled refresh, an on-premises data gateway. DirectQuery through a gateway requires standard mode.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Downloading the Connector Bundle
chunks.text: 1. Download **`iomete-odbc-connector.zip`** from the iomete-artifacts repository. 2. Extract the ZIP file. It contains `IOMETEConnector.mez`, the Power BI connector, and `arrow-odbc-iomete.zip`, the ODBC driver.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Installing the ODBC Driver
chunks.text: Install the driver on every machine that runs IOMETE queries: your Power BI Desktop machine and every gateway node. 1. Extract **`arrow-odbc-iomete.zip`** to `C:\Program Files\IOMETE Connector`. 2. In `C:\Program Files\IOMETE Connector\arrow-odbc-iomete`, right-click **`register-arrow-odbc-iomete`** and select **Run as administrator**. The script registers the driver with Windows.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connecting From Power BI Desktop
chunks.text: 1. Copy **`IOMETEConnector.mez`** to `C:\Users\ \Documents\Power BI Desktop\Custom Connectors`, replacing ` ` with your Windows username. Create the folder if it does not exist, then restart Power BI Desktop. 2. In Power BI Desktop, select **Get Data** → **More...**, search for **IOMETE Arrow Flight Connector**, and select **Connect**. If the connector is not listed, see Troubleshooting. 3. Fill in the connection settings and select **OK**. 4. Enter your IOMETE username and access token, and select **Connect**. The Navigator then lists the catalogs and tables you can access, and you can start building your report.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connection Settings
chunks.text: Server URL: Value Host and port of your IOMETE Arrow Flight endpoint, Example dev.iomete.com:443. Cluster: Value Name of the compute cluster, Example medium-cluster. Data Plane: Value Kubernetes namespace where the compute cluster runs, Example spark-resources. Certificate Path: Value Optional. Leave blank to use the Windows certificate store. See Trusting the Server Certificate., Example C:\certs\iomete-ca.pem. Data Connectivity mode: Value Import copies data into the report; DirectQuery queries IOMETE live, Example DirectQuery.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Refreshing Through an On-premises Data Gateway
chunks.text: The Power BI Service refreshes published reports through the on-premises data gateway, so every gateway node needs the driver and the connector. The gateway runs as a Windows service, `NT SERVICE\PBIEgwService` by default, so it cannot see files in your user profile or certificates in your personal certificate store.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Setting Up Each Gateway Node
chunks.text: Repeat these steps on every node of the gateway cluster, and use the same connector version everywhere: 1. Install the ODBC driver. 2. Copy **`IOMETEConnector.mez`** to a folder the gateway service account can read, for example `C:\Program Files\IOMETE Connector\Custom Connectors`. 3. In the on-premises data gateway app, open **Connectors**, and under **Load custom data connectors from folder**, select that folder. `IOMETEConnector` then appears in the list of loaded connectors. 4. Make sure the node trusts the IOMETE server certificate. See Trusting the Server Certificate. 5. Restart the gateway from **Service Settings** in the gateway app. Then, once per gateway cluster, allow custom connectors in the Power BI Service. Go to **Settings** → **Manage connections and gateways** → **On-premises data gateways**, open your gateway cluster's **Settings**, and select **Allow user's custom data connectors to refresh through this gateway cluster**.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Creating the Gateway Connection
chunks.text: The gateway matches a connection to a report on **Server URL**, **Cluster**, and **Data Plane**, so the connection must use exactly the values in your report. The easiest way to get them right is to start from the published report: 1. Publish your report to the Power BI Service and open its semantic model's settings. 2. Under **Gateway and cloud connections**, expand your gateway cluster, and next to the IOMETE data source, select **Manually add to gateway**. Power BI opens a new connection with **IOMETE Arrow Flight Connector** selected and the **Server URL**, **Cluster**, and **Data Plane** copied from your report. Leave **Certificate Path** blank. 3. Select **Basic** authentication and enter your IOMETE username and access token. 4. Create the connection. Power BI tests it before saving. 5. Back in **Gateway and cloud connections**, map the IOMETE data source to the new connection, and select **Apply**. You can also create the connection from **Settings** → **Manage connections and gateways**, but then you must type the values exactly as they appear in your report. The connection test always uses the gateway node's Windows certificate store, even when your report sets a **Certificate Path**. If your nodes trust the server only through

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Creating the Gateway Connection
chunks.text: in your report. The connection test always uses the gateway node's Windows certificate store, even when your report sets a **Certificate Path**. If your nodes trust the server only through a PEM file, the test fails, so select **Skip test connection** before creating the connection. Scheduled refresh still uses the **Certificate Path** from your report.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Trusting the Server Certificate
chunks.text: The driver always verifies the TLS certificate of your IOMETE server. **Certificate Path** only decides which certificate authority (CA) the driver trusts for that check. It is not a client certificate and never contains a private key. Blank (recommended): The driver trusts The certificates already in the Windows certificate store, Use it when The root CA that issued your server certificate is in the Windows certificate store. Path to a PEM file: The driver trusts Only the certificates in that file, Use it when You cannot change the Windows certificate store, or you want to trust a single CA. The driver only uses root CA certificates that are already in the store. Browsers work differently: Windows downloads a publicly trusted root CA the first time a browser needs it. So a newly installed machine, such as a fresh gateway node, can fail to verify a certificate from a public CA that every browser accepts. To check, run `certlm.msc` and look under **Trusted Root Certification Authorities** → **Certificates** for the root CA named by the OpenSSL command below. If the root CA is missing, whether it's public or your organization's own, import it into **Trusted Root Certification Authorities** for the **local

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Trusting the Server Certificate
chunks.text: CA named by the OpenSSL command below. If the root CA is missing, whether it's public or your organization's own, import it into **Trusted Root Certification Authorities** for the **local computer**. Do this in `certlm.msc`, or from an administrator PowerShell window: Import-Certificate -FilePath C:\certs\root-ca.pem -CertStoreLocation Cert:\LocalMachine\Root The local computer store works for both Power BI Desktop and the gateway service account, whereas the current user store is invisible to the gateway. If you use a PEM file instead, it must contain the root CA certificate as Base64 text starting with `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----`. Put the file at the same path on every machine that runs the report, including every gateway node, and make sure the user running Power BI or the gateway service can read it. To see which CA issued your server certificate, run this from any machine with OpenSSL, replacing ` : ` with your **Server URL**. If your Server URL has no port, the connector uses `443`. The last `i:` line names the root CA: openssl s_client -connect : -showcerts </dev/null | grep -E 's:|i:'

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Upgrading From an Earlier Connector Version
chunks.text: Connector versions earlier than `24.0.0-iomete.2` required **Certificate Path** and could not be used with an on-premises data gateway. To check which version you have, open the connection dialog in Power BI Desktop: if the field reads **Certificate Path** instead of **Certificate Path (optional)**, you have an earlier version. After you replace `IOMETEConnector.mez` with the current version: - Power BI Desktop asks for your credentials again the next time you refresh. You can remove the old entry under **File** → **Options and settings** → **Data source settings**. - Recreate any gateway connections that were created with the earlier version. - Republish reports that you edit in Power BI Desktop. A report published with an earlier version keeps its old data source until you republish it, so it cannot be mapped to a connection created with the current version. - Earlier versions ignored **Certificate Path** and always used the Windows certificate store. The current version uses the file you enter, so if your reports pass a path that does not point to a valid PEM file, clear it or fix the file before you refresh.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Upgrading From an Earlier Connector Version
chunks.text: a valid PEM file, clear it or fix the file before you refresh.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.text: When a report works in Power BI Desktop but fails through the gateway, the cause is usually something installed for your Windows user instead of for the gateway service account. Check the gateway node setup first.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Power BI Desktop Does Not List the Connector
chunks.text: - Check that `IOMETEConnector.mez` is in `Documents\Power BI Desktop\Custom Connectors`, and restart Power BI Desktop after copying it. If your Documents folder is redirected to OneDrive, use that Documents folder. - Power BI Desktop blocks uncertified connectors by default. Go to **File** → **Options and settings** → **Options** → **Security**, and under **Data Extensions**, select **(Not Recommended) Allow any extension to load without validation or warning**. Select **OK** and restart Power BI Desktop.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connection Fails With "Could not finish writing before closing"
chunks.text: The driver shows this generic error when the connection closes before login finishes, and the real cause isn't passed on. It most often means a wrong **Server URL**, **Cluster**, or **Data Plane**, such as a data plane that doesn't contain the cluster. It can also come from an invalid access token or an untrusted server certificate. Check the three connection values first, then your credentials, then Trusting the Server Certificate.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connection Fails With "No client transport implementation for arrow-flight-reuse-connection"
chunks.text: ODBC driver versions earlier than `24.0.0-iomete.3` show this error on IOMETE 4.0 and later, in both **Test Connection** and queries. Download and install the current driver.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: "Data source name not found and no default driver specified"
chunks.text: The ODBC driver is not registered on the machine running the query. Install the ODBC driver on that machine. For gateway refreshes, install it on every gateway node.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Saving Gateway Credentials Fails
chunks.text: Power BI tests the connection on a gateway node before it saves the credentials, so the test depends on that node's setup, not on your Desktop machine. The banner only says that Power BI was unable to connect to the data source. Expand it to see the driver's error. - **"3 arguments were passed to a function that expects 4"**: the node runs an earlier connector version. Install the current `IOMETEConnector.mez` on every gateway node, restart the gateway, and recreate the connection. See Upgrading From an Earlier Connector Version. - **Any other error**: check that the driver is registered on every node and that the server's CA is in the **local computer** certificate store. If your nodes trust the server only through a PEM file, the test cannot pass, so select **Skip test connection**.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: IOMETE Arrow Flight Connector Is Not Listed as a Connection Type
chunks.text: The gateway hasn't loaded the connector, or the cluster doesn't allow custom connectors. In the gateway app, check that **Connectors** lists `IOMETEConnector`. In the Power BI Service, check that **Allow user's custom data connectors to refresh through this gateway cluster** is selected in the gateway cluster's settings. Then wait a minute for the gateway to report in, and reload the page. See Setting Up Each Gateway Node.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Refresh Does Not Use the Gateway Connection
chunks.text: If the semantic model settings show the IOMETE data source without a mapped connection, the **Server URL**, **Cluster**, or **Data Plane** on the gateway connection differs from the values in your report. They must match character for character, including the port, so `dev.iomete.com` and `dev.iomete.com:443` count as different data sources. Recreate the connection with **Manually add to gateway**, as described in Creating the Gateway Connection.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connection Fails With "Could not open certificate"
chunks.text: The file in **Certificate Path** does not exist or cannot be read on the machine running the query. On a gateway, that means every gateway node, and the gateway service account needs read access to the file. Fix the path, or clear **Certificate Path** to use the Windows certificate store.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connection Fails With a Certificate Verification Error
chunks.text: The driver could not verify the server certificate. Check that: - The CA that issued the server certificate is trusted where the query runs. On a gateway, it must be in the **local computer** store, because the gateway cannot see your user store. - A PEM file in **Certificate Path** contains the CA certificate, not the server's own certificate, and is Base64 text starting with `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----`. - **Server URL** uses the host name on the server certificate, not an IP address or an alias the certificate does not cover. See Trusting the Server Certificate.

chunks.title: Power BI (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Sign-in Fails
chunks.text: Check your IOMETE username and that your personal access token has not expired or been revoked. The gateway stores its own copy of the credentials, so after you rotate a token, update the credentials on the gateway connection as well.

chunks.title: Power BI (Thrift ODBC) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Power BI (Thrift ODBC) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.text: If you need to connect to the default Spark Catalog, and work with Iceberg and Metastore tables, please refer to Power BI (Thrift) documentation. However, if you need to connect to an additional Spark Catalog, you must use the ODBC driver. This guide will show you how to connect Power BI to IOMETE using the ODBC driver. Let’s get started.

chunks.title: Power BI (Thrift ODBC) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Create ODBC Data Source
chunks.text: First, you need to create an ODBC Data Source. Go to the Windows search bar and type `ODBC Data Sources` and click on the `ODBC Data Sources (64-bit)`. This will open the ODBC Data Source Administrator. Click on the `User DSN` tab and then click on the `Add` button. Choose the "Simba Spark ODBC Driver" from the list of drivers and click `Finish`. If you don't see the driver in the list, you can download it from the Simba website or contact us for assistance.

chunks.title: Power BI (Thrift ODBC) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Data Source Details
chunks.text: Please refer to the IOMETE Platform to get the connection details. Go to the Lakehouse you want to connect and open Power BI tab in the Connections section. Now, fill in the connection details in the ODBC Data Source Administrator as shown below. Optionally, you can click on the `Advanced` button and add additional properties. Finally, click on the `Test` button to verify the connection. If everything is correct, you will see a success message.

chunks.title: Power BI (Thrift ODBC) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connecting Power BI
chunks.text: Click “Get Data” from the menu and select `ODBC` as a data source. Then choose the ODBC Data Source you created and click `Connect`. After clicking the `OK` button, you will be directed to an authentication page where you can establish a connection and input your username and password. You will need to create a Personal Access Token and use as the password. Now in the next step, you will see your databases and tables. Select the tables you want to use in Power BI. You will have to wait a couple of minutes before Power BI will load the data sets. Congratulations, you have successfully connected Power BI to IOMETE. From this point, you can create, save and publish your reports. You can learn how to create dashboards and detailed visualizations with Power BI resources. Thanks.

chunks.title: Power BI - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Choose a Connection Method
chunks.text: IOMETE supports three ways to connect Power BI. Choose the guide that matches the connector and protocol you want to use. Arrow Flight (recommended): Connector IOMETE Arrow Flight ODBC connector, Guide Arrow Flight. Thrift: Connector Power BI's built-in Spark connector, Guide Thrift. Thrift ODBC: Connector Simba Spark ODBC driver, Guide Thrift ODBC.

chunks.heading: Power BI (Thrift) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.text: This guide explains how to effortlessly integrate IOMETE with yet another popular BI tool: Power BI. Let’s get started. First, you have to add a new Data Source. Click “Get Data” from the menu and select Spark as a data source. In the next Form, you will need to add connection details like in the screenshot below. For protocol, select HTTP, and in Data Connectivity mode select Import. Important Power BI recommends to use **Import** for connectivity mode. For relatively large data or real-time streaming switch to **DirectQuery** mode. Read more about connectivity modes and their use cases here . To fill in these values you can go to the IOMETE Platform and copy connection details from the lakehouse you are trying to connect. Switch to the Power BI tab in the Connections section and copy the `Server` parameter. After clicking the `OK` button, you will be directed to an authentication page where you can establish a connection and input your username and password. To fill in these values you can go to the IOMETE Platform and copy connection details from the lakehouse you are trying to connect. Switch to the Power BI tab in the Connections section and check

chunks.text: can go to the IOMETE Platform and copy connection details from the lakehouse you are trying to connect. chunks.text: Redash is an open-source business intelligence platform for data visualization and collaboration. It connects to various data sources, lets you write queries, and share dashboards with your team. This guide walks you through connecting Redash to your IOMETE compute cluster.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The IOMETE Tableau connector connects Tableau to IOMETE through the Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver. It adds an **IOMETE (Arrow Flight SQL)** connection dialog to Tableau and supports both live connections and extracts. The connector and JDBC driver are installed separately. If you need the older Thrift Server connection instead, see Tableau (Thrift).

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Supported Setup
chunks.text: Tableau: Supported value Desktop or Server 2024.2 and later. Platforms: Supported value Windows, macOS, and Linux. Connection modes: Supported value Live and extract. Authentication: Supported value IOMETE username and access token. Transport: Supported value JDBC with TLS.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text: Before you begin, make sure you have: - A running IOMETE compute cluster - An IOMETE username and personal access token - Administrator access to the computer or Tableau Server nodes where you install the connector - Tableau Desktop or Tableau Server 2024.2 or later

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Downloading the Connector and Driver
chunks.text: Download these files before installing the connector: 1. Open the Tableau connector releases page and select the latest `tableau-connector-v*` release. 2. Download the `.taco` connector, `iomete-taco.cer`, and `SHA256SUMS` files from that release. 3. Download the latest IOMETE Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver from the iomete-artifacts repository. Driver files follow the naming convention `flight-sql-jdbc-driver- -iomete. .jar`. The `.taco` file does not include the JDBC driver, so Tableau needs both files in their respective installation directories.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Installing on Tableau Desktop
chunks.text: Place the files in the directories for your operating system: macOS: .taco connector ~/Documents/My Tableau Repository/Connectors/, JDBC driver ~/Library/Tableau/Drivers/. Windows: .taco connector C:\Users\[user]\Documents\My Tableau Repository\Connectors, JDBC driver C:\Program Files\Tableau\Drivers. Create a missing directory if needed, then restart Tableau Desktop after installing or replacing either file.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Installing on Tableau Server
chunks.text: Place the connector and driver in these directories on every Tableau Server node: Linux: .taco connector /opt/tableau/connectors, JDBC driver /opt/tableau/tableau_driver/jdbc. Windows: .taco connector C:\Program Files\Tableau\Connectors, JDBC driver C:\Program Files\Tableau\Drivers. On Linux, create `/opt/tableau/connectors` only if it is missing, then copy both files: sudo mkdir -p /opt/tableau/connectors /opt/tableau/tableau_driver/jdbc sudo cp "/path/to/ .taco" /opt/tableau/connectors/ sudo cp "/path/to/ .jar" /opt/tableau/tableau_driver/jdbc/ Check the Tableau Server run-as username: tsm configuration get -k service.runas.username The following commands use `tableau`, the default run-as username. Replace it if the previous command returns another username: sudo chown tableau:tableau "/opt/tableau/connectors/ .taco" sudo chown tableau:tableau "/opt/tableau/tableau_driver/jdbc/ .jar" Files copied as `root` may remain `640 root:root`, which prevents the run-as user from loading them.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Trusting the Connector Certificate
chunks.text: IOMETE currently signs the `.taco` file with a self-signed certificate. Tableau does not trust that certificate automatically, so import `iomete-taco.cer` into Tableau's Java truststore before opening the connector. The same certificate signs each self-signed release. You only need to import it again if IOMETE rotates the certificate or a Tableau upgrade replaces the truststore. If the certificate import does not work in a test environment, see Testing With Signature Verification Disabled.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: macOS Desktop
chunks.text: Set `TABLEAU_JRE` to the JRE inside your Tableau application. The following example uses Tableau Desktop 2026.2 for Apple silicon, so adjust the application name and version for your installation: TABLEAU_JRE="/Applications/Tableau Desktop (Apple silicon) 2026.2.app/Contents/Plugins/jre" sudo cp "$TABLEAU_JRE/lib/security/cacerts" "$TABLEAU_JRE/lib/security/cacerts.bak" sudo keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias iomete-taco \ -file /path/to/iomete-taco.cer \ -keystore "$TABLEAU_JRE/lib/security/cacerts" -storepass changeit

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Windows Desktop
chunks.text: Run PowerShell as Administrator and adjust the Tableau version in the path: $TableauJre = 'C:\Program Files\Tableau\Tableau \Plugins\jre' Copy-Item "$TableauJre\lib\security\cacerts" "$TableauJre\lib\security\cacerts.bak" keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias iomete-taco ` -file C:\path\to\iomete-taco.cer ` -keystore "$TableauJre\lib\security\cacerts" -storepass changeit Restart Tableau Desktop after importing the certificate.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Tableau Server on Linux
chunks.text: Identify the running version and list every candidate truststore: tsm version find /opt/tableau/tableau_server -name cacerts Match the running version to its `repository. ` directory. If unsure, import the certificate into every `cacerts` under the current build. Run the following commands with root privileges, replacing ` ` with the current build directory name: JRE="/opt/tableau/tableau_server/packages/repository. /jre" sudo cp -p "$JRE/lib/security/cacerts" "$JRE/lib/security/cacerts.bak" sudo "$JRE/bin/keytool" -importcert -noprompt -alias iomete-taco \ -file /path/to/iomete-taco.cer \ -keystore "$JRE/lib/security/cacerts" -storepass changeit Verify the alias and compare the truststore with the backup: "$JRE/bin/keytool" -list -keystore "$JRE/lib/security/cacerts" \ -storepass changeit -alias iomete-taco ls -l "$JRE/lib/security/cacerts" "$JRE/lib/security/cacerts.bak" The truststore ownership should remain `root:root`. Its mode should match the backup, normally `644`, so Tableau services can read it. Do not change the owner to the Tableau Server run-as user. Restart Tableau Server and wait for every service to return to a healthy state: tsm restart tsm status -v Repeat these steps on every node in a multi-node cluster. A Tableau upgrade creates a new `repository. ` directory, so repeat the certificate import after each upgrade.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Tableau Server on Windows
chunks.text: Run PowerShell as Administrator. Check the running version and find the truststores under the default installation directory: tsm version Get-ChildItem 'C:\Program Files\Tableau\Tableau Server' -Filter cacerts -Recurse Adjust the base path for a custom installation. Match the running version to its `repository. ` directory, then replace ` ` below: $TableauJre = 'C:\Program Files\Tableau\Tableau Server\packages\repository. \jre' Copy-Item "$TableauJre\lib\security\cacerts" "$TableauJre\lib\security\cacerts.bak" & "$TableauJre\bin\keytool.exe" -importcert -noprompt -alias iomete-taco ` -file C:\path\to\iomete-taco.cer ` -keystore "$TableauJre\lib\security\cacerts" -storepass changeit & "$TableauJre\bin\keytool.exe" -list ` -keystore "$TableauJre\lib\security\cacerts" ` -storepass changeit -alias iomete-taco Restart Tableau Server and confirm that its services are healthy: tsm restart tsm status -v Repeat the import for every current-build truststore, on every node, and after each Tableau upgrade.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.text: 1. Start Tableau and open **Connect > To a Server > More**. 2. Select **IOMETE (Arrow Flight SQL)**. 3. Complete the connection dialog: Server: What to enter Your IOMETE hostname without https://. Port: What to enter 443, unless your deployment uses another port. Compute Cluster: What to enter The name of your running IOMETE compute cluster. Namespace: What to enter Your IOMETE namespace name. Catalog: What to enter Optional. Leave blank to browse all accessible catalogs, or enter a catalog to limit discovery. Username: What to enter Your IOMETE username. Access Token: What to enter Your IOMETE personal access token. Query Timeout: What to enter Optional. Maximum query duration in seconds; blank means no timeout. Connection Timeout: What to enter Optional. Connection timeout in seconds; blank uses the driver's 10-second default. Client Thread Pool Size: What to enter Optional. Number of parallel Flight endpoint workers; blank uses the driver default of 1. Disable Certificate Verification: What to enter Leave off unless the IOMETE endpoint uses a certificate Tableau does not trust. TLS encryption is always enabled. **Disable Certificate Verification** skips validation of the IOMETE server's TLS certificate, but it does not disable encryption or bypass `.taco` signature verification. 4. Confirm

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.text: trust. TLS encryption is always enabled. **Disable Certificate Verification** skips validation of the IOMETE server's TLS certificate, but it does not disable encryption or bypass `.taco` signature verification. 4. Confirm that the compute cluster is running, then select **Sign In**. 5. Select a catalog and schema, then drag tables onto the canvas to start building a data source. With the connection in place, continue to Building a Dashboard.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Testing With Signature Verification Disabled
chunks.text: If you cannot edit Tableau's truststore in a test environment, you can temporarily disable connector signature verification. Testing only Disabling signature verification allows Tableau to load any unsigned or untrusted connector. Do not use this setting as a permanent alternative to trusting `iomete-taco.cer`. On macOS, adjust the Tableau application name and version first: TABLEAU_APP="/Applications/Tableau Desktop (Apple silicon) 2026.2.app" "$TABLEAU_APP/Contents/MacOS/Tableau" \ -DDisableVerifyConnectorPluginSignature=true On Windows, run: & 'C:\Program Files\Tableau\Tableau \bin\tableau.exe' ` '-DDisableVerifyConnectorPluginSignature=true' On Tableau Server, disable verification through TSM and apply the pending change: tsm configuration set -k native_api.disable_verify_connector_plugin_signature -v true --force-keys tsm pending-changes apply The Desktop flags last only for that launch, but the TSM setting survives restarts. Re-enable verification as soon as the test finishes: tsm configuration set -k native_api.disable_verify_connector_plugin_signature -v false --force-keys tsm pending-changes apply

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: The Connector Does Not Appear
chunks.text: Confirm that the `.taco` file is in the correct connector directory and restart Tableau. If the connector still does not appear, import `iomete-taco.cer` into Tableau's JRE truststore or use the testing-only signature verification bypass.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Tableau Cannot Find the Driver
chunks.text: Confirm that the latest `flight-sql-jdbc-driver- -iomete. .jar` file is in the driver directory for the computer or Tableau Server node running the connection. On Tableau Server, check every node.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: The Connection Fails
chunks.text: Confirm that: - The compute cluster is running. - The server, port, compute cluster, and namespace match your IOMETE deployment. - The username and access token are valid. - The IOMETE endpoint's TLS certificate is trusted. Use **Disable Certificate Verification** only to diagnose a certificate validation problem.

chunks.title: Tableau (Arrow Flight) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Package Signature Verification Failed During Connection Creation
chunks.text: If Tableau reports `Package signature verification failed during connection creation.`, set these variables to the current Linux build and installed connector: JRE="/opt/tableau/tableau_server/packages/repository. /jre" TACO="/opt/tableau/connectors/ .taco" Then check the following: - Run the alias verification command against every `cacerts` under the current Tableau build. - Compare each truststore's mode with its `.bak` file and keep the owner as `root:root`. If the modes differ, run `sudo chmod --reference="$JRE/lib/security/cacerts.bak" "$JRE/lib/security/cacerts"`. - Confirm that the downloaded certificate matches the certificate embedded in the `.taco`. The two SHA256 fingerprints must match, and `jarsigner` must report `jar verified`: keytool -printcert -file /path/to/iomete-taco.cer | grep SHA256 "$JRE/bin/keytool" -printcert -jarfile "$TACO" | grep SHA256 "$JRE/bin/jarsigner" -verify -verbose -certs "$TACO" Tableau also requires a valid timestamp. If `jarsigner` reports that the signature does not include one, download a corrected `.taco`; importing the certificate cannot add a timestamp. - Run `tsm restart`, then confirm that services are healthy with `tsm status -v`. - Use Testing With Signature Verification Disabled only to confirm that signature verification is the failing step. Re-enable it immediately after the test. The connection dialog's **Disable Certificate Verification** checkbox does not bypass `.taco` signature verification. It only disables validation of the IOMETE endpoint's TLS certificate.
