chunks.title: Tableau - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Choose a Connection Method
chunks.text: IOMETE supports two ways to connect Tableau. Choose the guide that matches the protocol you want to use. Arrow Flight (recommended): Connector IOMETE Arrow Flight SQL connector, Guide Arrow Flight. Thrift: Connector Tableau's built-in Spark SQL connector or the CData Spark SQL connector, Guide Thrift.

chunks.title: Tableau - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Building a Dashboard
chunks.text: With either connection in place, you're ready to turn your IOMETE data into visualizations. 1. Select a schema, drag tables into the canvas, then click **Sheet 1** to open a new sheet. 2. Right-click a dimension or measure and select **Add to Sheet**. 3. Drag additional fields into rows, columns, or filters to refine the report. 4. Pick a visualization type and customize the layout to finish your dashboard.

chunks.title: Tableau (Thrift) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: If you're using Tableau for dashboards and reporting, you can point it straight at your IOMETE data. There's no need to copy anything into a separate analytics database. For the Arrow Flight SQL connection, see Tableau (Arrow Flight). Two Thrift connection methods are available: - **Spark SQL driver**: Tableau's built-in Spark SQL connector - **CData Spark SQL connector**: a third-party option from CData Both use the Thrift Server (Hive2 protocol) over HTTP transport, which is enabled by default on every IOMETE compute cluster.

chunks.title: Tableau (Thrift) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text: You'll need a few things in place before connecting Tableau to IOMETE: - A **running IOMETE compute cluster** (setup instructions) - **Tableau Desktop** or **Tableau Cloud** (download Tableau Desktop) - A **Personal Access Token** for authentication, since Tableau doesn't accept regular passwords (how to create one) - For the CData method only: the Spark SQL by CData connector

chunks.title: Tableau (Thrift) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Finding Connection Parameters
chunks.text: You don't need to assemble connection strings by hand. IOMETE generates them for each compute cluster. 1. Open **Compute** from the sidebar. 2. Click the cluster you want to connect. 3. Select the **Connections** tab. 4. Click the **Tableau** card. {/* 📸 SCREENSHOT NEEDED: Compute detail page showing the Connections tab with the Tableau card selected */} You'll see two parameter tables, one for the **Spark SQL Driver** and one for **Spark SQL by CData**. Every value is pre-filled for your environment. Hover over any value and click the copy button to grab it.

chunks.title: Tableau (Thrift) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connecting Using the Spark SQL Driver
chunks.text: This is the simplest path because Tableau ships with a built-in Spark SQL connector. Nothing extra to install. 1. Open Tableau and create a new workbook (or open an existing one). 2. Click **New Data Source**. 3. Go to the **Connectors** tab and select **Spark SQL**. 4. Fill in the Spark SQL connection dialog with these parameters: Connection: Value SparkThriftServer (Spark 1.1 and later). Server: Value Your IOMETE platform hostname (shown as HOST_NAME in the console). Port: Value 443 for HTTPS or 80 for HTTP (shown as PORT in the console). Authentication: Value Username and Password. Username: Value Your IOMETE user ID. Password: Value \. Transport: Value HTTP. HTTP Path: Value /data-plane/\/lakehouse/\. SSL: Value Check Require SSL if your platform uses HTTPS. Personal Access Token Required The **Password** field takes a **Personal Access Token**, not your account password. Generate one under **Settings > Access Tokens** in the IOMETE console. See Creating a Personal Access Token. HTTP Path Format The HTTP Path includes `lakehouse` in the URL (e.g., `/data-plane/default/lakehouse/my-compute`). Copy it exactly as shown in the IOMETE console, including the leading `/`. 5. Click **Sign In**. 6. Once connected, your IOMETE database appears. Select a **Schema** to browse its tables. 7.

chunks.title: Tableau (Thrift) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connecting Using the Spark SQL Driver
chunks.text: exactly as shown in the IOMETE console, including the leading `/`. 5. Click **Sign In**. 6. Once connected, your IOMETE database appears. Select a **Schema** to browse its tables. 7. Drag tables into the canvas to begin building your reports and dashboards.

chunks.title: Tableau (Thrift) - Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.heading: Connecting Using the CData Spark SQL Connector
chunks.text: If you need the extra configuration options that CData offers, use this method instead. It requires a separate connector install. 1. Install Tableau Desktop and the Spark SQL by CData connector. 2. Open Tableau. 3. Click **To a server**, then select **Spark SQL by CData**. 4. Enter the following connection parameters. **General tab:** Server: Value Your IOMETE platform hostname. Port: Value 443 for HTTPS or 80 for HTTP. Auth Scheme: Value Plain. User: Value Your IOMETE user ID. Password: Value \. **Advanced tab:** Transport Mode: Value HTTP. HTTP Path: Value /data-plane/\/lakehouse/\. Use SSL: Value True. Personal Access Token Required The **Password** field takes a **Personal Access Token**, not your account password. See Creating a Personal Access Token. 5. Click **Connect**. With the connection in place, continue to Building a Dashboard.

chunks.title: dbt Configuration Reference
chunks.heading: dbt Configuration Reference
chunks.text: For installation and a complete starter profile, see Getting Started with dbt. **Available Since** identifies the first published `dbt-iomete` version that supports a setting. When a setting gained new values later, its description identifies the newer version.

chunks.title: dbt Configuration Reference
chunks.heading: Profile Settings
chunks.text: Add connection settings under an IOMETE output in `~/.dbt/profiles.yml`. type: Available Since 1.0.0, Required Yes, Default —, Description Adapter type. Set this to iomete.. host: Available Since 1.0.0, Required Yes, Default —, Description IOMETE hostname without the protocol (e.g., example.iomete.com).. port: Available Since 1.0.0, Required No, Default 443, Description IOMETE port.. https: Available Since 1.7.0, Required No, Default true, Description Uses HTTPS when true and HTTP when false.. dataplane: Available Since 1.7.3, Required Yes, Default —, Description IOMETE namespace/data plane name (e.g., iomete-system).. domain: Available Since 1.7.4, Required Yes, Default —, Description IOMETE domain name (e.g., analytics).. lakehouse: Available Since 1.1.0, Required Yes, Default —, Description Compute cluster name.. catalog: Available Since 1.7.7, Required No, Default spark_catalog, Description Default catalog. The adapter also accepts database as the underlying dbt field name.. schema: Available Since 1.0.0, Required Yes, Default —, Description Default database or schema where dbt creates objects. The value cannot contain a period.. user: Available Since 1.0.0, Required Yes, Default —, Description IOMETE username.. token: Available Since 1.4.0, Required Yes, Default —, Description Personal access token. Use an environment variable instead of storing the token in the profile.. threads: Available Since 1.0.0, Required No, Default 1, Description Maximum number

chunks.title: dbt Configuration Reference
chunks.heading: Profile Settings
chunks.text: Yes, Default —, Description Personal access token. Use an environment variable instead of storing the token in the profile.. threads: Available Since 1.0.0, Required No, Default 1, Description Maximum number of dbt model tasks that can run concurrently.. connect_retries: Available Since 1.0.0, Required No, Default 0, Description Number of times to retry a failed connection.. connect_timeout: Available Since 1.0.0, Required No, Default 120, Description Seconds to wait between connection attempts when retries are enabled.. retry_all: Available Since 1.0.0, Required No, Default false, Description Retries every connection error when true. Otherwise, retries apply only to errors reported as pending or temporarily unavailable.. list_relations_threads: Available Since 1.8.2, Required No, Default 100, Description Maximum concurrent DESCRIBE EXTENDED queries used while listing relations. This does not change model-build concurrency.. Use `list_relations_threads` to tune metadata listing separately from model execution. Lower it if relation discovery creates too much load on the data plane: title="~/.dbt/profiles.yml" dbt_project: target: dev outputs: dev: type: iomete # Other connection settings omitted threads: 4 list_relations_threads: 25 connect_retries: 2 connect_timeout: 30 retry_all: false

chunks.title: dbt Configuration Reference
chunks.heading: Model Settings
chunks.text: Set model configuration in a model's `config()` block or under `models` in `dbt_project.yml`. materialized: Available Since 1.0.0, Applies to SQL and Python models, Default view, Description Materialization type. IOMETE supports view, table, and incremental for SQL models, and table and incremental for Python models. Because the default is view, set this explicitly in every Python model.. file_format: Available Since 1.0.0, Applies to SQL tables and incremental models, Default iceberg, Description Spark table provider. Incremental models require iceberg.. location_root: Available Since 1.0.0, Applies to SQL tables, Default —, Description Root storage location. The adapter appends the model alias to this path.. partition_by: Available Since 1.0.0, Applies to SQL tables and incremental models, Default —, Description Column name or list of columns used to partition the table.. clustered_by: Available Since 1.0.0, Applies to SQL tables, Default —, Description Column name or list of columns used to cluster the table. Set buckets with it.. buckets: Available Since 1.0.0, Applies to SQL tables, Default —, Description Number of buckets used with clustered_by. The adapter emits the clustering clause only when both settings are present.. options: Available Since 1.0.0, Applies to SQL tables, Default —, Description Mapping of Spark data source option names to values..

chunks.title: dbt Configuration Reference
chunks.heading: Model Settings
chunks.text: emits the clustering clause only when both settings are present.. options: Available Since 1.0.0, Applies to SQL tables, Default —, Description Mapping of Spark data source option names to values.. tblproperties: Available Since 1.7.9, Applies to SQL tables, views, snapshots, and seeds, Default —, Description Mapping of Spark table property names to values, applied when the relation is created.. persist_docs: Available Since 1.0.0, Applies to Tables and views, Default —, Description Persists relation descriptions and, for Iceberg tables, column descriptions.. This example creates a partitioned Iceberg table with table properties: title="models/events.sql" {{ config( materialized='table', file_format='iceberg', partition_by=['event_date'], tblproperties= ) }} select * from raw.events

chunks.title: dbt Configuration Reference
chunks.heading: Incremental Model Settings
chunks.text: Incremental models support the following additional settings. See Incremental Models for behavior, constraints, and examples. incremental_strategy: Available Since 1.0.0, Default merge, Description merge and append are available from 1.0.0; delete+insert and insert_overwrite are available from 1.8.3.. unique_key: Available Since 1.0.0, Default —, Description Column name or list of columns that identifies target rows for merge or delete+insert. Lists containing multiple columns are available from 1.7.7. Without a key, both strategies insert every source row.. on_schema_change: Available Since 1.0.0, Default ignore, Description Controls how dbt handles source and target column differences. Supports ignore, fail, append_new_columns, and sync_all_columns.. incremental_predicates: Available Since 1.7.9, Default —, Description List of predicates that limits target rows considered by merge or deleted by delete+insert. predicates is an alias.. merge_update_columns: Available Since 1.0.0, Default All columns, Description List of columns to update when a row matches.. merge_exclude_columns: Available Since 1.7.7, Default —, Description List of columns to exclude from matched-row updates. Do not combine this with merge_update_columns..

chunks.title: dbt Configuration Reference
chunks.heading: Python Model Settings
chunks.text: Python models run through an existing IOMETE Spark job and always write Iceberg tables. SQL-only table settings such as `location_root`, `clustered_by`, and `options` do not apply. spark_job_id: Available Since 1.7.1, Required Yes, Default —, Description ID of the IOMETE Spark job used to run the compiled Python model.. spark_job_overrides: Available Since 1.7.1, Required No, Default , Description Per-run overrides containing arguments, envVars, or sparkConf.. Replace `YOUR_SPARK_JOB_ID` with the ID of an existing IOMETE Spark job: title="models/my_python_model.py" def model(dbt, spark): dbt.config( materialized="table", spark_job_id="YOUR_SPARK_JOB_ID", spark_job_overrides={ "arguments": ["--environment", "production"], "envVars": , "sparkConf": , }, ) return dbt.ref("source_model")

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.text: Incremental models on IOMETE use Iceberg tables and support `append`, `merge`, `delete+insert`, and `insert_overwrite`. This page walks through every supported configuration with working SQL examples and shows the table state after each run. For how incremental models work and when to use them, see incremental models.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Incremental Models Configurations
chunks.text: Incremental models are trickier to get right than views or tables, so it helps to see every knob in one place before working through examples. The tables below summarize the configurations DBT exposes for incremental models on IOMETE. file_format: Default value iceberg, Expected values iceberg (only supported value). incremental_strategy: Default value merge, Expected values append, merge, delete+insert, insert_overwrite. on_schema_change: Default value ignore, Expected values ignore, append_new_columns, sync_all_columns, fail. **Incremental Strategies** append: Description Each run appends new rows to the table. Example: _append_. merge: Description Each run merges new rows with existing rows. Example: _merge-with-unique_key_. delete+insert: Description Each run deletes matching keys, then inserts the current result. Example: delete+insert. insert_overwrite: Description Each run replaces affected partitions. Example: insert_overwrite. **Strategy-Specific Settings** unique_key: Applies to merge, delete+insert, Behavior Identifies matching target rows. Without it, both strategies append every row. Examples: _merge without unique_key_, _merge with unique_key_, and delete+insert.. merge_update_columns: Applies to merge, Behavior Updates only the listed columns. Without it, every column is updated. Example: _merge with update columns_.. merge_exclude_columns: Applies to merge, Behavior Skips the listed columns and updates all others. Without it, every column is updated. Example: _merge with excluded columns_.. incremental_predicates: Applies to merge, delete+insert, Behavior Limits target rows scanned

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Incremental Models Configurations
chunks.text: Behavior Skips the listed columns and updates all others. Without it, every column is updated. Example: _merge with excluded columns_.. incremental_predicates: Applies to merge, delete+insert, Behavior Limits target rows scanned by merge or deleted by delete+insert. Example: _merge with incremental predicates_.. **Schema Changes** ignore: Description Ignores schema changes. Example: _ignore_. append_new_columns: Description Adds new fields and keeps removed ones. Example: _append-new-columns_. sync_all_columns: Description Adds new fields and drops missing ones. Example: _sync-all-columns_. fail: Description Fails the run when a schema change is detected. Example: _fail_.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Examples
chunks.text: Each example below pairs the SQL you'd write with the table state you'd see after each run. Pick the one that matches your use case as a starting template.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Append
chunks.text: title="models/incremental_strategies/models_iceberg/append.sql" {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'append' ) }} select cast(1 as bigint) as id, 'hello' as msg union all select cast(2 as bigint) as id, 'goodbye' as msg select cast(2 as bigint) as id, 'yo' as msg union all select cast(3 as bigint) as id, 'anyway' as msg Results

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 1st run

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 2nd run
chunks.text: > select * from append order by id +-----+----------+ +-----+----------+ 2: hello yo. 2: hello goodbye. 3: hello anyway. +-----+----------+ ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Delete+Insert
chunks.text: Use this strategy when the current result can contain duplicate `unique_key` values. title="models/incremental_strategies/models_iceberg/delete_insert_unique_key.sql" {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'delete+insert', unique_key = 'id' ) }} select cast(1 as bigint) as id, 'hello' as msg union all select cast(2 as bigint) as id, 'goodbye' as msg select cast(2 as bigint) as id, 'yo' as msg union all select cast(2 as bigint) as id, 'again' as msg union all select cast(3 as bigint) as id, 'anyway' as msg Results

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 2nd run
chunks.text: +-----+----------+ +-----+----------+ 2: hello yo. 2: hello again. 3: hello anyway. +-----+----------+ The delete and insert are separate statements. If the insert fails, rerun the model or perform a full refresh. ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Insert Overwrite
chunks.text: This example replaces only the dates present in the second run. Rows in other partitions stay unchanged. title="models/incremental_strategies/models_iceberg/insert_overwrite_partitions.sql" {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'insert_overwrite', partition_by = 'event_date' ) }} select 1 as id, date '2026-09-01' as event_date, 'keep' as msg union all select 2 as id, date '2026-09-02' as event_date, 'old' as msg select 3 as id, date '2026-09-02' as event_date, 'replacement' as msg Results

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 2nd run

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Merge Without unique_key
chunks.text: Without a merge key, the strategy quietly degrades to **append** mode. title="models/incremental_strategies/models_iceberg/merge_no_key.sql" {} select cast(1 as bigint) as id, 'hello' as msg union all select cast(2 as bigint) as id, 'goodbye' as msg select cast(2 as bigint) as id, 'yo' as msg union all select cast(3 as bigint) as id, 'anyway' as msg Results

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 1st run

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 2nd run
chunks.text: > select * from merge_no_key order by id; +-----+----------+ +-----+----------+ 2: hello yo. 2: hello goodbye. 3: hello anyway. +-----+----------+ ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Merge With unique_key
chunks.text: title="models/incremental_strategies/models_iceberg/merge_unique_key.sql" {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'merge', unique_key = 'id', ) }} select cast(1 as bigint) as id, 'hello' as msg union all select cast(2 as bigint) as id, 'goodbye' as msg select cast(2 as bigint) as id, 'yo' as msg union all select cast(3 as bigint) as id, 'anyway' as msg Results

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 1st run
chunks.text: > select * from merge_unique_key order by id; +-----+----------+ +-----+----------+ 2: hello goodbye. +-----+----------+

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 2nd run
chunks.text: > select * from merge_unique_key order by id; +-----+---------+ +-----+---------+ 2: hello yo. 3: hello anyway. +-----+---------+ ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 1st run

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: pay attention to id=2: msg changed, color unchanged
chunks.text: > select * from merge_update_columns order by id; +-----+---------+---------+ +-----+---------+---------+ 2: hello yo, blue red. 3: hello anyway, blue purple. +-----+---------+---------+ ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Merge With Exclude Columns
chunks.text: `merge_exclude_columns` is the inverse of `merge_update_columns`: the listed columns are preserved from the existing row, and everything else is updated. You can't use both on the same model. [code example] Results

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 1st run

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: id=2: msg updated to 'yo', but color stays 'red' (excluded from merge)
chunks.text: > select * from merge_exclude_columns order by id; +-----+---------+--------+ +-----+---------+--------+ 2: hello yo, blue red. 3: hello anyway, blue purple. +-----+---------+--------+ ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Merge With Incremental Predicates
chunks.text: `incremental_predicates` limits which target rows are scanned during the merge, so large tables avoid a full scan. Predicates must reference `DBT_INTERNAL_DEST`. `predicates` works as an alias for `incremental_predicates`. [code example] Results

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: After 1st run
chunks.text: > select * from merge_incremental_predicates order by id; +-----+----------+ +-----+----------+ 2: hello goodbye. 3: hello hey. +-----+----------+

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: id=2 is updated; id=3 is untouched (not in new data); id=4 is inserted.
chunks.text: > select * from merge_incremental_predicates order by id; +-----+---------+ +-----+---------+ 2: hello updated. 3: hello hey. 4: hello new. +-----+---------+ Keep your new data within the predicate window. If a source row falls outside it — for example `id=1` in this case — the merge can't find the existing target row and inserts a duplicate instead of updating it. ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Schema Changes
chunks.text: Source schemas drift over time, and `on_schema_change` decides how your incremental model reacts. The examples in this section all build on the same source model, shown below. [code example] > select * from source_data; +-----+---------+---------+---------+---------+ +-----+---------+---------+---------+---------+ 2: aaa ccc, bbb ddd, 111 222, TTT UUU. 3: aaa eee, bbb fff, 111 333, TTT VVV. 4: aaa ggg, bbb hhh, 111 444, TTT WWW. 5: aaa iii, bbb jjj, 111 555, TTT XXX. 6: aaa kkk, bbb lll, 111 666, TTT YYY. +-----+---------+---------+---------+---------+

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Ignore
chunks.text: The target schema stays frozen. New columns in the source are silently dropped on insert. title="models/incremental_on_schema_change/models/incremental_ignore.sql" {{ config( materialized='incremental', on_schema_change='ignore' ) }} WITH source_data AS (SELECT * FROM } ) SELECT id, field1, field2, field3, field4 FROM source_data WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id from } ) SELECT id, field1, field2 FROM source_data LIMIT 3 Results [code example] ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Append New Columns
chunks.text: New source fields are added to the target. Existing columns that disappear from the source are kept, and new rows get `NULL` for them. [code example] Results [code example] ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Sync All Columns
chunks.text: The target schema mirrors the source on every run. New columns are added and missing ones are dropped, so use this when you want the target to track the source exactly. [code example] Results [code example] ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Fail
chunks.text: The run fails as soon as a schema mismatch is detected. Use this when silent drift would hurt more than a broken pipeline. title="models/incremental_on_schema_change/models/incremental_fail.sql" {{ config( materialized='incremental', on_schema_change='fail' ) }} WITH source_data AS (SELECT * FROM } ) SELECT id, field1, field2 FROM source_data SELECT id, field1, field3 FROm source_data Results [code example] ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Bad Incremental Models
chunks.text: A few configurations look perfectly reasonable but fail at run time. Knowing them upfront saves you a debugging round trip.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Bad File Format
chunks.text: title="models/incremental_strategies/models_bad/bad_file_format.sql" } select 1 ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Unsupported File Format for Incremental
chunks.text: Incremental models only support the `iceberg` file format. Any other `file_format` value errors out immediately, regardless of `incremental_strategy`. title="models/incremental_strategies/models_bad/bad_file_format_incremental.sql" } select 1 **DBT Error on run** Invalid incremental file format provided: parquet We only support 'iceberg' file format ---

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Strategy Examples: merge, append, overwrite
chunks.heading: Bad Strategy
chunks.text: title="models/incremental_strategies/models_bad/bad_strategy.sql" {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'something_else', ) }} select 1 **DBT Error** Invalid incremental strategy provided: something_else Expected one of: 'append', 'merge', 'delete+insert', 'insert_overwrite'

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.text: Incremental models skip reprocessing your entire source dataset on every run, which can be the difference between a transformation that finishes in seconds and one that drags on for hours. They're built as tables in your data lake. The first run transforms _all rows_ of source data, and on later runs dbt transforms only the rows you filter for, then inserts them into the existing target table. For runnable examples of every strategy, see incremental models by example. Usually you filter for rows created or updated since the last run. That's why your model **gets built incrementally** with each dbt run. An incremental model limits how much data gets transformed on each run, which cuts runtime and lowers compute costs.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Using Incremental Materializations
chunks.text: Once you know an incremental model is the right fit, the setup is short. Incremental models work like other materializations in dbt: define them with a `select` statement and set the materialization in a config block. title="models/my_model.sql" } select ... To use incremental models, you also need to tell dbt: - How to filter the rows on an incremental run. - The uniqueness constraint of the model (if any).

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Filtering Rows on an Incremental Run
chunks.text: The filter is what keeps each run cheap, so this is the part that matters most. Wrap the filtering SQL inside the `is_incremental()` macro to tell dbt which rows to transform. Most of the time you want "new" rows: rows created since the last time dbt ran this model. The cleanest way to find that cutoff is to check the most recent timestamp already in your target table, and dbt makes that easy with the \} variable, which references the target table itself. Here's a model with a slow column transformation that benefits from incremental builds: title="models/my_model.sql" } select *, my_slow_function(my_column) from raw_app_data.events -- this filter will only be applied on an incremental run where event_time > (select max(event_time) from }) Optimizing Your Incremental Model For more complex incremental models built on Common Table Expressions (CTEs), the position of the `is_incremental()` macro affects query performance. Place it where it prunes data earliest in the pipeline.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Defining a Uniqueness Constraint (Optional)
chunks.text: If you re-run a model and don't want duplicate rows piling up, you need a `unique_key`. It tells dbt how to recognize an existing record so it can decide whether to update or insert, and each source row maps to a single row in your incremental model. Skip it, and dbt falls back to **append-only behavior**: every row returned by the model gets inserted into the target table, duplicates and all. This optional parameter accepts a single column or a list of columns that together uniquely identify a row. Set it in the config block at the top of your model. Pass `unique_key` as a string (a single column name) or as a list of single-quoted column names, for example `['col1', 'col2', …]`. If several columns identify a row, pass them as a list (`unique_key = ['user_id', 'session_number']`) instead of a string expression like `unique_key = 'concat(user_id, session_number)'`. The list form is portable, so dbt can template the columns into the merge statement the right way for your database. With a `unique_key` set, here's what happens to each row of "new" data your model returns: - If the same `unique_key` already exists in the target table, dbt updates the existing

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Defining a Uniqueness Constraint (Optional)
chunks.text: a `unique_key` set, here's what happens to each row of "new" data your model returns: - If the same `unique_key` already exists in the target table, dbt updates the existing row with the new values. On IOMETE (Iceberg), this runs through MERGE INTO syntax. - If the `unique_key` doesn't exist yet, dbt inserts the entire row, so the behavior is effectively `append-only`. `dbt-iomete` supports the following incremental strategies for Iceberg tables: - `merge` (default) updates matching rows and inserts new rows. - `append` inserts every row without changing existing rows. - `delete+insert` replaces rows that match the current result's `unique_key` values and accepts duplicate keys in the source. - `insert_overwrite` replaces affected partitions, or the whole table when `partition_by` is not set. For more, see Incremental models in the dbt docs.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: `unique_key` Example
chunks.text: Consider a model that calculates daily active users (DAUs) from an event stream. As new source data arrives, you want to recalculate DAUs for the day dbt last ran and every day since. The model looks like this: {{ config( materialized='incremental', unique_key='date_day' ) }} select date_trunc('day', event_at) as date_day, count(distinct user_id) as daily_active_users from raw_app_data.events -- this filter will only be applied on an incremental run where date_day >= (select max(date_day) from }) group by 1 Without `unique_key`, this model would produce one row per day for every dbt run on that day, leading to duplicates. With `unique_key` set, dbt updates the existing row instead.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: How Do I Rebuild an Incremental Model?
chunks.text: Eventually your model logic will change, and the new transformations no longer match the historical rows already sitting in your target table. When that happens, you need to rebuild the model from scratch. Use the `--full-refresh` flag to force a complete rebuild. dbt drops the existing target table and rebuilds it for all time: dbt run --full-refresh --select my_incremental_model+ The trailing `+` rebuilds downstream models too, which is usually what you want. For full usage details, see the dbt run documentation.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Understanding Incremental Models
chunks.text: Before reaching for `incremental` on every model, it helps to know when it's the right tool and how it behaves under the hood. This section covers when to use one, how the `is_incremental()` macro decides what to run, what IOMETE does behind the scenes, and how schema drift is handled.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: When Should I Use an Incremental Model?
chunks.text: Building models as tables makes downstream queries fast, which is why it's often the right default for a data lakehouse. The plain `table` materialization works the same way, but it rebuilds the whole table on every run. That gets expensive when: - Source tables hold millions or billions of rows. - Transformations on the source data are slow (think complex regex or UDFs). In either case, an incremental model can save substantial runtime and compute. Like most things in programming, incremental models trade complexity for performance. They aren't as plug-and-play as `view` or `table`, but on a long-running pipeline the speedup is usually worth it.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Understanding the is_incremental() Macro
chunks.text: The macro gates your filter logic, so it helps to know exactly when it fires. `is_incremental()` returns `True` when all of these conditions hold: - The destination table already exists in the database. - dbt is _not_ running in full-refresh mode. - The running model is configured with `materialized='incremental'`. Your model's SQL must stay valid whether `is_incremental()` evaluates to `True` or `False`.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: How Do Incremental Models Work Behind the Scenes?
chunks.text: A quick note on what IOMETE does once dbt hands off the SQL. Incremental models are supported on Iceberg tables, the platform's default table format. If you explicitly set `file_format` to anything other than `iceberg` (for example, `file_format = 'parquet'`), the incremental build won't work. Iceberg's ACID transaction management runs the incremental write as a single unit of work, so a partial update can't leave the table in a broken state.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Python Models
chunks.text: Prefer Python over SQL for the transformation? Incremental models support both. A Python incremental model takes the same config options (`unique_key`, `incremental_strategy`, `on_schema_change`, and so on) and uses `dbt.is_incremental()` to branch its logic. title="models/my_model.py" def model(dbt, session): dbt.config( materialized="incremental", unique_key="id", ) df = dbt.ref("my_source") if dbt.is_incremental(): max_id = session.sql(f"select max(id) from ").collect()[0][0] df = df.filter(df.id > max_id) return df

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: What If the Columns of My Incremental Model Change?
chunks.text: Schema drift is the most common reason teams end up running `--full-refresh` more often than they'd like. The optional `on_schema_change` parameter lets dbt keep going when columns are added or removed, so full refreshes become rarer. Configure `on_schema_change` in one of two places.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Option 1. Globally
chunks.text: In `dbt_project.yml`: title="dbt_project.yml" models: +on_schema_change: "sync_all_columns"

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Option 2. Per Model
chunks.text: In the model configuration: title="models/my_model.sql" {{ config( materialized='incremental', unique_key='date_day', on_schema_change='fail' ) }} The supported values are: - `ignore`: Default behavior (see below). - `fail`: Raises an error when source and target schemas diverge. - `append_new_columns`: Adds new columns to the existing table. It does _not_ remove columns that are absent from the new data. - `sync_all_columns`: Adds new columns and removes any that are now missing. This is _inclusive_ of data type changes. None of the `on_schema_change` behaviors backfill old records with values for newly added columns. To populate those values, run manual updates or trigger a `--full-refresh`. Default Behavior Here's what `on_schema_change: ignore` actually does (it's the default, and the behavior on older dbt versions). Add a column to your incremental model and run `dbt run`, and the column won't show up in the target table. Remove a column and run again, and the column stays in the target table. So whenever the model logic changes, run a full-refresh on the incremental model and any downstream models.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: About incremental_strategy
chunks.text: The strategy decides how new rows land in the target table. IOMETE supports `merge` (the default), `append`, `delete+insert`, and `insert_overwrite`. Set it globally or per model.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Configuring Incremental Strategy
chunks.text: Set `incremental_strategy` on individual models, or globally for every model in `dbt_project.yml`.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Option 1. Globally
chunks.text: In `dbt_project.yml`: title="dbt_project.yml" models: +incremental_strategy: "append"

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Option 2. Per Model
chunks.text: In the model configuration: title="models/my_model.sql" {{ config( materialized='incremental', unique_key='date_day', incremental_strategy='merge', ... ) }} select ...

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Using `delete+insert`
chunks.text: Use `delete+insert` when one run can return several rows with the same `unique_key`. Spark rejects duplicate source keys during a `merge`, but this strategy keeps them. Without a `unique_key`, it behaves like `append`. {{ config( materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='delete+insert', unique_key='order_id' ) }} select ... - The delete and insert are separate statements. If the insert fails after the delete succeeds, rerun the model or perform a full refresh to restore the missing rows. - `incremental_predicates` limit only the delete rows; every row from the current result is still inserted.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Using `insert_overwrite`
chunks.text: Use `insert_overwrite` when each run returns the complete contents of every partition it updates. Existing rows in an affected partition are removed even if the current result has no replacement for them. Partitions absent from the result stay unchanged. {{ config( materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='insert_overwrite', partition_by='days(event_time)' ) }} select ... Without `partition_by`, the current result replaces every row in the target table. The overwrite is one atomic Iceberg operation, and values map to target columns by name. A target column missing from the current result receives `NULL`.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: Strategy-Specific Configs
chunks.text: The settings below refine `merge` behavior. `incremental_predicates` also applies to the delete step of `delete+insert`.

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: `merge_update_columns`
chunks.text: With the `merge` strategy and a `unique_key`, dbt overwrites every column on a matched row by default. To narrow that down, pass a list of column names to `merge_update_columns`. dbt then updates _only_ those columns and leaves the rest untouched. {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', unique_key = 'id', merge_update_columns = ['email', 'ip_address'], ) }} select ...

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: `merge_exclude_columns`
chunks.text: The inverse of `merge_update_columns`: list the columns you want to _exclude_ from the update, and dbt updates everything else. You can't use both options on the same model. {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', unique_key = 'id', merge_exclude_columns = ['created_at'], ) }} select ...

chunks.title: dbt Incremental Models: How They Work and When to Use Them
chunks.heading: `incremental_predicates`
chunks.text: Scanning every row of a large target table gets expensive fast. `incremental_predicates` is an optional list of predicates that limits the target rows considered by `merge` or deleted by `delete+insert`. `predicates` is accepted as an alias for `incremental_predicates`, and both behave the same. {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', unique_key = 'id', incremental_predicates = ['DBT_INTERNAL_DEST.updated_at >= dateadd(day, -3, current_date)'], ) }} select ... Predicates reference `DBT_INTERNAL_DEST` (the target table alias). A wrong predicate can silently skip rows during the merge, so run `--full-refresh` to recover.

chunks.title: Materializations
chunks.heading: DBT Materializations
chunks.text: Materializations determine how dbt persists your models in the warehouse, and the choice you make has a direct impact on query speed, freshness, and build time. The `dbt-iomete` adapter supports three of them: - table - view - incremental

chunks.title: Materializations
chunks.heading: Configuring Materializations
chunks.text: dbt uses `view` materialization by default. You can override this globally in `dbt_project.yml` or per model in the model file itself. See the configuration reference for every IOMETE-specific model setting.

chunks.title: Materializations
chunks.heading: Option 1. Globally
chunks.text: Set the materialization in `dbt_project.yml` to apply it across folders of models at once.

chunks.title: Materializations
chunks.heading: └── stg_event_sessions.sql
chunks.text: name: my_project version: 1.0.0 config-version: 2 models: my_project: events: # materialize all models in models/events as tables +materialized: table csvs: # this is redundant, and does not need to be set +materialized: view

chunks.title: Materializations
chunks.heading: Option 2. Per Model
chunks.text: Set the materialization directly inside a model's SQL file when you want to override the project default for a single model. } select * from ...

chunks.title: Materializations
chunks.heading: Materializations
chunks.text: Each materialization trades off freshness, query speed, and build time differently. Pick the one that fits how the model will be used downstream.

chunks.title: Materializations
chunks.heading: View
chunks.text: With the `view` materialization, dbt rebuilds your model as a view on every run using a `create view as` statement. - **Pros**: No extra data is stored, and views over source data always reflect the latest records. - **Cons**: Views that perform heavy transformations, or stack on top of other views, are slow to query. - **Advice**: - Start with views and switch to another materialization only when you hit performance issues. - Views work best for lightweight transformations like renaming or recasting columns.

chunks.title: Materializations
chunks.heading: Table
chunks.text: With the `table` materialization, dbt rebuilds your model as a table on every run using a `create table as` statement. - **Pros**: Tables are fast to query. - **Cons**: - Tables can take a long time to rebuild, especially for complex transformations. - New records in the underlying source data don't flow into the table automatically. - **Advice**: - Use tables for any model queried by BI tools, so end users get a faster experience. - Use tables for slow transformations that feed many downstream models.

chunks.title: Materializations
chunks.heading: Incremental
chunks.text: `incremental` models let dbt insert or update only the records that changed since the last run, which keeps build times short on large datasets. - **Pros**: Build times drop significantly because dbt only transforms new records. - **Cons**: Incremental models need extra configuration and are an advanced dbt pattern. See Incremental models on IOMETE for details. - **Advice**: - Incremental models suit event-style data best. - Reach for them when your `dbt run` gets too slow. Don't start there.

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Getting Started with DBT
chunks.text: If your team already runs analytics with version control, tests, and CI, dbt fits the same workflow for SQL transformations. dbt is an open-source tool for writing SQL models, testing them, and deploying them like any other software project. The **dbt-iomete** adapter wires dbt into your IOMETE lakehouse with full Iceberg support, so you get versioned transformations on top of open table formats. This guide walks you through your first dbt project on IOMETE.

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text: Before you start, make sure you have: - A running IOMETE compute cluster (see Compute Clusters for setup details). - Python 3.9 or later.

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Setting Up Sample Data
chunks.text: Your dbt project needs something to transform, so start by seeding two small Iceberg tables. Run the following in the SQL editor: CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS iomete_analytics.dbt_database; CREATE TABLE iomete_analytics.dbt_database.employees ( emp_no INT, first_name STRING, last_name STRING ) USING iceberg; CREATE TABLE iomete_analytics.dbt_database.salaries ( emp_no INT, salary INT ) USING iceberg; -- Add as many rows as needed INSERT INTO iomete_analytics.dbt_database.employees VALUES (1, 'John', 'Doe'), (2, 'Jane', 'Smith'); -- Add as many rows as needed INSERT INTO iomete_analytics.dbt_database.salaries VALUES (1, 50000), (2, 60000);

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Installing and Configuring dbt-iomete
chunks.text: With the source tables in place, the next step is getting the adapter onto your machine and pointed at your lakehouse.

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Installing the Adapter
chunks.text: Work inside a virtual environment to keep dbt-iomete isolated from your system Python:

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Install dbt-iomete in a virtual Python environment
chunks.text: virtualenv .env source .env/bin/activate pip install --upgrade dbt-iomete

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Initializing the Project
chunks.text: `dbt init` asks for connection details, so grab them first. In the IOMETE console, open your compute instance, switch to the **Connect** tab, and select **dbt**. Now run the init command and answer the prompts. When it asks for a schema, enter `dbt_database` (the database you created earlier). dbt init dbt_project [code example] dbt writes your answers to `~/.dbt/profiles.yml`. Pull sensitive values from environment variables so credentials never end up in source control:

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: ~/.dbt/profiles.yml
chunks.text: dbt_project: target: dev outputs: dev: type: iomete host: dev.iomete.cloud port: 443 https: true dataplane: spark-resources-1 domain: workflow-governance lakehouse: demo-spark-compute catalog: iomete_analytics schema: dbt_database user: "}" token: "}" threads: 1 connect_timeout: 120 connect_retries: 0

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Testing the Connection
chunks.text: Before writing any models, confirm dbt can actually reach IOMETE. `dbt debug` validates your profile and runs a connection test: cd dbt_project dbt debug ➜ dbt debug Configuration: profiles.yml file [OK found and valid] dbt_project.yml file [OK found and valid] Required dependencies: - git [OK found] Connection: host: dev.iomete.cloud port: 443 dataplane: spark-resources-1 lakehouse: demo-spark-compute database: iomete_analytics schema: dbt_database Connection test: [OK connection ok] All checks passed!

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Running Your First Transformation
chunks.text: In dbt, you write a `SELECT` and the adapter handles the DDL. A model is a **SELECT statement** in a `.sql` file, and the file name becomes the model name.

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Creating a View Model
chunks.text: By default, dbt materializes models as views. Drop the following file into your models directory, then run dbt to create the `employee_salaries` view: title="dbt_project/models/example/employee_salaries.sql" SELECT e.emp_no, e.first_name, e.last_name, s.salary FROM dbt_database.employees e JOIN dbt_database.salaries s ON e.emp_no = s.emp_no; dbt run ➜ dbt run Concurrency: 1 threads (target='dev') 1 of 1 START sql view model dbt_database.employee_salaries ..................... [RUN] 1 of 1 OK created sql view model dbt_database.employee_salaries ................ [OK] Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=1

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Switching to a Table Materialization
chunks.text: Views work well for lightweight transformations, but a physical table is faster for anything you query repeatedly. Switching takes one line: add a `config` block at the top of the model. IOMETE supports `table`, `view`, and `incremental` materializations (see dbt-iomete materializations for the full picture). title="dbt_project/models/example/employee_salaries.sql" } SELECT e.emp_no, e.first_name, e.last_name, s.salary FROM dbt_database.employees e JOIN dbt_database.salaries s ON e.emp_no = s.emp_no; A view with the same name already exists from the previous run, so drop it first in the SQL editor: DROP VIEW dbt_database.employee_salaries; Then run dbt again: dbt run This time the result is an Iceberg table instead of a view:

chunks.title: Getting started with DBT
chunks.heading: Next Steps
chunks.text: You now have a working dbt project on IOMETE. From here: - Use the configuration reference for connection, model, and Python model settings. - Explore dbt-iomete materializations for `table`, `view`, `incremental`, and snapshots. - Learn about incremental models to handle large datasets efficiently. - See incremental models by example for hands-on patterns. - Check integration release notes before upgrading the adapter.

chunks.title: Dataiku
chunks.text: This guide walks you through connecting Dataiku to IOMETE using the Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver.

chunks.title: Dataiku
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text: - A running IOMETE cluster with an active compute resource - Access to the Dataiku Administration panel - Your IOMETE username and personal access token

chunks.title: Dataiku
chunks.heading: Download the JDBC Driver
chunks.text: Download the IOMETE custom build from the iomete-artifacts GitHub repository, where files follow the naming convention `flight-sql-jdbc-driver- -iomete. .jar`. See the Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver guide for proxy configuration, JDBC URL parameters, and details on the standard upstream driver alternative. Save the JAR file to a directory accessible by your Dataiku instance.

chunks.title: Dataiku
chunks.heading: Step 1: Open the Administration Panel
chunks.text: Navigate to the **Administration** section from the Dataiku home screen.

chunks.title: Dataiku
chunks.heading: Step 4: Configure the Connection
chunks.text: You will see the connection setup form: Fill in the following settings: JDBC driver class: Value org.apache.arrow.driver.jdbc.ArrowFlightJdbcDriver. JDBC URL: Value Your IOMETE compute JDBC connection string (remove any embedded username/password). Driver jars directory: Value Path to the directory containing the downloaded JAR file. SQL dialect: Value SparkSQL (via JDBC). User: Value Your IOMETE username. Password: Value Your IOMETE personal access token. Can browse catalogs: Value ✓ Enabled. Finding Your JDBC URL You can find the JDBC connection string in the IOMETE console under your compute resource's connection details. Make sure to remove any `user` and `password` parameters from the URL, as these are configured separately.

chunks.title: Dataiku
chunks.heading: Verify the Connection
chunks.text: After saving your configuration, use Dataiku's **Test** button to verify the connection. Once successful, you can start creating datasets and running queries against your IOMETE lakehouse.

chunks.title: DBeaver
chunks.text: DBeaver is a cross-platform database tool. It connects to IOMETE over the Arrow Flight SQL protocol using a JDBC driver. You can choose between two Arrow Flight drivers, and both work the same way: - **IOMETE custom build**: adds proxy support, a connection-level query timeout, and named parameters. See the Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver guide for the details. - **Apache Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver**: the standard upstream build, also fully compatible. There's also a **legacy Hive JDBC driver** that connects over the _deprecated_ HiveServer2 protocol. It's slower and has known compatibility issues with schema selection and catalog names. Use Arrow Flight SQL unless you have a specific reason to use the Hive driver. The steps below apply to either Arrow Flight driver.

chunks.title: DBeaver
chunks.heading: Downloading the Driver
chunks.text: DBeaver needs the JDBC driver JAR on disk before it can connect to IOMETE. Download the IOMETE custom build from the iomete-artifacts GitHub repository, where the files follow the naming convention `flight-sql-jdbc-driver- -iomete. .jar`. To use the standard upstream driver instead, download it from the Apache Arrow releases page.

chunks.title: DBeaver
chunks.heading: Registering the Driver in DBeaver
chunks.text: DBeaver doesn't ship with the Arrow Flight SQL driver. Register the JAR once, then reuse it for every IOMETE connection. 1. Open DBeaver and go to **Database → Driver Manager**. 2. Click **New** to create a driver. 3. On the **Libraries** tab, click **Add File** and select the JAR you downloaded. Then click **Find Class** to let DBeaver resolve the driver class. 4. Switch to the **Settings** tab and confirm: - **Driver Name**: `IOMETE Arrow Flight SQL` - **Driver Type**: `Generic` - **Class Name**: `org.apache.arrow.driver.jdbc.ArrowFlightJdbcDriver` 5. Click **OK** to save.

chunks.title: DBeaver
chunks.heading: Connecting to IOMETE
chunks.text: With the driver registered, you can open a connection and browse your data. 1. Click **New Database Connection** and select the **IOMETE Arrow Flight SQL** driver. 2. Find your connection details in the IOMETE Console: **Compute → select a compute → Connections tab → Arrow Flight**. Copy the JDBC connection string. 3. Paste it into the **JDBC URL** field (it looks like `jdbc:arrow-flight-sql:// :443?cluster= &data-plane= `), then enter your credentials in the **Username** and **Password** fields below it. Use an **Access Token** generated in the IOMETE Console as the password. 4. Click **Test Connection**, then **Finish**. If the connection succeeds, the **Database Navigator** lists your catalogs, schemas, and tables so you can start querying.

chunks.title: DBeaver
chunks.heading: Java Version Requirements
chunks.text: If Arrow Flight connections fail the moment you hit **Test Connection**, a modern version of Java is usually the cause. DBeaver bundles and runs its own copy of Java, independent of any Java installed on your machine. On **Java 16 and newer**, the Arrow Flight SQL driver needs a couple of extra startup flags. Without them, it can't set up its memory and the connection fails right away, usually with a `Could not initialize class ...RootAllocator` error. See Symptoms Without the Flags in the driver guide for the full error messages. Auto-Update Can Trigger This Overnight A DBeaver update can silently swap its bundled Java for a newer version. A setup that worked yesterday then starts failing, even though you never touched your driver or connection. So if Arrow Flight breaks right after a DBeaver update, apply the flags below. Add the required flags to `dbeaver.ini`: 1. Locate `dbeaver.ini`: - **macOS**: `DBeaver.app/Contents/Eclipse/dbeaver.ini` (right-click the app → **Show Package Contents**) - **Windows**: `dbeaver.ini` next to `dbeaver.exe` in the install folder - **Linux**: `dbeaver.ini` in the install directory 2. Add each flag on its own line **after** the `-vmargs` line (every argument in `dbeaver.ini` must be on a separate line): -vmargs --add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED

chunks.title: DBeaver
chunks.heading: Java Version Requirements
chunks.text: **Linux**: `dbeaver.ini` in the install directory 2. Add each flag on its own line **after** the `-vmargs` line (every argument in `dbeaver.ini` must be on a separate line): -vmargs --add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow Each flag does the following: - `--add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED` opens Java's internal `java.nio` package so the driver can reach the direct memory it needs. Java's module system blocks this by default on **Java 16 and newer** (JEP 396). - `--sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow` re-enables the internal `Unsafe` memory API the driver relies on. **Java 24** only prints a deprecation warning, but **Java 25 and newer** deny it by default, so without this flag the driver can't initialize its memory allocator (JEP 498). Include `--sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow` only if DBeaver's bundled Java is **version 24 or newer**; on older versions it prevents startup. When unsure, add `--add-opens` first, retry, and add the second flag only if the failure persists. 3. **Fully quit and restart** DBeaver (a window reload isn't enough), then retry **Test Connection**. For the per-version flag matrix and the reasoning behind each flag, see Java Version Requirements in the driver guide.

chunks.title: Git Integration
chunks.text: Starting from version 3.1.0 of the IOMETE platform, we now support Git integration, with GitLab as our initial Git provider. The initial support focuses on hosting SQL worksheets in Git repositories that can be accessed through the SQL editor tab within the platform. This document outlines the process for setting up the integration and accessing SQL files hosted on Git.

chunks.title: Git Integration
chunks.heading: Registering a Git Repo
chunks.text: To integrate a repository within the platform, first register it through the Git Integration tab or by using the "Checkout Git Repo" button directly from the SQL editor. We can now fill in the details requested. Git Repository URL: The URL of the repository for the current configuration. eg. https://gitlab.com/namespace/project.git Name: The name that you want to be used in, used to display the specified repository. Provider: The Git provider in use. Currently only Gitlab is supported.

chunks.title: Git Integration
chunks.heading: Select or create a token
chunks.text: Once all the repository related details are filled in, we need to provide the token via which we want to interact with git. If you don't have a token configured already we can create a new token by clicking on the Create new button inside token drop down. Tokens can also be managed from the Git Integration tab. A token belongs to the user who created it, and each user links their own token to a repository. Users without the **Manage Git Repository** permission can still link their token from the repository's **Configure** option in the SQL Editor. See Git Repository Worksheets. Token values are never shown after you save them. To change a token, use **Configure** on it, and leave the token field blank to keep the current value. Once the token is set click on the create button to register the repository. We can now see the content of the git repo and execute the Sql queries present in them.

chunks.title: Integrations Overview
chunks.heading: Integrations

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.text: --- A searchable data catalog is only useful if it stays in sync with what's in your warehouse. The **Data Catalog Sync Job** scans every catalog in your IOMETE environment and indexes the tables it finds. Indexed tables appear on the **Data Catalog** page, where you can add documentation, assign owners, define classifications, and set maintenance properties. - **Version:** see the Marketplace Jobs release notes for the latest version (requires IOMETE `3.16.x` or later) - **Source:** View on GitHub

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Marketplace
chunks.text: Open **Job Templates** and click **Marketplace**. Find the **catalog-sync** card, click the **⋮** menu, and select **Deploy**. The job form opens pre-filled with recommended defaults.

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Manual Setup
chunks.text: Open **Job Templates** in the sidebar and click . **1. Name & Schedule** - **Name:** any name you like, for example `catalog-sync` - **Schedule:** `0 * * * *` (runs every hour). Use any cron expression that fits your needs. - **Concurrency:** `Forbid`, which prevents overlapping runs if a previous execution is still in progress. **2. Application** - **Application type:** `JVM (Java, Scala)` - **Docker image:** `iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/iom-catalog-sync: ` (see Marketplace Jobs release notes for the latest version) - **Main Class:** `com.iomete.catalogsync.App` - **Main application file:** `spark-internal` **3. Exclusion Rules Config** This step is optional and applies to both Marketplace and manual installs. Without a config file, the job falls back to its built-in defaults and indexes everything. To control which catalogs, schemas, or tables are excluded, add a Config Map: - **File path:** `/etc/configs/application.json` - **Content:** your exclusion rules JSON (see Exclusion Rules) **4. Instance Resources** - **Deployment type:** `Standard` - **Node driver / Node executor:** choose any instance type that fits your workload - **Executor count:** `1` Click to save the job.

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: How It Works
chunks.text: Once deployed, the job runs on its own. It fires on a schedule (hourly by default), scans every catalog in your environment, and indexes the tables it finds. Anything matching an exclusion rule is skipped. You can change the schedule or trigger a run manually at any time.

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Running the Job
chunks.text: The schedule handles most cases. If you need a fresh index right now (say, after creating a batch of new tables), open the job and click .

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Deleted Tables
chunks.text: Dropping a table doesn't erase its history from the catalog. That history is useful when you need to know what existed before and when it disappeared. When a table is dropped from a source catalog, the sync job marks it as **deleted** and hides it from the default view instead of removing the record. To review what was removed and when, use the **Deleted** toggle in the Data Catalog UI. Deleted entries are kept indefinitely for now. Automatic cleanup of old deleted entries is planned for a future release.

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Exclusion Rules
chunks.text: Not every catalog needs to be indexed. For example, you may want to skip: - An external catalog (e.g., Oracle) with millions of tables that would clutter search results - Catalogs or schemas containing sensitive data that shouldn't appear in the Data Catalog - Personal or sandbox environments used for development Exclusion rules let you skip specific catalogs, namespaces (schemas/databases), or tables during sync.

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Default Rule
chunks.text: For a single rule that covers everything, start here. The default rule applies at **all levels**: catalogs, schemas, and tables. Any asset with a matching property is excluded from indexing. { "exclusion_rules": { "default_rule": { "filter_by_properties": } } } With this rule in place, setting `iomete.governance.index=false` on any catalog, schema, or table excludes it from the sync. One rule, applied wherever you need it via properties.

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Excluding Catalogs
chunks.text: For catalog-level control, exclude catalogs **by name**, **by property**, or both.

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: By Name
chunks.text: List catalog names directly. These catalogs are always skipped, regardless of their properties. { "exclusion_rules": { "catalogs": } }

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: By Property
chunks.text: Set `iomete.governance.index` to `false` on the catalog in the **Admin Portal** when you create or edit it. Then add the matching filter: { "exclusion_rules": { "catalogs": { "filter_by_properties": } } }

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Combining Both
chunks.text: Use names and properties together. A catalog is excluded if it matches **either** condition. { "exclusion_rules": { "catalogs": { "names": ["sandbox_dev", "legacy_warehouse"], "filter_by_properties": } } }

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Excluding Namespaces (Schemas/Databases)
chunks.text: To keep a catalog in the index but skip a few schemas inside it, use namespace exclusion. It's property-based. Set the property in SQL to mark a namespace for exclusion: ALTER DATABASE my_catalog.my_schema SET DBPROPERTIES ('iomete.governance.index' = 'false'); Verify the property: DESCRIBE DATABASE EXTENDED my_catalog.my_schema; To re-enable indexing later, flip the property back: ALTER DATABASE my_catalog.my_schema SET DBPROPERTIES ('iomete.governance.index' = 'true'); Then add the exclusion rule: { "exclusion_rules": { "schemas": { "filter_by_properties": } } }

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Excluding Tables
chunks.text: Tables work the same way as namespaces. Set a property on the table, then define the matching rule. ALTER TABLE my_catalog.my_schema.my_table SET TBLPROPERTIES ('iomete.governance.index' = 'false'); Verify the property: SHOW TBLPROPERTIES my_catalog.my_schema.my_table; To remove the property later: ALTER TABLE my_catalog.my_schema.my_table UNSET TBLPROPERTIES ('iomete.governance.index'); Then add the exclusion rule: { "exclusion_rules": { "tables": { "filter_by_properties": } } }

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Multiple Properties (OR Logic)
chunks.text: When a table exclusion rule lists multiple properties, a table is excluded if **any** of them match. { "exclusion_rules": { "tables": { "filter_by_properties": } } } A table is excluded if `iomete.governance.index` is `false` **or** `hidden` is `true`. It doesn't need to match both.

chunks.title: Data Catalog Sync Job
chunks.heading: Full Example
chunks.text: A complete configuration that uses every exclusion level: { "exclusion_rules": { "catalogs": { "names": ["sandbox_dev", "legacy_warehouse", "user_personal_spaces"], "filter_by_properties": }, "schemas": { "filter_by_properties": }, "tables": { "filter_by_properties": }, "default_rule": { "filter_by_properties": } } }

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.text: --- The **Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job** helps find table folders that still exist in object storage even though the corresponding tables are no longer active in the catalog. Use this job when tables were dropped without purging their physical files. It can run in dry-run mode to report candidate folders, and it deletes folders only when deletion is explicitly enabled. - **Version**: `0.1.5` - **Source**: View on GitHub This job can delete data from object storage. Always run it in dry-run mode first, review the candidates and audit table, and only enable deletion after confirming the output.

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Installation
chunks.text: You can deploy this job from the Marketplace or create the job template manually. The Marketplace flow is recommended because it pre-populates the image, main class, and default configuration.

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Marketplace
chunks.text: - Open **Job Templates** from the left sidebar. - Click to open the list of preconfigured Marketplace jobs. - Find `cleanup-untracked-table-folders`, open the actions menu, and click . - The Marketplace template opens a pre-filled **Create New Job** form. Review the defaults and update the configuration for your environment.

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Manual Setup
chunks.text: Create a job template manually with **New Job Template** if you do not use the Marketplace flow. Specify the following parameters when creating the job manually: Name: Value cleanup-untracked-table-folders. Docker image: Value iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/cleanup-untracked-table-folders:0.1.5. Main class: Value com.iomete.cleanup.untrackedtablefolders.App. Main application file: Value spark-internal. Config file path: Value /etc/configs/application.json. Config file name: Value application.json.

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Running the Job
chunks.text: The Marketplace template includes a default configuration under the **Config Maps** tab. Review the databases and safety settings before creating the job.

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Dry-Run Example
chunks.text: Use dry-run mode first to inspect candidates without deleting data. { "catalog": "spark_catalog", "databases": ["analytics"], "exclude_paths": [], "exclude_database_folders": [], "older_than_hours": 24, "dry_run": true, "delete_enabled": false, "max_candidate_folders_per_database": 10 }

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Delete-Enabled Example
chunks.text: Enable deletion only after reviewing the dry-run output. { "catalog": "spark_catalog", "databases": ["analytics"], "exclude_paths": [ "s3a://bucket/data/analytics/protected_table" ], "exclude_database_folders": [], "older_than_hours": 24, "dry_run": false, "delete_enabled": true, "max_candidate_folders_per_database": 5 }

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Configuration Fields
chunks.text: catalog: Default required, Description Catalog to inspect, for example spark_catalog.. databases: Default required, Description List of database names to scan. The job does not scan all databases automatically.. exclude_paths: Default [], Description Full object-storage paths that must never be selected as candidates. Each entry must include a scheme and bucket, such as s3a://bucket/data/analytics/manual_archive; otherwise the job fails at startup.. exclude_database_folders: Default [], Description Database-relative folder exclusions in the format database.folder. The database must be listed in databases, and the folder must be an immediate child folder name without /.. older_than_hours: Default 24, Description A folder becomes a candidate only when the newest object inside it is at least this old.. dry_run: Default true, Description Reports candidates without deleting data.. delete_enabled: Default false, Description Must be true together with dry_run=false before deletion can happen. Setting dry_run=false without delete_enabled=true stops the job at startup.. max_candidate_folders_per_database: Default 10, Description Safety limit. If more candidates are detected for a database, the database is skipped.. report_only_storage_roots: Default , Description Optional. Additional storage locations per database to list for review. Nothing in them is deleted. See Storage Roots.. collect_size_statistics: Default ignored, Description Deprecated and ignored. Object count and size are always collected for candidate folders. You

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Configuration Fields
chunks.text: to list for review. Nothing in them is deleted. See Storage Roots.. collect_size_statistics: Default ignored, Description Deprecated and ignored. Object count and size are always collected for candidate folders. You can remove this field.. Unknown fields in `application.json` are rejected at startup, so check the spelling of every field name.

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Recommended Workflow
chunks.text: 1. Run with `dry_run=true` and `delete_enabled=false`. 2. Review the driver logs and audit table output. 3. Check the `STORAGE ROOTS` section of the report and any `partial_scan_coverage` status for table locations the cleanup did not cover. 4. Add `exclude_paths` or `exclude_database_folders` for anything that must be protected. 5. Keep `max_candidate_folders_per_database` low for the first delete-enabled run. 6. Enable deletion only after the dry-run output is reviewed. 7. Query the audit table after the run.

chunks.title: Cleanup Untracked Table Folders Job
chunks.heading: Safety Controls
chunks.text: The job is designed to fail closed. If it cannot prove that a path is safe to delete, it does not delete it. dry_run=true by default: Purpose Reports candidates without deleting data.. delete_enabled=false by default: Purpose Requires explicit confirmation before destructive cleanup.. Explicit database list: Purpose Limits cleanup scope to configured databases.. Scan-root validation: Purpose Prevents scanning outside the database storage boundary.. Bucket-root and warehouse-root rejection: Purpose Never scans a database whose location is a bucket root, or equals or contains the catalog warehouse root, where other databases live.. Supported storage only: Purpose Refuses databases on storage other than S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure storage.. Active table protection: Purpose Protects folders that are active table locations, contain active table locations, or sit inside them.. Other database protection: Purpose Protects storage of other databases visible in the catalog that sits inside the cleanup root.. Iceberg write path protection: Purpose Protects folders named by an Iceberg table's write..path properties.. Visible table anchor: Purpose Blocks deletion when no visible table is stored under the cleanup root.. Pre-delete recheck: Purpose Re-discovers active table locations and write paths immediately before deletion, and stops if a table's storage can no longer be resolved.. exclude_paths:
