chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Docker Tag Aliases allow you to define and manage custom aliases for Docker image tags. These aliases let you reference meaningful names (e.g., `latest`, `experimental`, `spark-3-latest`, `sample-job-latest`) instead of hard-coded version numbers in Spark jobs or deployment configurations. This provides greater flexibility in version management and simplifies updates across your deployment environment. To view Docker Tag Aliases, navigate to the **Settings** menu item, switch to the **Docker Settings** tab, and then select the **Docker Tag Aliases** tab. ---

chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Global Aliases
chunks.text: Global aliases are predefined aliases managed by system administrators. These are defined in HELM files at the time of IOMETE installation and provide consistent references across all environments. **Key characteristics:** - Defined during platform installation - Cannot be modified by users - Provide standardized version references across the entire platform - Ensure consistency across different domains and environments

chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Domain Aliases
chunks.text: Domain aliases are custom aliases that you can create and manage within your specific domain. Use these to define your own tag mappings for easier version management and deployment flexibility. **Key characteristics:** - Created and managed by domain users - Provide flexibility for domain-specific versioning - Can be modified or deleted as needed - Ideal for custom deployments and version control strategies ---

chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Adding a New Tag Alias
chunks.text: To add a new tag alias: 1. Navigate to **Settings** > **Docker Settings** > **Docker Tag Aliases** tab 2. Ensure you're in the **Domain aliases** section 3. Click on the **New tag alias** button 4. Enter the alias name (e.g., `latest`, `stable`, `experimental`) 5. Enter the corresponding Docker tag/version (e.g., `3.9.1`, `2.1.0`) 6. Click **Save** to save the tag alias

chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Changing an Alias Value
chunks.text: If you want to update the tag version for an existing alias: 1. Locate the alias in the Domain aliases table 2. Click on the three dots menu (⋮) next to the alias 3. Select **Change value** 4. Enter the new tag version 5. Click **Save** --> ---

chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Using Tag Aliases in Spark Jobs
chunks.text: Tag aliases can be used in Spark jobs to reference Docker images without hard-coding specific version numbers. This makes it easier to update versions across multiple jobs by simply updating the alias mapping.

chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Syntax
chunks.text: To use a tag alias in a Spark job, reference it using the `$` syntax in the Docker image field: iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/spark-py:$ Instead of using a hard-coded version: iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/spark-py:3.9.1

chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Steps to Use Tag Aliases
chunks.text: 1. Navigate to **Spark Jobs** and create or edit a job 2. In the **Application** section, locate the **Docker image** field 3. Enter the Docker image path with the alias syntax: - Example: `iomete.azurecr.io/iomete/spark-py:$` - Example: `myregistry.io/custom-spark:$` 4. Save and run the job

chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Benefits
chunks.text: - **Easy version management**: Update the alias mapping once to affect all jobs using that alias - **Consistent deployments**: Use meaningful names like `stable` or `production` across your environment - **Simplified rollbacks**: Quickly revert to previous versions by updating the alias - **Better organization**: Group related versions under meaningful aliases ---

chunks.title: Docker Tag Aliases
chunks.heading: Best Practices
chunks.text: 1. **Use descriptive alias names**: Choose names that clearly indicate the purpose (e.g., `stable`, `beta`, `prod-latest`) 2. **Document your aliases**: Maintain documentation of which aliases map to which versions 3. **Test before updating**: When changing an alias value, test with a single job before updating production workloads 4. **Avoid frequent changes**: Establish a process for updating aliases to prevent unexpected behavior 5. **Monitor dependencies**: Before deleting an alias, check which resources reference it

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.text: IOMETE provides a custom release of the Apache Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver. It's functionally identical to the upstream driver, with a few IOMETE-specific additions: - **HTTP CONNECT proxy tunneling**: routes gRPC/Flight connections through an enterprise HTTP proxy › - **Connection-level query timeout**: sets a per-connection default timeout applied to every statement › - **Named parameters**: allows `:name` syntax as an alternative to positional `?` markers › - **Catalog scoping for BI tools**: pins a connection to one catalog for clients that aren't catalog-aware (such as Oracle) › - **Default string column length**: reports a length for Spark `STRING` columns to tools that size columns from JDBC metadata (such as Oracle BI Publisher) › It also supports standard mutual TLS and can present a client certificate when your endpoint requires one. See Client Certificates (mTLS).

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Download the Driver
chunks.text: IOMETE maintains its own build of the Arrow Flight SQL driver. Download the latest release from the iomete-artifacts GitHub repository. Driver artifacts follow the naming convention `flight-sql-jdbc-driver- -iomete. .jar`, where ` ` is the Arrow Flight SQL version and ` ` is the IOMETE release number (e.g. `flight-sql-jdbc-driver-19.0.0-iomete.3.jar`).

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Query Timeout
chunks.text: *Requires IOMETE **≥ 3.17.1**.* Without a timeout, a slow or stuck query can hold a connection open indefinitely. To cap that, set a default timeout for all statements on a connection: add `queryTimeout= ` to the JDBC URL, or pass it as a connection property if your client supports one. jdbc:arrow-flight-sql:// : ?user= &password= &queryTimeout=30 The timeout applies to every statement executed on that connection. A value of `0` (the default) means no timeout. Individual statements can still override this via the standard `Statement.setQueryTimeout()` method.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Named Parameters
chunks.text: *Requires IOMETE **≥ 3.16.0**.* Named parameters keep prepared statements readable when a query has many bind variables. Instead of counting `?` positions, you reference each value by name. Prepared statements support `:name` syntax as an alternative to positional `?` markers. The driver automatically translates named parameters to positional placeholders before sending the query. NamedPreparedStatement ps = (NamedPreparedStatement) conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = :status AND region = :region"); ps.setString("status", "active"); ps.setString("region", "europe"); ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery(); The same name can appear multiple times in a query, and the driver binds the value to every occurrence. Positional `?` and named `:name` markers cannot be mixed in the same statement.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Catalog Scoping for BI Tools
chunks.text: *Requires driver **≥ 19.0.0-iomete.3**.* Some JDBC clients aren't catalog-aware. Business Intelligence (BI) tools such as **Oracle Analytics Server and BI Publisher** assume a two-part `schema.table` name hierarchy and drop the catalog prefix entirely. Since IOMETE organizes data in three parts (`catalog.schema.table`), these clients mix schemas and tables from every catalog together in their object lists, and their queries fail because two-part names don't say which catalog to use. Catalog scoping fixes this by pinning the connection to a single catalog: the client keeps using two-part names, and the driver supplies the catalog they leave out. To enable it, set `compatibilityMode=oracle` (or `catalogFilterEnabled=true`) and name the catalog in the `schema` parameter. compatibilityMode: Values oracle, Default unset, Effect Turns on catalog filtering for Oracle-style tools. Other values have no effect.. catalogFilterEnabled: Values true / false, Default false, Effect Turns catalog filtering on or off directly. An explicit value always overrides compatibilityMode.. schema: Values catalog[.namespace], Default unset, Effect The first (catalog) part becomes the metadata filter. Anything after the first dot is an execution hint only, not a metadata filter.. When scoping is on, the driver limits metadata calls (`getCatalogs`, `getSchemas`, `getTables`, `getColumns`, and the key-metadata calls) to the catalog you name. Scoping

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Catalog Scoping for BI Tools
chunks.text: execution hint only, not a metadata filter.. When scoping is on, the driver limits metadata calls (`getCatalogs`, `getSchemas`, `getTables`, `getColumns`, and the key-metadata calls) to the catalog you name. Scoping works at the catalog level: within the pinned catalog, all schemas and tables stay visible. To reach more than one catalog from a client that isn't catalog-aware, define one connection per catalog.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Scoping Examples
chunks.text: Append the catalog parameters to your base JDBC URL (`jdbc:arrow-flight-sql:// : ?user= &password= `):

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Turn on scoping for a non-Oracle tool that isn't catalog-aware
chunks.text: ...&catalogFilterEnabled=true&schema=spark_catalog - Existing connections are unaffected: without `compatibilityMode` or `catalogFilterEnabled`, `schema` behaves exactly as before. - If `schema` is malformed, the driver ignores the filter and logs a warning instead of failing the connection.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Default String Column Length
chunks.text: *Requires driver **≥ 19.0.0-iomete.7**.* Spark `STRING` columns have no declared length, so the driver reports their precision and display size in `ResultSetMetaData` as `0`. Most clients ignore this, but tools that size string columns from that metadata, such as **Oracle BI Publisher**, render those columns empty. To report a length instead, set `defaultStringColumnLength` to a positive integer in the JDBC URL or as a connection property: jdbc:arrow-flight-sql:// : ?user= &password= &defaultStringColumnLength=255 The driver then reports that value as the precision and display size of every string column in a query result. Choose a length that fits the longest values in your string columns, because tools that size columns from this metadata may cut off longer values. - Existing connections are unaffected: without `defaultStringColumnLength`, string columns report `0` as before. A blank value counts as unset. - A length sent by the server always takes precedence over the configured value. - The setting applies to query result metadata only. `DatabaseMetaData` results, including `COLUMN_SIZE` from `getColumns`, are unchanged. - An invalid value (`0`, a negative number, or a non-numeric value) makes queries fail with an error that names the property.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Default String Column Length
chunks.text: (`0`, a negative number, or a non-numeric value) makes queries fail with an error that names the property.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: HTTP Proxy Configuration
chunks.text: You configure the proxy through query parameters on the JDBC URL, so your application code doesn't change. The proxy must support **HTTP CONNECT tunneling** (standard for HTTPS/gRPC traffic). SOCKS proxies are not supported. Proxy authentication (proxy username/password) isn't currently supported, so the proxy must allow unauthenticated CONNECT.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Connection Parameters
chunks.text: proxyHost: Type string, Default —, Description Hostname or IP of the HTTP proxy. proxyPort: Type integer, Default —, Description Port of the HTTP proxy. proxyBypassPattern: Type string, Default —, Description Hosts to connect directly, bypassing the proxy (see format below). proxyDisable: Type string, Default —, Description Set to force to disable proxy resolution entirely. `proxyHost` and `proxyPort` must be set together. If only one is provided, the explicit proxy is ignored and the driver falls back to the JVM's system proxy selector.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Resolution Priority
chunks.text: When establishing a connection, the driver resolves the proxy in this order: 1. `proxyDisable=force` → connect directly, no proxy 2. Target host matches `proxyBypassPattern` → connect directly 3. `proxyHost` + `proxyPort` are both set → use this explicit proxy 4. JVM system proxy (`java.net.ProxySelector`) → use the first non-DIRECT proxy found 5. No proxy found → connect directly

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: `proxyBypassPattern` Format
chunks.text: Uses the same format as the JVM `http.nonProxyHosts` system property: - Patterns separated by `|` - `*` is a wildcard matching any sequence of characters - Matching is case-insensitive localhost: Matches localhost only. .internal: Matches db.internal, api.internal, etc.. localhost\: Matches .internal\, 10.0., any of the above.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: JVM System Proxy Fallback
chunks.text: If `proxyHost`/`proxyPort` are not set, the driver automatically falls back to the JVM's proxy selector. Standard JVM proxy properties are respected: java -Dhttps.proxyHost=proxy.corp.internal -Dhttps.proxyPort=3128 -jar your-app.jar You can also set `proxyHost`/`proxyPort` directly in the JDBC URL to use a connection-specific proxy, independently of the JVM-level proxy. So you can route general Java traffic through one proxy and IOMETE JDBC connections through another. To suppress JVM proxy resolution for a specific connection without changing JVM properties, add `proxyDisable=force` to the JDBC URL.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Proxy Examples
chunks.text: All examples use the base JDBC URL format: jdbc:arrow-flight-sql:// : ?user= &password= Replace ` `, ` `, ` `, and ` ` with your cluster's connection details from the IOMETE console.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Route all traffic through a proxy
chunks.text: Uses `proxyHost` and `proxyPort`. jdbc:arrow-flight-sql:// : ?user= &password= &proxyHost=proxy.corp.internal&proxyPort=3128

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Bypass proxy for internal hosts
chunks.text: Uses `proxyHost`, `proxyPort`, and `proxyBypassPattern` to route internal traffic directly. jdbc:arrow-flight-sql:// : ?user= &password= &proxyHost=proxy.corp.internal&proxyPort=3128&proxyBypassPattern=*.internal|localhost

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Disable proxy entirely
chunks.text: Uses `proxyDisable=force` to override any JVM-level proxy configuration for this connection. jdbc:arrow-flight-sql:// : ?user= &password= &proxyDisable=force

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Client Certificates (mTLS)
chunks.text: If your IOMETE endpoint requires mutual TLS, the driver can present a client certificate during the handshake. It does so only when all three properties below are set, so a missing `useEncryption=true` silently drops the certificate. Enable TLS: Property useEncryption, Value true (required, or the certificate is never attached). Client certificate: Property clientCertificate, Value Filesystem path to the client certificate PEM. Client key: Property clientKey, Value Filesystem path to the client key PEM. jdbc:arrow-flight-sql:// : ?user= &password= &useEncryption=true&clientCertificate=/path/to/client-cert.pem&clientKey=/path/to/client-key.pem

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Java Version Requirements
chunks.text: For performance reasons, the Apache Arrow JDBC driver manages its own memory directly instead of leaving it to Java's garbage collector. It does this through low-level Java internals that recent Java versions lock down by default. As a result, on **Java 16 and newer** you must add one or two extra startup flags to whichever program loads the driver, whether that's DBeaver, Oracle BI, your own Java application, or another JDBC client. Without them, the driver fails while setting up its memory, usually at connect time or on the first query. The exact flags depend on your Java version (see the matrix below). This is a known requirement of every Arrow-based driver (upstream and the IOMETE build alike), not an IOMETE-specific bug. Apache Arrow documents it in its Installing Java Modules guide. It can't be fixed inside the driver: a driver can't change the Java startup options of the program that loads it.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Flag Matrix
chunks.text: Find your Java version below to see which flags to add. 8–15 : Flags to add None, Why No limits on direct-memory access. 16–23 : Flags to add --add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED, Why Java's module system now blocks the driver's direct-memory access (JEP 396). 24 : Flags to add --add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow _(recommended)_, Why The driver still works on Java 24 with only --add-opens, but its use of the internal Unsafe memory API now prints a deprecation warning; allow silences it (JEP 498). 25+ : Flags to add --add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow, Why Java now denies the internal Unsafe memory API by default; without allow the driver can't initialize its memory allocator and fails at connect time (JEP 498). `--sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow` exists only on **Java 24 and newer**. Adding it on an older version stops Java from starting, so add it only when you actually run Java 24 or later. Use exactly `=allow`. The other accepted values (`=warn`, `=deny`) both make the driver fail to initialize its allocator, even on Java 24 where the default (flag omitted) otherwise works.

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Symptoms Without the Flags
chunks.text: If the flags are missing, the connection fails while the driver sets up its memory. The exact error depends on your Java version. On **Java 16–23**, you get a reflective-access error, one of: InaccessibleObjectException: module java.base does not "opens java.nio" to unnamed module UnsupportedOperationException: sun.misc.Unsafe or java.nio.DirectByteBuffer. (long, int) not available On **Java 24**, the driver still connects with only `--add-opens`, but prints a deprecation warning on first use: WARNING: A terminally deprecated method in sun.misc.Unsafe has been called WARNING: sun.misc.Unsafe::allocateMemory has been called by ...io.netty.util.internal.PlatformDependent0 Add `--sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow` to silence it. On **Java 25 and newer**, the same `Unsafe` access is denied by default, so the driver fails outright while initializing its allocator (from the bundled Netty library): ExceptionInInitializerError: Could not initialize class ...RootAllocator Caused by: UnsupportedOperationException ... EmptyByteBuf.memoryAddress()

chunks.title: Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Passing the Flags
chunks.text: Add the flags to the **program that loads the driver**. For an application you launch yourself: java --add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED \ --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow \ -jar your-app.jar If you can't edit the launch command (for example, a tool that starts its own Java runtime), set the `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS` environment variable instead. Java reads it automatically: For GUI database tools and application servers, the flags go in that product's own Java settings, not in your application: - **DBeaver**: add them to `dbeaver.ini`. See Java Version Requirements in the DBeaver guide. - **Oracle BI / BI Publisher (WebLogic)**: add them to the domain's Java options, for example `setDomainEnv.sh` via `EXTRA_JAVA_PROPERTIES`, or the `JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS` environment variable, then restart the server. Apache Arrow documents the longer form `--add-opens=java.base/java.nio=org.apache.arrow.memory.core,ALL-UNNAMED`. Because the driver ships Arrow shaded on the classpath (the unnamed module), the `ALL-UNNAMED` target is the part that matters; the shorter form above is sufficient. See Arrow's Installing Java Modules guide.

chunks.title: Hive JDBC Driver
chunks.text: The Hive JDBC driver connects a BI tool, dbt, or any other HiveServer2-aware client to IOMETE. IOMETE exposes a **HiveServer2** endpoint that's compatible with the Apache Hive JDBC driver, so it behaves like a standard SQL-over-JDBC connection. Looking for the Arrow Flight JDBC Driver? For high-performance binary data transfer or HTTP CONNECT proxy support, use the Arrow Flight SQL JDBC Driver instead. It uses a different JDBC URL scheme (`jdbc:arrow-flight-sql://`).

chunks.title: Hive JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Download the Driver
chunks.text: Before you can connect, you need the driver JAR. Download the latest release from the iomete-artifacts GitHub repository. The standalone build bundles every dependency, so you don't need to install anything else: hive-jdbc-4.0.1-standalone.jar

chunks.title: Hive JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Using the Driver in a Java Project
chunks.text: To use IOMETE in your own Java application, declare the standalone JAR as a system-scoped Maven dependency: org.apache.hive hive-jdbc 4.0.1 system $/src/main/resources/hive-jdbc-4.0.1-standalone.jar Then point your connection at IOMETE using this JDBC URL format: jdbc:hive2:// /;transportMode=http;ssl=true;httpPath=/data-plane/ /lakehouse/ To avoid assembling the URL by hand, copy the exact connection string for your compute from the IOMETE Console under **Compute → select a compute → Connections tab → JDBC**.

chunks.title: Hive JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Known Issues
chunks.text: A few SQL clients behave oddly with the Hive driver. Both issues below have workarounds, so you don't need to switch drivers. Schema Selection Error Some SQL clients (including DBeaver) throw a "schema not found" error when you select an active schema from a dropdown or top menu. Two workarounds: 1. Use the `USE` statement to switch schemas: `USE schema_name;` 2. Use fully qualified table names: `catalog_name.schema_name.table_name` Catalog Not Included in Fully Qualified Table Names Some clients leave out the catalog name when they generate fully qualified table references, such as when you drag a table into a SQL editor. Queries that span catalogs then fail with a `TABLE_NOT_FOUND` error. Two workarounds: 1. Use the `USE` statement when switching between catalogs. 2. Always use fully qualified names: `catalog_name.schema_name.table_name`

chunks.title: Hive JDBC Driver
chunks.heading: Related Drivers
chunks.text: Binary transport over gRPC. Use it for faster queries and enterprise proxy support. Connect DBeaver to IOMETE using either the Hive or Arrow Flight JDBC driver.

chunks.title: IOMETE SQLAlchemy Driver
chunks.text: The `iomete-sqlalchemy` package provides a SQLAlchemy dialect for IOMETE that communicates over Arrow Flight SQL (`adbc-driver-flightsql`) — offering faster, binary-efficient transport compared to the legacy Thrift/Hive driver.

chunks.title: IOMETE SQLAlchemy Driver
chunks.heading: Requirements
chunks.text: - Python 3.9+ - SQLAlchemy >= 2.0.30 - adbc-driver-flightsql >= 1.1.0 - pyarrow >= 16.0

chunks.title: IOMETE SQLAlchemy Driver
chunks.heading: Parameters
chunks.text: host: Description IOMETE host, Default Required. port: Description gRPC port, Default 443. catalog: Description Top-level catalog (e.g. spark_catalog), Default Required. schema: Description Schema / database inside the catalog, Default Required. cluster: Description IOMETE compute cluster name, Default Required. data_plane: Description IOMETE data plane name, Default Required. tls: Description Use grpc+tls transport, Default true. max_msg_size: Description Max gRPC message size in bytes, Default 134217728 (128 MB). You can find the host, port, cluster, and data plane values from the **Connection Details** tab of your lakehouse in the IOMETE console.

chunks.title: IOMETE SQLAlchemy Driver
chunks.heading: Basic Connection
chunks.text: from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text engine = create_engine( "iomete:// : @ :443" "/spark_catalog/default" "?cluster= &data_plane= " ) with engine.connect() as conn: result = conn.execute(text("SELECT 1")).scalar() print(result) # 1

chunks.title: IOMETE SQLAlchemy Driver
chunks.heading: Querying Data
chunks.text: from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text engine = create_engine( "iomete:// : @ :443" "/spark_catalog/default" "?cluster= &data_plane= " ) with engine.connect() as conn: rows = conn.execute(text("SELECT * FROM my_table LIMIT 10")).fetchall() for row in rows: print(row)

chunks.title: IOMETE SQLAlchemy Driver
chunks.heading: Schema Inspection
chunks.text: All reflection methods are fully implemented, making `iomete-sqlalchemy` compatible with schema inspection tools and data catalog integrations. from sqlalchemy import create_engine, inspect engine = create_engine( "iomete:// : @ :443" "/spark_catalog/default" "?cluster= &data_plane= " ) inspector = inspect(engine) print(inspector.get_schema_names()) print(inspector.get_table_names(schema="spark_catalog.default"))

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.text: Email configuration allows IOMETE to send transactional and notification emails through your SMTP server. Only one configuration can exist at a time, and it applies across the entire account. Once configured, features such as notification settings automatically use this SMTP server for event-driven emails. This page acts as both the setup screen and the management view. If no configuration exists, you’ll see a blank form ready for setup. After saving, the page switches to edit mode and displays your stored values (except the password), so you can update them anytime.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Configuring Email
chunks.text: Setting up email for the first time takes a single form. The fields are grouped into four areas: server connection, security, authentication, and sender information. 1. Go to **Admin Console** > **Email Config** in the sidebar. 2. The form loads with defaults: connection security set to **STARTTLS**, port set to `587`, and authentication enabled. 3. Fill in the fields described in the sections below. 4. Click **Save**. If everything validates, a "Saved" notification appears and the form switches to edit mode.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: SMTP Host and Port
chunks.text: These two fields identify your mail server. - **SMTP host** (required): your mail server's address (for example, `smtp.gmail.com`). - **Port** (required): the SMTP port number, from `1` to `65535`. This updates automatically when you change the security type: STARTTLS: Suggested port 587. SSL/TLS: Suggested port 465. No encryption: Suggested port 25. You can always override the suggested port after selecting a security type.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Connection Security
chunks.text: This controls how the connection between IOMETE and your SMTP server is encrypted. Three options appear as radio cards: - **STARTTLS** (recommended): a secure, encrypted connection supported by most modern email providers. This is the default. - **SSL/TLS** (legacy): a fully encrypted connection from the start, supported by some older providers. - **No encryption** (not secure): sends email without encryption. Use this only for internal or testing environments. Self-Signed Certificates If your SMTP server uses a self-signed or internal certificate, add it to the truststore. Changing the security type has two side effects: 1. The **Port** field updates to the suggested port for that type. 2. If you select anything other than **No encryption**, the **Require authentication** checkbox locks on and can't be unchecked.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Authentication
chunks.text: The **Require authentication** checkbox controls whether IOMETE sends credentials to the SMTP server. - With **STARTTLS** or **SSL/TLS**, authentication is required. The checkbox stays checked and disabled, showing the message: "Authentication is required for encrypted SMTP connections." - With **No encryption**, you can uncheck the box to allow anonymous connections. When authentication is on, two extra fields appear: - **Username** (required): your SMTP server username. - **Password** (required): your SMTP server password.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Sender Information
chunks.text: These fields control the "From" line on outgoing emails. - **Default sender email** (required): the address that appears in the "From" field (for example, `noreply@example.com`). Must be a valid email format. - **Default sender name** (required): the display name shown alongside the sender email (for example, `Example Company`).

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Updating the Configuration
chunks.text: If a configuration already exists, the form loads in edit mode with your stored values pre-filled. Here's what to do when you need to change something. 1. Go to **Admin Console** > **Email Config**. 2. Modify whatever fields you need. 3. Re-enter your SMTP password. The password field is always cleared on page load for security, so you'll see a "Re-enter your SMTP password" placeholder. 4. Click **Update**. If the update succeeds, a "Saved" notification appears. Password Re-Entry Required You must re-enter your SMTP password every time you update the configuration. The stored password is never sent back to the browser. If you click **Update** without entering the password, validation blocks the submission.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Testing the Connection
chunks.text: Before you commit to saving, try firing off a test email to verify your SMTP settings. The test uses the current form values without persisting them, so it's safe to experiment. 1. Fill in all required fields in the email configuration form. 2. Click **Test Connection** (in the form footer, next to **Save** or **Update**). 3. If any required fields are empty or invalid, a notification reads: "Please fill in all required email configuration fields first." Fix the errors and try again. 4. If validation passes, a **Test Connection** modal opens. 5. The **Select email recipients** field is pre-filled with your email address. Change it to any valid address if you prefer. 6. Click **Send Test Email**. If the test succeeds, a notification confirms: "Connection successful! A test email was sent, please check your inbox." The modal closes and a green checkmark appears on the **Test Connection** button. The test email arrives with the subject "IOMETE Email Configuration Test" and a message confirming your email integration works. Test Doesn't Save The test sends form values directly to your SMTP server without saving them. You still need to click **Save** or **Update** to persist the configuration.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Testing the Connection
chunks.text: The test sends form values directly to your SMTP server without saving them. You still need to click **Save** or **Update** to persist the configuration.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Deleting the Configuration
chunks.text: If you no longer need email, deleting the configuration removes all stored SMTP settings. Any features that depend on email (like notification settings) stop sending until you create a new configuration. 1. Click the **actions menu** (three-dot icon) at the top-right corner of the page. 2. Click **Delete config**. 3. A confirmation dialog asks: "Are you sure?" 4. Click **Yes, delete it** to confirm, or **Cancel** to back out. After deleting, the form resets to create mode so you can set up a new configuration right away. Immediate Deletion Deleting the email configuration takes effect immediately. Any active notification settings that rely on email delivery stop working until you configure a new SMTP server.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Access Permissions
chunks.text: Only administrators can manage email configuration. The table below lists the required roles for each action. View configuration: Required role Any admin role, Description Any user with Admin Console access can view the email configuration.. Create or update: Required role ADMINISTRATION_MANAGER, Description Needed to save or modify the SMTP configuration.. Delete: Required role ADMINISTRATION_MANAGER, Description Needed to remove the configuration.. Test connection: Required role ADMINISTRATION_MANAGER, Description Needed to send a test email.. The `ADMINISTRATION_MANAGER` role covers system configurations and event logs. Users without it can view the form but can't make changes.

chunks.title: Email Configuration
chunks.heading: Related Resources
chunks.text: - Truststore: add self-signed or internal certificates so IOMETE can connect to private SMTP servers over encrypted connections.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.text: Event Stream is a real-time event ingestion service that receives events and continuously makes them available in Apache Iceberg tables in near real time. ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Event Stream provides a simple way to ingest events into your data lakehouse without managing complex infrastructure like Kafka. You send HTTP requests with JSON data, and the service handles writing to Iceberg tables on your behalf. **Key benefits:** - Simple HTTP API - no client libraries required - Batch support for high throughput - Data available in Iceberg tables in near real-time - No need to manage message queues or streaming infrastructure ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: How It Works
chunks.text: 1. **Create an Event Stream** - Deploy an ingestion service via the IOMETE console 2. **Create an Iceberg table** - Define your table schema with the fields you want to capture 3. **Send events** - POST JSON data to your Event Stream endpoint 4. **Query your data** - Events appear in your Iceberg table for analysis ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.text: Before using Event Stream, you need a **Personal Access Token (PAT)** for authentication. Generate one from the IOMETE console under your account settings. ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Creating an Event Stream
chunks.text: 1. Navigate to **Event Streams** in the IOMETE console 2. Click **New Event Stream** button in the top right corner The Event Streams list page displays all your existing streams with their status, namespace, and replica health at a glance.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: General Settings
chunks.text: In the create form configure the basic settings for your Event Stream. Name: Description A unique name for your Event Stream (e.g., sales-event-stream). Resource Bundle: Description Select who can access this resource. Namespace: Description Kubernetes namespace for deployment. Resources: Description Number of replicas and CPU/memory allocation per replica. Volume: Description Persistent storage for the Event Stream. Without a volume, data is continuously persisted but a very small amount of recent data may be lost if the service restarts. Attach an On-Demand PVC for full durability guarantees.. When no volume is selected, a warning message appears: *"No storage volume is attached. Your data is continuously persisted, but a very small amount of recent data may be lost if the service restarts. For full durability guarantees, attach a persistent volume (On-Demand PVC)."*

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Resource Tags (Optional)
chunks.text: Add custom key/value tags to categorize and organize your Event Stream resources. Tags help with filtering and resource management across your organization.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Review & Create
chunks.text: Before creating, review all your settings in a summary view. Verify the configuration is correct, then click **Create** to deploy your Event Stream.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Deployment Status
chunks.text: After clicking Create, the Event Stream begins deploying. The status shows **Starting** with replicas ready count while pods are being provisioned. Once at least 1 replica is running, the status changes to **Active** with showing replicas ready count. Your Event Stream is now ready to receive events. ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: View Status and Logs
chunks.text: The Event Stream details page provides four tabs for monitoring: - **Details** - Overview of configuration, status, and resource allocation - **Connect** - Endpoint URL and code snippets for integration - **Logs** - Real-time container logs for debugging and monitoring - **Kubernetes events** - Deployment events and pod lifecycle information The **Logs** tab shows real-time container output, useful for debugging ingestion issues or monitoring service health. The **Kubernetes events** tab displays pod lifecycle events including volume claims and pod creation.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Configure
chunks.text: Click the **Configure** button to modify your Event Stream settings. The edit form allows you to change the resource bundle, namespace, resources, and volume configuration. After making changes, click **Review & Save** to apply them.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Scale
chunks.text: To adjust the number of replicas, select **Scale** from the three-dot menu. A modal dialog appears where you can set the desired replica count using the slider or input field, then click **Scale** to apply.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Terminate and Start
chunks.text: Click **Terminate** to stop the Event Stream. The status changes to **Stopped** and the service stops accepting events. The **Start** button appears to restart the service when needed.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Delete
chunks.text: To permanently remove an Event Stream, select **Delete** from the three-dot menu. This action cannot be undone. ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Creating an Iceberg Table
chunks.text: Create a table to store your events. The table schema should match the JSON fields you plan to send. CREATE TABLE analytics.events.sales ( event_id STRING, customer_id STRING, product_id STRING, quantity INT, price DOUBLE ); Additional metadata columns (`__id__`, `__ts__`, `__write_id__`) will be added automatically by the system. __id__: Description Unique event identifier (auto-generated UUID). __ts__: Description Event ingestion timestamp (auto-generated). __write_id__: Description Write batch identifier for data organization. ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Sending Events
chunks.text: Once your Event Stream is active, you can send events using any HTTP client.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Endpoint URL
chunks.text: Navigate to the **Connect** tab to find your endpoint URL and ready-to-use code snippets in multiple programming languages (cURL, Java, Kotlin, C#, JavaScript, Python, Go, Ruby).

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Request Format
chunks.text: Method: Value POST. Content-Type: Value application/json. Headers: Value Authorization - Your Personal Access Token. : Value table - Target table in format catalog.database.table. Body: Value JSON array of events.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Single Event
chunks.text: [{"event_id": "e001", "customer_id": "c123", "product_id": "p456", "quantity": 2, "price": 29.99}]

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Batch Events (Recommended)
chunks.text: For better throughput, send multiple events in a single request: [ {"event_id": "e001", "customer_id": "c123", "product_id": "p456", "quantity": 2, "price": 29.99}, {"event_id": "e002", "customer_id": "c124", "product_id": "p789", "quantity": 1, "price": 49.99}, {"event_id": "e003", "customer_id": "c125", "product_id": "p456", "quantity": 5, "price": 29.99} ] ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: cURL
chunks.text: curl -X POST "https:// /data-plane/ /event-stream/ /ingest" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Authorization: " \ -H "table: analytics.events.sales" \ -d '[{"event_id": "e001", "customer_id": "c123", "product_id": "p456", "quantity": 2, "price": 29.99}]'

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Python
chunks.text: endpoint = "https:// /data-plane/ /event-stream/ /ingest" headers = { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Authorization": " ", "table": "analytics.events.sales" } events = [ {"event_id": "e001", "customer_id": "c123", "product_id": "p456", "quantity": 2, "price": 29.99}, {"event_id": "e002", "customer_id": "c124", "product_id": "p789", "quantity": 1, "price": 49.99} ] response = requests.post(endpoint, json=events, headers=headers) print(response.status_code) ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Use Batch Requests
chunks.text: Instead of sending events one at a time, collect events on the client side and send them in batches. This significantly improves throughput.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Recommended: Batch events
chunks.text: batch = [] batch_size = 100 for event in events: batch.append(event) if len(batch) >= batch_size: send_to_event_stream(batch) batch = []

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Match JSON Fields to Table Schema
chunks.text: Ensure your JSON field names match your Iceberg table column names. Mismatched fields will be ignored. event_id: JSON Field "event_id": "value". customer_id: JSON Field "customer_id": "value".

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Store Flexible Data with String Columns
chunks.text: For complex or dynamic event fields (such as nested objects or fields with varying structures), define the Iceberg column as a string type. The Event Stream will automatically cast these values to strings, allowing you to store flexible data without strict schema requirements.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Use Persistent Volume for Production
chunks.text: When creating an Event Stream for production workloads, always attach a persistent volume. Without a volume, in-flight events may be lost if the service restarts.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Handle Errors Gracefully
chunks.text: Implement retry logic in your client for transient failures: def send_with_retry(events, max_retries=3): for attempt in range(max_retries): response = requests.post(endpoint, json=events, headers=headers) if response.status_code == 200: return response time.sleep(2 ** attempt) # Exponential backoff raise Exception("Failed after retries") ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: HTTP Status Codes
chunks.text: 200: Error Code OK, Cause Success, Solution Event(s) ingested successfully. 400: Error Code BAD_REQUEST, Cause Missing table header, Solution Add table header with format catalog.database.table. 400: Error Code BAD_REQUEST, Cause Invalid table name format, Solution Use format catalog.database.table (three parts separated by dots). 400: Error Code BAD_REQUEST, Cause Invalid JSON, Solution Verify JSON syntax is valid. 400: Error Code BAD_REQUEST, Cause Expected JSON array, Solution Wrap events in array: [] even for single events. 400: Error Code BAD_REQUEST, Cause Schema mismatch, Solution Ensure JSON field types match table column types. 401: Error Code UNAUTHORIZED, Cause Missing authorization header, Solution Add Authorization header with your Personal Access Token. 401: Error Code UNAUTHORIZED, Cause Invalid or expired token, Solution Generate a new Personal Access Token. 403: Error Code FORBIDDEN, Cause No access to Event Stream, Solution Request access to the Event Stream service. 403: Error Code FORBIDDEN, Cause No INSERT permission, Solution Request INSERT permission on the target table. 404: Error Code NOT_FOUND, Cause Table not found, Solution Verify the table exists in the specified catalog and database. 429: Error Code TOO_MANY_REQUESTS, Cause Server overloaded, Solution Reduce request rate or increase replicas. 500: Error Code INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, Cause Server error, Solution Check Event

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: HTTP Status Codes
chunks.text: in the specified catalog and database. 429: Error Code TOO_MANY_REQUESTS, Cause Server overloaded, Solution Reduce request rate or increase replicas. 500: Error Code INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, Cause Server error, Solution Check Event Stream logs for details. 503: Error Code SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, Cause Service draining, Solution Wait for service to restart or check deployment status.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Common Issues
chunks.text: Events not appearing in table: Solution Check logs in the Event Stream details page; verify table name is correct. Service not starting: Solution Review Kubernetes events for resource issues (CPU/memory limits). Slow ingestion: Solution Increase batch size; add more replicas; attach persistent volume. Connection refused: Solution Verify Event Stream status is Active with ready replicas (e.g., 2/2). ---

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Advanced Configuration
chunks.text: Event Stream uses sensible defaults that work well for most use cases. However, for specific scenarios, you can override these settings using environment variables before starting or creating an Event Stream. These are advanced configuration options. The default values are optimized for typical workloads and should not need modification in most cases.

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Environment Variables
chunks.text: RUST_LOG: Default info, Min -, Max -, Description Log level for the ingestion service. Valid values: trace, debug, info, warn, error. Use debug or trace for troubleshooting.. WRITE_PARTITION_SIZE_IN_BYTES: Default 100000000 (100 MB), Min 50 MB, Max 200 MB, Description Maximum write partition size in bytes before creating a new partition. Increase for higher throughput workloads.. CATALOG_REFRESH_INTERVAL_MINUTES: Default 5, Min 2, Max 15, Description How often (in minutes) to refresh catalog configurations from the API. Lower values detect catalog changes faster but increase API calls.. INCREMENTAL_COMPACTION_THRESHOLD: Default 20, Min 10, Max 50, Description Number of files processed before triggering incremental compaction. Lower values compact more frequently, improving query performance but using more resources.. DISK_BACKPRESSURE_PERCENT: Default 50, Min 1, Max 99, Description Disk usage of the event stream volume at which ingestion pauses. The loader reports not ready, and the ingestion service applies backpressure until the loader catches up.. DISK_RECOVER_PERCENT: Default 40, Min 1, Max 99, Description Disk usage at which ingestion resumes. Keep it below DISK_BACKPRESSURE_PERCENT so a value sitting on the threshold does not toggle backpressure repeatedly.. SCAN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: Default 1800 (30 min), Min 1, Max -, Description How long without a completed folder scan before the loader reports unhealthy and

chunks.title: Event Stream
chunks.heading: Environment Variables
chunks.text: the threshold does not toggle backpressure repeatedly.. SCAN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: Default 1800 (30 min), Min 1, Max -, Description How long without a completed folder scan before the loader reports unhealthy and is restarted. A scan takes as long as the backlog it works through, so keep this well above the slowest cycle.. MAX_COMPACTION_ATTEMPTS: Default 3, Min 1, Max -, Description How many times a write batch is allowed to fail its final compaction before the loader gives up on it. The data is already stored; only the compaction is skipped, and the files stay queryable.. COMPACTION_LOCK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: Default 300 (5 min), Min 1, Max -, Description How long the final compaction waits for an in-progress compaction of the same write batch before leaving it for the next cycle.. EMPTY_FOLDER_TTL_DAYS: Default 10, Min 10, Max 30, Description Minimum age (in days) before empty folders are eligible for cleanup..

chunks.title: LDAP Group Inheritance Feature Flag
chunks.text: When LDAP groups contain other groups, this flag makes IOMETE take that hierarchy into account for authorization: a group's members inherit any access granted to its parent groups, the same way users inherit access from the groups they belong to directly. See LDAP Configuration for the full LDAP sync feature. This only affects **group-to-group** relationships built during LDAP sync (a group nested inside another group in the directory). Direct LDAP user-to-group membership is a separate code path this flag does not touch, and always syncs regardless of the flag. Scope: ldapGroupInheritance Global only — no per-domain override. Default: ldapGroupInheritance Enabled.

chunks.title: LDAP Group Inheritance Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Minimum compatible version
chunks.text: IOMETE `4.0.0` or later to control it through this feature flag — before that, `ldapGroupInheritance` can only be set through the Helm chart value, which requires a normal redeploy to change.

chunks.title: LDAP Group Inheritance Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Deployment setup changes
chunks.text: None beyond having LDAP itself configured. This flag has no effect unless group searching and updating is enabled on the LDAP integration and at least one synced group is nested inside another.

chunks.title: LDAP Group Inheritance Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Services to restart
chunks.text: None **when changed through the feature-flag admin API**. Toggling a global override takes effect automatically, within about a minute, without restarting `iom-identity` or any other service — the change applies starting with the next LDAP sync. If you instead change the underlying Helm value this flag falls back to (`features.ldapGroupInheritance.enabled`) with no override set, that's an ordinary Helm upgrade — it goes through your normal deploy process like any other chart value.

chunks.title: LDAP Group Inheritance Feature Flag
chunks.heading: LDAP Sync
chunks.text: Every LDAP sync (manual or periodic full sync) always clears and rebuilds the group-to-group hierarchy table for LDAP-origin groups — that part isn't gated by this flag. What the flag controls is what happens next: - **Enabled:** any group-to-group relationships found in that sync (a group listed as a member of another group) are rebuilt into the hierarchy. - **Disabled:** the sync logs that group hierarchy creation was skipped and leaves the hierarchy table empty for LDAP-origin groups. Direct user-to-group mappings sync normally either way.

chunks.title: LDAP Group Inheritance Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Authorization
chunks.text: The group hierarchy is what lets access granted to a parent group also apply to its child groups' members. This is read at the point IOMETE builds the user-to-groups mapping used for authorization: each user's groups are expanded to include ancestor groups from the hierarchy table. - **Enabled:** a user in a child group is treated as if they're also in every ancestor group, for authorization purposes. - **Disabled:** only a user's direct group memberships are considered — ancestor groups are not added, so no inherited access applies.

chunks.title: LDAP Group Inheritance Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Rollout Considerations
chunks.text: Enabling `ldapGroupInheritance` takes effect starting with the next LDAP sync — it does not retroactively re-derive authorization decisions that were already cached before that sync completes. If your LDAP directory has nested groups with access granted at a parent level, trigger a full sync after enabling so those relationships are picked up.

chunks.title: LDAP Group Inheritance Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Rollback Considerations
chunks.text: **Breaking, not safe.** The group-to-group hierarchy table is always cleared on the next LDAP sync, flag or no flag — disabling this flag just means it isn't rebuilt afterward. Concretely: any user who only has access because of an inherited (not direct) group membership silently loses that access once the next sync runs and authorization re-reads the (now-empty) hierarchy. Direct group memberships and any access granted through them are unaffected. Before disabling, confirm no access grant relies solely on inherited group membership, and notify affected users first. If you re-enable later, the hierarchy is rebuilt from the current LDAP directory state on the next sync, not restored from what existed before you disabled it.

chunks.title: LDAP Group Inheritance Feature Flag
chunks.heading: References
chunks.text: - LDAP Configuration - Groups --- See Feature Flags for other flags.

chunks.title: Managing Feature Flags
chunks.text: From release `4.0.0` forward, you manage feature flags directly in the admin panel, under **Administration → Feature Flags**. Changes take effect at runtime — within about a minute, without redeploying or restarting any service.

chunks.title: Managing Feature Flags
chunks.heading: What a Feature Flag Is
chunks.text: A feature flag is a runtime switch for one piece of platform behavior. When a release changes how an existing feature works — the SQL Editor engine, for example — the new behavior ships behind a flag, so you can turn it on when you're ready and switch back without a redeploy if it causes problems. Flags ship with the platform itself, so what you see depends on your version, and the list grows over time: new releases add flags for new behavior, and once a behavior has proven stable, its flag is removed and the behavior becomes permanent. Available flags lists the current flags, each with its own documentation page. Every admin panel user can view the flags. Changing one requires the Administration Manager admin role; without it, the controls are disabled with an access tooltip.

chunks.title: Managing Feature Flags
chunks.heading: Viewing Flags
chunks.text: The list shows the feature flags in your platform version, each with its flag key, current status, and a short description. The status reflects the flag's global default: Enabled: Meaning The flag is on by default everywhere.. Disabled: Meaning The flag is off by default everywhere.. Not set: Meaning Nothing is configured; the flag falls back to its Helm chart value, or off where the chart doesn't define one..

chunks.title: Managing Feature Flags
chunks.heading: Reviewing a Flag Before Toggling
chunks.text: Click a flag to open its details. Each flag documents what it controls, what it requires, which surfaces it touches, and what happens if you roll it back — plus links to its documentation. The **Global default** card also shows who last changed the flag and when. A flag nobody has touched shows the value inherited from the Helm chart, recorded as _Default from helm (values.yaml)_ by `system`.

chunks.title: Managing Feature Flags
chunks.heading: Changing the Global Default
chunks.text: Toggle the **Global default** switch. Before anything changes, a confirmation dialog repeats the flag's affected surfaces and rollback considerations, so you see the impact before you commit: Confirming applies the change at runtime. Services pick it up automatically within about a minute — no restart, no redeploy. Rollback considerations differ per flag — some are safe to flip back freely, others are breaking — so read the dialog (or the flag's page under Available flags) before disabling anything.

chunks.title: Managing Feature Flags
chunks.heading: Scope
chunks.text: Flags in the current release support **global changes only** — a toggle applies everywhere at once, and each flag's documentation page records this as _Global only — no per-domain override_. Per-domain overrides, which will let you enable a feature for specific domains before turning it on everywhere, are planned for a future release.

chunks.title: Feature Flags
chunks.text: From release `4.0.0` forward, feature flags let IOMETE turn a feature on or off at runtime, without a redeploy. Admins control them from the admin panel under **Administration → Feature Flags** — see Managing Feature Flags.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.text: Enables structured `secretObject` references for compute, Spark jobs, Jupyter containers, and storage configs, backed by IOMETE-managed Kubernetes secrets or read-only HashiCorp Vault integrations. See Secrets Management for the full feature. This is purely additive: the existing `$` inline-placeholder syntax is a separate code path that this flag does not touch, in any of the areas below. Toggling this flag only changes whether the _new_ `secretObject` syntax works — nothing that currently uses `$` changes behavior, whether the flag is on or off. This flag is also what makes **HashiCorp Vault-backed secrets usable at all**. The legacy `$` placeholder only ever resolves IOMETE-managed Kubernetes secrets; there's no Vault path in it. A `secretObject` is the only way to reference a Vault-backed secret in a workload, so Vault integrations are only useful once this flag is on. Console users are already using secretObject The console's secret selector — "Use existing secret" / "Create new secret", the recommended way to attach a secret to a workload — produces a `secretObject` by default, not the legacy placeholder. If this flag is off, secrets picked through that selector won't resolve into the workload (see Impact Area), even though the selector itself doesn't check the flag

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.text: the legacy placeholder. If this flag is off, secrets picked through that selector won't resolve into the workload (see Impact Area), even though the selector itself doesn't check the flag before letting you pick one. Scope: secretsV2 Global only — no per-domain override. Default: secretsV2 Disabled.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Minimum compatible version
chunks.text: IOMETE `4.0.0` or later to control it through this feature flag — before that, `secretsV2` can only be set through the Helm chart value, which requires a normal redeploy to change.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Deployment setup changes
chunks.text: None. No additional Helm values, infrastructure, or configuration are needed to turn this flag on or off.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Services to restart
chunks.text: None **when changed through the feature-flag admin API** — that's what "no restart" means on this page. Toggling a domain or global override takes effect automatically, within about a minute, without restarting `iom-core`, `iom-cluster`, or any other service. If you instead change the underlying Helm value this flag falls back to (`features.secretsV2.enabled`) with no override set, that's an ordinary Helm upgrade — it goes through your normal deploy process like any other chart value.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Impact Area
chunks.text: Enabling `secretsV2` lets API payloads use a `secretObject` in place of an inline `$` placeholder, per surface below. Existing `$` placeholders keep working regardless of the flag, so workloads can migrate one field at a time.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Secret Object
chunks.text: A `secretObject` identifies a secret and its backend: { "key": "secret_key_in_store", "source": } key: Description Secret key name in the store. source.type: Description KUBERNETES (IOMETE-managed) or VAULT (HashiCorp Vault). source.id: Description Domain name for Kubernetes, or Vault config ID for Vault. When the flag is off, a `secretObject` entry resolves to nothing instead of a value — the environment variable or Spark config key is simply absent from the workload, with no error at deploy time.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Compute
chunks.text: **Endpoint:** `POST/PUT /api/v2/domains//compute` The same two secrets, expressed both ways — a `DB_PASSWORD` environment variable and an S3 secret key in Spark config: " }, "sparkConf": " } } } { "sparkConfig": { "envSecrets": [ { "key": "DB_PASSWORD", "secretObject": { "key": "db_password", "source": } } ], "sparkConfSecrets": [ { "key": "spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.secret.key", "secretObject": { "key": "s3_secret_key", "source": } } ] } } `envVars`/`sparkConf` (plain values) and `envSecrets`/`sparkConfSecrets` (`secretObject` references) are separate fields inside the same `sparkConfig` object — you can keep non-secret settings in the plain fields while migrating secrets one at a time.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Spark Jobs
chunks.text: **Endpoints:** `POST/PUT /api/v2/domains//spark/jobs`, `POST/PUT /api/v2/domains//spark/streaming/jobs`, `POST/PUT /api/v2/domains//sdk/spark/jobs` — all three job types use the same structure under `template`. The same two secrets, expressed both ways — an `API_KEY` environment variable and an S3 access key in Spark config: " }, "sparkConf": " } } } { "template": { "envSecrets": [ { "key": "API_KEY", "secretObject": { "key": "api_key", "source": } } ], "sparkConfSecrets": [ { "key": "spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.access.key", "secretObject": { "key": "s3_access_key", "source": } } ] } }

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Jupyter Containers
chunks.text: **Endpoint:** `POST/PUT /api/v1/domains//jupyter-containers` The same secret, expressed both ways — a `DB_PASSWORD` environment variable: " } } } { "config": { "envSecrets": [ { "key": "DB_PASSWORD", "secretObject": { "key": "db_password", "source": } } ] } }

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Storage Configs
chunks.text: **Endpoint:** `POST/PUT /api/v1/domains//storage-configs` Unlike the other surfaces, storage configs keep a legacy plaintext field as a real fallback, not just a separate code path. The same S3 secret key, expressed both ways: { "storageSecret": { "key": "s3_secret_key", "source": } } When both fields are set, the structured reference takes precedence; when the flag is off, resolution falls back to the plaintext field if one was ever saved, or comes back blank if it wasn't.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Vault Config Usage Authorization
chunks.text: Creating or updating a compute cluster, Spark job, streaming job, or Jupyter container checks that the requesting user has **Use** permission on any Vault configuration referenced in its `secretObject` entries, at request time, before the resource is created. While the flag is off, this check is skipped (consistent with the fact that those references won't resolve to anything anyway) — so a request containing a Vault-backed `secretObject` the user doesn't have **Use** permission for is accepted rather than rejected. This has no effect on Kubernetes-backed secrets or on `$` placeholders, which were never gated by this permission.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Rollout Considerations
chunks.text: Enabling `secretsV2` requires no migration of existing workloads (see above) and can be turned on ahead of anyone actually using `secretObject`. The only extra setup: to reference a Vault-backed secret through `secretObject`, a Vault integration must already be configured for the domain — see Vault Integrations.

chunks.title: Secrets V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Rollback Considerations
chunks.text: Disabling `secretsV2` is a breaking change once anything is relying on it, not a safe no-op: every case in Impact Area where an entry resolves to nothing or falls back also applies here, in reverse. Concretely: any compute, Spark job, streaming job, or Jupyter container whose secrets are set **only** through `secretObject` (no `$` placeholder) loses those environment variables/Spark config values on its next deploy, silently and without error, and any storage config set up only through a structured secret reference loses its connection secret the same way. Before disabling, confirm nothing depends solely on a structured secret reference, and let affected users know first.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.text: Switches the SQL Editor, Query Monitoring and the SQL that Table Maintenance runs to the V2 engine. V2 brings more reliable query execution, automatic recovery of interrupted queries, better handling of large results, real-time status updates, and faster monitoring and search. A single flag controls all three: the SQL Editor, Query Monitoring and the SQL that Table Maintenance runs. When the flag is disabled, all three run on the V1 engine. Scope: sqlEditorV2 Global only — no per-domain override. Default: sqlEditorV2 Disabled.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Minimum Compatible Version
chunks.text: IOMETE `4.0.0` or later. Compute clusters must run Spark image `3.5.7-v4` or later (including Spark 4.x). Queries submitted through V2 against a compute on an older image fail with a message asking to update the compute — so update your compute clusters to a compatible image **before** enabling the flag.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Deployment Setup Changes
chunks.text: None. No additional Helm values, infrastructure, or configuration are needed to turn this flag on or off.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Services to Restart
chunks.text: None. Toggling the flag takes effect automatically — users get the new engine the next time they load or reload the SQL Editor or Query Monitoring page.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: SQL Editor
chunks.text: Query submission, execution, results, cancellation, and query history all run through the selected engine. On V2, queries survive service restarts and are recovered automatically, large results are handled more reliably, and query status updates arrive in real time.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Query Monitoring
chunks.text: The Query Monitoring (Activity Monitoring) pages and APIs read from the selected engine's history. V2 monitoring is faster and search is more responsive. Queries are recorded by the engine that ran them: queries submitted on V2 are visible in V2 monitoring, and queries submitted on V1 are visible in V1 monitoring.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Table Maintenance
chunks.text: **Rewrite Data Files** and **Rewrite Manifest Files** run as Spark SQL, so they use the selected engine. **Expire Snapshots** and **Cleanup Orphan Files** run directly on the `iom-maintenance` service and aren't affected by this flag. See Execution Model.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Rollout Considerations
chunks.text: 1. Update all compute clusters to a V2-capable Spark image (`3.5.7-v4` or later, including Spark 4.x) — see Minimum Compatible Version. 2. Enable the `sqlEditorV2` flag. 3. Users switch to V2 the next time they load or reload the SQL Editor or Query Monitoring page — queries already running on V1 at that moment continue to completion on V1. No data migration is needed to enable the flag.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: Rollback Considerations
chunks.text: Disabling the flag is safe: users switch back to V1 on the next page reload, with no deployment needed. Keep in mind: - Queries running on V2 at the moment of rollback continue to completion and remain recorded, but V2-submitted queries are not visible in V1 monitoring while the flag is off. - New queries run through the V1 engine, so V1 limitations return: queries can be lost on service restarts, large results are handled less reliably, and monitoring is slower.

chunks.title: SQL Editor V2 Feature Flag
chunks.heading: References
chunks.text: - SQL Editor - Query Monitoring - Table Maintenance --- See Feature Flags for other flags.

chunks.title: GCS Bucket Access
chunks.text: IOMETE is a hybrid (cloud & on-premises) platform that allows users to store, manage, and analyze large amounts of data. One of the key features of IOMETE is the ability to connect any `Google Cloud Storage Buckets` and access data from them. In order to do this, you need to provide permission to the `Lakehouse Service Account`. Identify the Lakehouse Service Account Go to the IOMETE **Console > Settings > Data Plane > General** to locate the `Lakehouse Service Account` email address, which will be in the form ` @ .iam.gserviceaccount.com`. `What is the Lakehouse Service Account?` The Lakehouse Service Account is a Google Cloud IAM service account that is used by IOMETE Data Plane compute resources to access GCS buckets. The Lakehouse Service Account is created during the IOMETE Data Plane installation process.

chunks.title: GCS Bucket Access
chunks.heading: Provide access to GCS bucket
chunks.text: 1. Go to your Google Cloud Console and select your desired bucket. 2. Click on the "Permissions" tab, and then click on "Add". 3. Add the `Lakehouse Service Account` as a member and provide the necessary permissions. See Permission Levels for the available permission levels.

chunks.title: GCS Bucket Access
chunks.heading: Permission Levels
chunks.text: Google Cloud Storage provides several permission levels that you can assign to the Lakehouse Service Account: - **Storage Object User**: Allows the Lakehouse Service Account to view, create, and delete objects in the bucket (read-write access). - **Storage Object Viewer**: Allows the Lakehouse Service Account to view objects in the bucket (readonly access). - **Storage Object Admin**: Allows the Lakehouse Service Account to view, create, and delete objects in the bucket (full admin access). Please, consult the IAM roles for Cloud Storage and IAM permissions for Cloud Storage documentation for more information.

chunks.title: Global Spark Settings
chunks.text: IOMETE offers a convenient feature for configuring Spark settings through an autocomplete interface. --- To view Global Spark Settings, navigate to the `Settings` menu item and switch to the `Global Spark Settings` tab.

chunks.title: Global Spark Settings
chunks.heading: Add config
chunks.text: To add a new configuration item, click on the `Add config` button. If you want to remove a configuration item, simply click on the button. Once you have configured all the necessary Spark settings, click on `Save changes`.

chunks.title: Global Spark Settings
chunks.heading: Autocomplete
chunks.text: As you begin typing in the `Key` input, the autocomplete feature will suggest relevant Spark settings based on your input. These suggestions include common Spark configuration parameters. Users can easily discover and select appropriate Spark settings, even if they are not familiar with the complete list of available options. Autocomplete Autocomplete speeds up configuration by suggesting relevant settings, cutting down on manual input and potential errors. This feature ensures that settings are properly formatted and aligned with Spark's requirements, reducing configuration problems and runtime errors.

chunks.title: Admin Roles
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Admin roles are built-in, predefined roles that grant permission to manage specific areas of the IOMETE platform. You assign admin roles to users directly or to groups, and group members inherit the role automatically. Most admin roles scope a user to one management area — IAM, domains, Spark catalogs, data security, compute, or system administration — so you can grant only the access a person needs. Admin roles are different from **Resource Bundles** (see Resource Bundles), which grant resource-scoped access to the resources within a bundle. Admin roles always apply platform-wide within the area they manage; they don't scope down to individual resources.

chunks.title: Admin Roles
chunks.heading: Available Admin Roles
chunks.text: IOMETE ships with seven built-in admin roles. The list is fixed — you can't create new admin roles or edit the permissions of existing ones. DOMAIN_MANAGER: Label Domain Manager, Description Manage domains and their resource mappings. Domain managers are owners of all domains, meaning they can do everything across all domains.. IAM_MANAGER: Label IAM Manager, Description Manage users, groups, admin roles, LDAP, SSO, and SCIM operations.. SPARK_CATALOG_MANAGER: Label Spark Catalog Manager, Description Manage Spark catalogs — create, update, and delete.. DATA_SECURITY_AND_AUDIT_MANAGER: Label Data Security and Audit Manager, Description Manage data security, Spark catalog permissions, and audit operations.. COMPUTE_RESOURCES_MANAGER: Label Compute Resources Manager, Description Manage compute resources — Docker registries, volumes, and node types.. ADMINISTRATION_MANAGER: Label Administration Manager, Description Manage system configurations and event logs.. READ_ONLY_ADMIN: Label Read-Only Admin, Description Read-only (GET) access to all admin APIs. Cannot create, update, or delete.. Unlike the six management roles, which each govern one area, **Read-Only Admin** is cross-cutting: it grants read-only (`GET`) access across every admin API rather than management rights over a single area. A user or group can hold multiple admin roles. Any admin role grants read access to the IAM section (you can view users, groups, and admin roles), but

chunks.title: Admin Roles
chunks.heading: Available Admin Roles
chunks.text: single area. A user or group can hold multiple admin roles. Any admin role grants read access to the IAM section (you can view users, groups, and admin roles), but write access is gated by `IAM_MANAGER`.

chunks.title: Admin Roles
chunks.heading: Assigning Admin Roles
chunks.text: You assign admin roles in two places: - **To a user** — open the user's detail page from Users and add the admin role under the user's role assignments. - **To a group** — open the group's detail page from Groups and add the admin role to the group. All current and future group members inherit it. Assigning or removing an admin role requires the `IAM_MANAGER` admin role. Without it, the assignment controls are disabled.

chunks.title: Admin Roles
chunks.heading: Admin Roles vs. Resource Bundles
chunks.text: Admin roles and Resource Bundles cover different layers of the platform: Admin roles: Scope Platform-wide, fixed set, What it controls Management actions in IAM, domains, catalogs, security, compute, and system settings, Where to manage IAM > Admin Roles. Resource Bundles: Scope Resource-scoped, What it controls Granular access to resources within a bundle, Where to manage Resource Bundles. Use admin roles to delegate platform administration. Use resource bundles to govern day-to-day access to data and compute resources.

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: Domain Authorization
chunks.text: The **Domain Authorization** feature transitions domain security from a role-mapping model to a granular permission model within the **Resource Authorization System (RAS)**. This change simplifies and unifies how access is granted to domains and their associated resources. Feature Flag This feature is controlled by the `domainLevelBundleAuthorization` feature flag and is available starting from **IOMETE version 3.16.x**. When enabled, it activates the new authorization flows and V2 API endpoints described in this guide. You can verify if this feature is enabled for your environment by checking the `GET /api/v1/modules` endpoint. With this feature enabled, domain access is no longer managed through role assignments. Instead, permissions are granted directly to users or groups, providing more precise control over domain resources.

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: 1. Granular Permission Management
chunks.text: Previously, domain access and permissions were managed by creating **Domain Roles** and mapping them to users or groups. In the new flow, this role-mapping system is replaced by direct, granular permissions. This allows administrators to grant specific access rights (e.g., only "View Secrets" or only "Create Compute") without needing to manage complex role definitions.

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: 2. Zero-Trust Default
chunks.text: When this feature is enabled, no default permissions are assigned to users or groups upon joining a domain. All access must be explicitly granted by the domain owner within the Resource Bundle interface or via API.

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: 3. Flexible Ownership
chunks.text: Domain ownership is no longer restricted to individual users. A domain can now be owned by a **User** or a **Group**. Group ownership allows for collaborative management, where any member of the owning group can manage the domain and its permissions. ---

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: Domain Creation
chunks.text: The Domain Creation form now includes an **Owner Type** selection (User or Group). Administrators must select an owner at the time of creation. This owner is automatically granted full management rights over the domain and its associated Resource Bundle.

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: Member Management
chunks.text: The "Members" tab within the domain view now directs administrators to the RAS permission interface. Instead of assigning roles, you now manage granular permissions (e.g., `Create Compute`, `Manage Spark Settings`) for each user or group. When adding or editing a member, you can select specific granular permissions: ---

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: API Migration Guide
chunks.text: For users managing permissions via API, the transition involves moving to V2 endpoints and adopting a two-step "Discovery and Action" flow.

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: 1. Identity & Discovery
chunks.text: To manage domain-level permissions via API, you must first discover the `bundleId` associated with the domain. Permissions are managed on the **Resource Bundle**, not the Domain ID directly. There are three primary ways to discover a domain's `bundleId`:

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: Option A: Logged-in User API (V2) - Recommended for Users
chunks.text: If you are managing domains you have access to, use the V2 user endpoint. * **Endpoint:** `GET /api/v2/user` * **Action:** Locate the domain in the `domains` array and extract the `bundle.bundleId`. // GET /api/v2/user response snippet { "domains": [ { "id": "marketing-dept", "bundle": { "bundleId": "7f2a8b3c-1234-5678-abcd-ef9012345678", "isOwner": true } } ] }

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: Option B: Admin Domain API (V1) - Recommended for Admins
chunks.text: Administrators can fetch details for any specific domain to see its bundle information. * **Endpoint:** `GET /api/v1/admin/domains/` * **Action:** Look for the `bundle.bundleId` field in the response.

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: Option C: Resource Bundle Search - Direct Lookup
chunks.text: You can search for the "Domain Bundle" directly using the domain ID. * **Endpoint:** `GET /api/v1/bundles?domain=&bundleType=DOMAIN&scope=DOMAIN` * **Action:** The response will return the specific bundle associated with that domain.

chunks.title: Domain Authorization
chunks.heading: 2. Domain Management (Admin)
